#1512. Man Utd, the crazy week (which might not be enough)

We don’t know if this will be enough to save Michael Carrick’s place. But at least this Manchester United showed some heart in this crazy week. Winners of AS Roma in the Champions League (3-2) after being led 2-0, the Red Devils snatched a draw against Aston Villa (4-4), in a meeting where they were twice two goals behind.

It’s difficult to know whether to see the glass half full, or whether to remember the new defensive wanderings of the Mancunians, who made two disastrous starts during each period.

When he looked at his watch, Michael Carrick noticed that we had only been playing for four minutes, while his team had already conceded two goals: a strike from Alysson, who too easily deceived Senne Lammens (0-1, 1st), and a goal from Nicolas Jackson, the only one to feel the blow on a ball pushed back by the Belgian goalkeeper (0-2, 4th).

Man Utd therefore reacted for the first time, with a penalty converted by Bruno Fernandes, on a (rare) error from Boubacar Kamara (1-2, 16th), and a goal from Youri Tielemans (2-2, 44th). But the Red Devils shot themselves a second time in the foot, with a penalty stupidly conceded by Diogo Dalot, sanctioned by John McGinn (2-3, 48th), and a goal from Leon Goretzka, after a missed intervention by Leny Yoro (2-4, 53rd). This time it took less than eight minutes after returning from the locker room…

For what will perhaps be his last match, Michael Carrick managed to revive his team with his coaching, since it was two entrants who snatched the draw, Joshua Zirkzee (3-4, 90th+2) and Patrick Dorgu (4-4, 90th+6). So there is still a little life, but it remains a seventh match without a victory in the Premier League for Manchester United, well and truly relegated (18th) after this day.

#1511. Thomas Tuchel faces fight to win trust of England players

Thomas Tuchel faces a fight to regain the full trust of his England players, despite claiming that “99.9 per cent” of supporters do not talk about the semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Telegraph Sport reported that players were shocked and disappointed by Tuchel’s approach to the final 30 minutes of the World Cup semi-final.

It can now be revealed that doubts linger among England players over Tuchel’s ability to get the best out of his squad and ultimately lead them to glory in the next European Championship.

There is also some lasting unhappiness over Tuchel’s perceived unwillingness to take ultimate responsibility for England’s World Cup exit and his claim that ball possession was not in “the DNA” of the nation’s players.

Tuchel has spoken of fostering a “brotherhood” within the England squad, but a source told Telegraph Sport: “He still has work to do to get all the players fully behind him again. What happened at the World Cup and some of his comments caused some damage that has not just disappeared.”

Tuchel has no concerns over the commitment of his players and said: “I have no doubt how keen they are. No doubt. I know them, I was seven weeks with them. We had a qualification campaign together, we are 18 months together, I have no doubt that we step up and produce performances in the next cycle. I’m responsible for that.”

One player who did not travel to the World Cup and is not part of Tuchel’s latest England squad for four Nations League games is Morgan Gibbs-White. His partner, Britney De Villiers, took a swipe at Tuchel by posting an image on Instagram that referenced the fact the Nottingham Forest man is the only Premier League player to have created five or more chances in every match he has played this season.

There is no immediate sign that Tuchel is ready to change his approach, as he refused to accept the country were angered by his tactics and substitutions in the Argentina game.

In an attempt to gloss over the nature of England’s missed opportunity in the United States, Tuchel claimed that the bronze-medal victory over France was “one of the nicest experiences ever” for supporters and that he did not lose any sleep over his World Cup squad selection.

Tuchel’s defence of the World Cup campaign also included the revelation that his Football Association bosses had assured the England head coach that his job was safe before the last-16 victory over Mexico.

“I tell you something, like 99.9 per cent of the fans don’t speak about substitutions, tactical twists,” Tuchel said. “They speak about where they have watched the Mexico game, they speak about the second half, the energy of the Croatia match, they speak about how nerve-wracking it was to watch our match against Congo and where they celebrated.

“This is how it should be, this is what a World Cup is for, to connect with the people and to give them experiences that they will not forget. And this is the feedback that I get.”

Asked if he had received any negative feedback at all since the World Cup, Tuchel answered: “No. Not at all. Do you think that’s necessary? I had some quite bad stuff between Argentina and France. [But] No [not since I’ve been back in England].”

The FA publicly backed Tuchel after the defeat by Argentina, but the German has now revealed that he was privately told his job was safe well before that.

Even if England had lost to Mexico and failed to reach the last eight of the World Cup, Tuchel has claimed he would not have been sacked. He said: “There was a moment, a very special moment, before the Mexico game where we had a talk and my bosses told me ‘we know that anything can happen in a football match, we know that anything can happen in a match in Mexico, in a World Cup match, but don’t worry, we see what’s going on and we want to continue like this’.

“It was a beautiful moment for me as a coach. I felt this kind of freedom to take my choices and to just coach freely, and there was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their mind.”

England secured their best World Cup finish since 1966 by winning the bronze-medal game against France in a chaotic match in Miami.

“If you look at the 6-4 against France, people talk about it like it’s one of their nicest experiences ever, to watch a football match,” Tuchel said. “So maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control, for a little bit more chaos, embrace the chaos, and maybe it brings out the best.”

Tuchel has named his first England squad since the World Cup for four Nations League games against Spain, Czech Republic (home and away) and Croatia. He has recalled Cole Palmer and Trent Alexander-Arnold to his squad, but insists he has lost no sleep over not taking the pair to the World Cup.

“I was very happy with the [World Cup] squad selection, we put a lot of effort and emphasis into the squad selection,” Tuchel said. “And I had a lot of sleepless nights, but I had not one sleepless night about our selection, because I was more than seven weeks with this group of players, and they were nothing but fantastic. I think the spirit that we built and the mentality that we showed brought us to the place that we got.

“It feels unfulfilled, but, yeah, that’s how it is. We need to move forward with the decisions in the Argentina game. And sometimes as a coach, you can only win if you win. So now we know the result, and we didn’t win. Of course, I reflect and, of course, I’m very critical of myself. But the question that is also still lingering around is, who knows what would have happened? Who knows if we hadn’t made any substitutions what would have happened? And would we have the same sleepless nights?

“So, there’s not much sense in torturing ourselves, looking back. It’s moving forward, but the team, like I said, did brilliantly. And I will not allow 30 minutes against Argentina to override how we view this World Cup.”

Tuchel had warnings for Palmer and Alexander-Arnold, as he said: “It is one thing to be nominated, by the way, with Cole and getting your ticket back in the squad, but it’s another thing to play and keep your place. It’s about when he comes and he needs to show these kinds of performances.”

On Alexander-Arnold, Tuchel added: “Now it’s time to fight for his place. He always said he’s up for a fight, especially for England. So it’s a need to prove that.”

Tuchel said that Alexander-Arnold has been called up as a right-back, rather than a midfielder. Asked if the Real Madrid player offers enough defensively, he answered by saying: “He has to, he has to. It’s necessary. My conviction is that he will, but he has no choice.”

Tuchel has now finished his broadcast duties. It was quite a strange performance from him. I don’t recall ever seeing him read from notes before. His little joke about his bosses telling him off was awkward and felt rehearsed, and the stuff about 99.9 per cent of England fans talking about Mexico and the second half against Croatia was delusional.

It was also jarring to hear him claim that the FA had basically assured Tuchel that his job was safe straight after England beat Mexico. It was a special night, undoubtedly, but did it really deserve that sort of reaction?

“I wanted to give Jarrad a chance. It was a 51 per cent decision on Jarrad.

“I don’t have a clear picture on what he is all about and have a very clear picture on what Levi can bring us.”

“It makes no sense to nominate three, four, five number 10s. It just does not help anyone. We can see the form that Morgan [Gibbs-White] is in.

“It’s one thing to be nominated, but it’s another thing to perform. This also counts, especially Cole needs to step up to justify the nomination.”

“The minimum I can do is back my bosses. They have my full support on that.

“I’m grateful that I can talk about football because that’s my little bit of knowledge, not sports politics.”

“That’s the beauty of high-level sport, you can’t always win and it makes you feel alive. Not in a very nice way, still you feel that pain of these high-pressure moments.

“As soon as you enter knockout football, it’s a new level of pressure.”

Tuchel has now claimed that people say the 6-4 against France is “maybe one of their best experiences (watching football) ever”.

Again, not something anyone has said to me. Where is Tuchel finding these people?!

Tuchel on Alexander-Arnold: “He comes as a right back.” Sounds like he agrees with Mourinho that the Real Madrid player is not a midfielder.

Tuchel: “There was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their (the FA’s) mind.”

Tuchel says that 99.9 per cent of fans don’t talk about substitutions. He says they speak about the Mexico game and the Croatia game, their emotions and where they watched the matches.

Sorry, Thomas, that’s not my experience at all. Everyone I speak to says he blew the Argentina game. This sounds a bit deluded. According to Tuchel, I must speak to 0.01 per cent of England fans....

FA technical director John McDermott, who has taken a position at the back of the room to listen, had a little laugh when Tuchel joked that he got told off in his FA review for “my substitutions.”

Tuchel says he felt the “full support from my bosses”.

Warning for Palmer: “It’s one thing to get your ticket back, but it’s another thing to keep it.”

He’s expecting Palmer to step up and show him his Chelsea form.

“When you are a coach, you only win when you win...There’s not much sense torturing ourselves by looking back. I will not allow 30 minutes of the World Cup to determine how we view the World Cup.”

Tuchel says he has no regrets over not taking Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to the World Cup. He says he didn’t have a single sleepless night over his squad selection.

Tuchel says the direction in sports is always forwards and never backwards. “The target is to win the home Euros, of course.”

Tuchel says his feelings on the World Cup are mixed. He thinks there are very positive things to take from the World Cup, but says it was also unfulfilled. He says it’s important to recognise that England won a bronze medal, but says he acknowledges they did not push it over the line.

He says the downside of having the belief they could go and win it is that it hurts even more that they did not.

Tuchel has said the France third-place game “directs the narrative” of what’s coming for England.

Tuchel will be happy with this so far. Very gentle start from the broadcasters.

No questions from the broadcasters about blowing the lead against Argentina and Tuchel’s opinion about the World Cup. Weird.

Ben White pulled out with an injury after being back to his best. It is unfortunately, a bit of a story for him. Josh King was very close and is on the radar.

Tuchel seems to be referring to notes as he speaks. He keeps looking down at a piece of paper he brought in with him.

“The door is always open through performance, behaviour and commitment.”

“They had a good start to the season. Now it’s a new competition. Some positions have injuries. Palmer has his numbers back and a point to prove. Trent was never non-selectable and comes in as a right back.”

We will be hearing from Tuchel very soon. Lots to discuss but the Palmer and Alexander-Arnold call-ups and his World Cup reflections are at the top of the list.

Jason Steele’s inclusion is effectively a call-up. He was at the World Cup as a “fourth” goalkeeper for training – and going to country and western gigs in Kansas – but was not part of the official 26-man squad.

The big ‘loser’ from the World Cup squad in being left out by Thomas Tuchel is Arsenal’s Noni Madueke. There’s a return to the Three Lions squad for a number of players following the start of the new campaign with their clubs, with the likes of Cole Palmer, Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Lewis Hall, Rio Ngumoha, Jarrad Branthwaite, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Alex Scott all selected.

#1509. How Declan Rice's new role has turned him into the Premier League assist king, saves him from burnout and reduces Arsenal's reliance on set-piece goals

Published: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026

For so long, Declan Rice was Mikel Arteta’s lighthouse. ‘You just look at him and you know where to head,’ said the Arsenal boss. ‘A focal point giving clarity and direction to everybody.’

Only, not any more. Arteta had a chat with his midfield general at the start of the season, one Rice described as a ‘really honest conversation’, to discuss how he wanted his role to evolve.

After setting up Kai Havertz’s winner against Liverpool with a superb overlap run and cross on Sunday, Rice revealed what Arteta had told him.

‘I’ve done well but he believes I can still do more and he's drilled that into me,’ said Rice. ‘This season I've really tried to attack that part going forward, trying to come up with assists, create chances, create moments. Being behind the ball as well, linking the play. Being involved with all aspects, for me, is my best position.’

He’s certainly doing the creative part of that assignment. Rice’s assist for Havertz at Anfield was his fifth of the season, the most of any player in the Premier League, and puts him on track to obliterate his previous high of eight in 2023-24. Remarkably, for the corner specialist at the league's renowned set-piece kings, all five have come from open play.

Rice, too, revealed he’d discussed overlapping before the Liverpool game and told Havertz to attack balls into the box. That’s just what they both did.

Arsenal's Declan Rice is top of the assist charts in the Premier League this season with five

His latest came at Anfield on Sunday when he made an overlapping run around Noni Madueke who picks up the ball on the edge of the box...

...Madueke plays the ball into Rice's path and he crosses for Kai Havertz (arm raised) to finish at the back post

In truth, Rice’s role has evolved throughout his time at Arsenal.

In the very early days at the Emirates, Rice spent most of his time sitting in a defensive midfield role.

As the seasons have progressed, especially after Martin Zubimendi’s arrival last summer, Rice has been freed to drive further up the pitch, and occupy that space in the left channel.

You can see from his heat map over his Arsenal career, where the redder zones reflect more touches in that area, how much that role has shifted.

In his first season at Arsenal, Rice pops up all over the pitch...

...the following year he appears as an attacking force on the left side of the pitch...

...as he did again last season alongside Martin Zubimendi when Arsenal went on to win the title...

...but this season he is popping up more on the right-hand side, as seen at Anfield for Havertz's winning goal

What’s most noticeable about this season, following the arrival of Bruno Guimaraes and Arteta’s ability to use converted left back Myles Lewis-Skelly in midfield, is that Rice has now shifted to the right.

That has enabled him to link up more effectively with Bukayo Saka or Noni Madueke on that side.

What is perhaps less obvious, but even more telling, is that despite the sight of Rice bursting into the box on the overlap down the right to set up Havertz, he is actually doing most of his creative work and tempo-setting from deeper on the pitch.

As Rice put it, ‘Being behind the ball as well’.

Early in this campaign, he spent a large portion of games picking up possession between Arsenal's centre backs, allowing the champions to create overloads when building up play and bypass an opposition press.

He’s averaging just one touch in the opposition box per game in the league, the lowest number in any season of his Arsenal career. He’s only played a handful of passes all season beyond the edge of the 18-yard box.

In Arsenal’s victory over Sunderland, in which Rice set up one goal and created another two chances, he was the deepest sitting of all Arteta’s midfielders (No 41)

And yet it’s making him more influential than ever. He’s playing more forward passes than in any season at the club. More passes into the final third, more line-breaking passes. And he's carrying the ball towards goal more frequently than at any point in his Arsenal career.

At the same time, he’s having less defensive responsibility, averaging the fewest ball recoveries and possession wins in the final third of any of his seasons at the club.

There is a small caveat to add here. For as clearly effective and influential as he has been in this evolved role, Rice is still overperforming his numbers a little.

His five assists have come from a total open-play expected assists (xA) tally of just 1.07. No one has overperformed that metric – which measures how likely the chances you’ve created are to result in a goal – as much as Rice.

You only need to look back at a few of those assists this season. His one for Madueke against Nottingham Forest was a simple pass out to the touchline where the winger then did all the work to cut inside and bend a beauty into the far corner.

He did the same for Havertz on the other flank for his equaliser against Chelsea. And it was a little sideways pass to Guimaraes against Sunderland that his midfield partner then whacked into the top corner from long range.

By contrast, Martin Odegaard, for so long his side’s creative hub, is yet to claim an assist from open play despite having an xA of 1.9, the fourth-highest in the division.

But that is not to take away from the superb work Rice is doing. Where he’s really showing his expertise is in how simply he’s making those forward creative passes look. Take these examples:

After his assist at Anfield, Rice creates another chance for Jurrien Timber, poking a little pass that cuts out two Liverpool players to open up space for a long-range shot

Against Everton, he knocks another through the lines into space for Madueke to turn and run on to

And even though Havertz still had everything to do for his goal against Chelsea, Rice’s pass to him takes out four blue shirts

The xA on the above pass might not be high but it creates the opportunity for Havertz to conjure some magic. Short, simple passes that help open up defences.

Rice is doing all this while running less, too. He’s averaging 6.8 miles per game. Over the previous two campaigns, he travelled 7.1.

Perhaps it was always going to have to be this way. It was over the World Cup this summer that the sheer weight of games Rice had played in 2025-26 – 69 for club and country – finally took its toll.

He played through a hamstring injury from Christmas onwards and was substituted early in England’s victory over Croatia with ‘neural pain’ in his back.

'The body's been through a lot this season,’ he said after the semi-final defeat by Argentina. 'I think you can see I'm mentally done, physically done. I need a break now.’

Now, with the likes of Guimaraes and Lewis-Skelly as well as Zubimendi around him, Rice is able to keep starting every game but also do what great midfield metronomes like Rodri and Paul Scholes did before him: control matches without having to bust a gut.

It has allowed Rice to be more selective in his runs forward. Guimaraes, especially, is dynamic enough to sit in for those moments – like at Anfield – when Rice spots the opportunity to make his move.

Rice's movement and backheel allowed space for Bruno Guimaraes to fire in the winning goal against Leeds last month

He did similar against Leeds to set up Guimaraes’ winner, charging into the box to play a neat little backheel to the Brazilian, who fired into the bottom corner.

It allows Arteta, too, to find different ways to open up defences in open play, whether they are sitting deep or pressing man-to-man. Rice is now able to exploit the gaps or pick the locks.

Arsenal have not always had this luxury and, when they frequently struggled to do so in the past, had to turn to set-pieces. Not any more.

Rice may no longer be Arteta's lighthouse but he continues to find new ways to lead Arsenal to glory.

#1508. Bloodthirsty Brighton feast on rattled Arsenal

Overpowered and overrun, Arsenal were subjected to the sort of gruelling treatment they usually inflict on their opponents. Mikel Arteta’s side did not look anything like Premier League champions here, as Brighton and Hove Albion produced a stunning performance full of swarming energy and breathless bravery.

In the biggest test of their season so far, Arsenal fell woefully short of the standards they have set themselves over the past few campaigns. This sort of thing simply does not happen to Arteta’s side. Well, it did not happen. Not before this monstering on the south coast, where the Brighton fans were whipped into a frenzy by the brilliance of Fabian Hürzeler’s players.

Brighton were everything that Arsenal are expected to be: aggressive, inventive and dominant across the field. They even scored with a set-piece, as one of Arsenal’s great strengths became a sudden weakness. Everywhere Arteta looked, the foundational truths of his team were being shaken by a Brighton storm. It was their first defeat by a three-goal margin since May 2023, also against Brighton.

Remarkably, this is now the third consecutive season in which Brighton have beaten the reigning Premier League champions. They are rarely happier than when they are on the hunt against more illustrious opponents, working as a team to snap at heels and then attacking in numbers. They are known as the Seagulls, but they played more like a pack of bloodthirsty wolves. The ferocity of their off-the-ball work, especially in the first half, was extraordinary.

Not for a long time have Arsenal been as rattled as they were here. David Raya misplaced passes, Gabriel Magalhães lost duels and Bruno Guimarães chased the ball in vain. It was Brighton’s Pascal Gross, rather than Arsenal’s Martin Odegaard, who shaped the game in midfield. It was Brighton’s Charalampos Kostoulas, rather than Arsenal’s Kai Havertz, who offered incisive class in attack.

Gross and Kostoulas both struck from range in a one-sided first half, before Chema Andrés added the third after the break. At half-time, Arteta had sprinted down the tunnel towards the dressing room. Whatever messages he gave to his players, they either did not sink in or did not work. By the end, Arsenal were lucky the scoreline was not even more humiliating.

Arteta’s players had come through some tricky assignments in winning their first seven matches of this season, but this was their toughest test yet and they failed it badly. They did not handle the emotions of the occasion particularly well, either: in stoppage time, a frustrated Declan Rice kicked out at Malick Yalcouyé. He was perhaps fortunate to avoid a red card.

It was the first time that Rice and Guimarães had started alongside each other for Arsenal and it quickly became clear that their £180m partnership will need some work. Arsenal would have hoped their experience in the Premier League would allow for an instant connection but, evidently, that is not the case. Guimarães was hooked after 60 minutes, but might easily have been removed at the break.

Both managers had a similar assessment of the match and how it was won: Brighton did the basics far better than Arsenal. “How we wanted to approach this game was getting into it through small wins,” Hürzeler said. “Everyone speaks about a goal or chance as a win, but a small win can be the first throw-in, the first corner, win the first header, win the first tackle. These small things. If you win these small steps, and celebrate them as a win, then you can gain bigger and bigger wins.”

It was typical of Brighton that one of their new signings produced an excellent performance in midfield. Andrés, a 21-year-old Spaniard signed from Stuttgart at the end of the transfer window, looks to be the latest gem identified by their data-led recruitment model. No one inside the Amex Stadium was thinking about Carlos Baleba, sold to Manchester United, when Andrés made his tackles and won his headers.

Another new signing, centre-back Luka Vuskovic, was similarly impressive at the back. Signed for £46m from Tottenham Hotspur, Vuskovic looks more than capable of going to the top of the game.

This was perhaps the first occasion this season in which Arsenal missed William Saliba, the injured centre-back who has been so fundamental to their success in recent years. The Frenchman can always be relied on to provide calmness and composure at the back, even under intense pressure. Without him, Arsenal were uncharacteristically jittery.

“The amount of technical errors we did in our own half...” Arteta bemoaned. “We didn’t respect any principle of play that you have to get out of those man-to-man situations. That put us always on the back foot.”

Gross, who at 35 is playing as well as ever, opened the scoring with a low shot from range after 31 minutes. Kostoulas then struck the second, from a similar distance, after some end-to-end action resulted in Arsenal’s midfield and defence melting away. The third was the most simple, as Andrés headed in at the back post from an inswinging corner.

Arsenal did have some chances, with Havertz missing the best of them, but there was never a sense that Brighton were vulnerable. The pressure on the home side was never sustained. For Arteta, who now has an extended international break in which to ruminate on this defeat, it all made for an unfamiliar and unexpected pain.

Mikel Arteta said his Arsenal players failed to “respect the game” as their perfect start to the season was ended in stunning style by a brilliant Brighton performance.

Arsenal’s capitulation on the south coast led to their first defeat of the campaign and Arteta admitted that Brighton had a different “edge” and “bite” throughout the match. The Arsenal manager also said the 3-0 loss represented a “big lesson” for his players.

“There are certain basics you need to accomplish in football, especially in the Premier League, that we were very far from,” Arteta said. “From the first throw-in you could sense it, it was so clear.

“It was a really disappointing result and performance. Brighton were another gear up from us. We were extremely poor technically and were not respecting the game.

“It is not going to take away what the team has done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup. What we have done and the way we have competed, and the amount of games we have won, has been remarkable. But this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level.”

Arteta added that his team did not “respect the principles of play” that were required against Brighton’s intense pressing, and also said his players were guilty of numerous technical errors.

“Credit to Brighton for what they have done because they have overcome us and they had another edge,” Arteta said. “There are a lot of moments when the ball is 50/50 and it changes hands and most of the time it was for them.”

Brighton are the Premier League’s top scorers this season with 16 goals in five matches so far, and this emphatic victory took them up to third place in the table.

“It was a special win,” Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton head coach, said. “Not only because we played the best team in England but because of the performance. I am really proud of my team. It’s always important to enjoy these moments. We were horrible to play against. My players really trust each other on the pitch.”

Two things, one give credit to them. In the manner that they played and committed to every single action. We were below the standards that are required for us but in the Premier League as well.

When you miss chances like we did it becomes impossible. I want to congratulate Brighton for what they’ve done. It’s a big lesson for us to learn. If I have to describe how the team has played and competed in the last six or seven weeks, has been expectational but today has been a big lesson.

A very disappointing result and performance. Full credit to Brighton the manner they went about the game, they were a different gear from us. We didn’t do the basics right for long periods, especially in the first half. We didn’t win enough duels, and any second balls and that stretches you.

We were poor technically when we had the ball in our own half, we didn’t apply the principles that you need against a team that wants to press you man to man.

Arteta: "There are certain basics that you need to accomplish in the Premier League that we were very far from. The amount of technical errors we did... we didn't respect any principle of play. We were always on the back foot. They had another edge."

Beating the current champions and maybe the best team in England is something special. The result is nice but the performance is what makes it special, the boys showed real courage, real intensity and they were horrible to play against because we did the basics right.

Intensity, intensity, winning the personal duels...we have to have the belief to compete with the best teams in the league. My players really trust each other on the pitch. If one player is out then another can replace him.

Overall we wanted to be really good in every phase. We needed to be at the highest level. We go game by game. After the international break we have a lot of games. After wins like this we have to stay humble and understand why we had this win. We have to keep on going.

I thought we showed great intensity, waited for mistakes and punished Arsenal. It was a strong performance, a very complete performance.

We won the ball high up and attacked really fast. After the last two wins we are full of confidence and wanted to finish really strong before the international break.

I feel really good. I can’t complain. I just try to help the team when I can. I really enjoy life in Brighton, I’m loving it.

I know after the international break we play every three days and a lot of the lads are not used to that. It will be tough. I hope we can compete. We have a big squad this season.

Brighton have beaten the reigning Premier League champions in three consecutive seasons.

Like Everton, Newcastle labour to a home win which should have been more comfortable. It would have been had Wissa scored his penalty, but it was a nervy finish as Hull pushed for an equaliser after Cho’s goal.

Everton up to fifth but they made hard work of that against Ipswich’s 10 men, but Thierno Barry’s goal proves the difference. Barry unfortunate that his second did not stand because of a contentious offside check.

One of the outstanding team performances of the season so far from Brighton, and it will take some beating between now and May. Arsenal were loose defensively in open play and from set-pieces, and were smothered by Brighton’s pressing. Arteta’s team beaten for the first time this season and emphatically so. Arsenal’s first defeat by a three-goal margin since May 2023.

Just three minutes of stoppage time remaining, but Hull are still pushing bodies forward.

Hull are knocking on the door at St James’ Park, and Newcastle are hanging on to their lead rather than pressing for a third goal.

Matt O’Riley has missed two great chances to make it four. Brighton have not given Arsenal a sniff. It will be interesting to hear how stern Arteta is in his post-match assessment.

Kai Havertz shoots straight at the goalkeeper when clean through, and that is surely Arsenal’s last chance of an unlikely comeback gone. Brighton have pushed Arsenal back for much of the season half, they have not been sitting on a lead.

At St James’ Park, Hull have pulled a goal back through Cho to set up a nervy finish for Newcastle.

The forward is shown a second yellow card for diving, and Ipswich’s hopes appear to be dwindling at the Hill Dickinson Stadium.

What a farcical five minutes we have had, from an absurd disallowed goal for Everton to a ridiculous red card for Abdul Fatawu, banished for a second bookable offence - which was diving. These are the situations with which I struggle most - if players do not appeal for a wrongdoing, if they don’t feel they have been the victims of an injustice, why are officials getting involved?

Thierno Barry thought he had made it two for Everton, but the goal has been ruled out because Brennan Johnson was judged to be interfering with play and offside. You’re never getting those this weekend after the Enzo Fernandez incident.

Arsenal undone from a corner, swung to the back post and Chema Andres rose above everyone to head home.

This is a remarkable performance by Brighton, who have battered and bullied the champions from the start. Three-nil, and they have even beaten Arsenal at their own game by scoring a set-piece.

I am struggling to remember the last time Arsenal were overrun and outplayed as comprehensively as this. It’s a thrashing.

No half-time subs from Mikel Arteta, which is a little surprising given Arsenal’s predicament.

The undisputed highlight of the afternoon so far – Raspberry Beret has just been played during the half-time interval and you will agree that this is Prince’s finest work. We feel the need to bring this to your attention because, really, the final 15 minutes of the first half were a hotchpotch and if Everton don’t raise themselves, they will find trouble.

Another shot from outside the box as Arsenal’s defenders backed off, and the Greek striker found the bottom corner. What a first half for Brighton, Arsenal need to pull something out of the fire in the second half. Just before the goal, Saka had a chance after a deflected Odegaard shot.

Brighton’s second goal was an even better hit than their first. End-to-end football resulted in Kostoulas having space 20 yards from Arsenal’s goal. It’s another thumping low finish. Brilliant, breathless half of football by Brighton.

As half-time approaches, Arsenal have mustered just one shot on goal worth 0.03 expected goals. When they have moved the ball beyond Brighton’s press, they have not done anywhere near enough with it.

This fixture last season was especially bad-tempered, with the Brighton fans (and manager) repeatedly accusing Arsenal of time-wasting. The memories of that defeat are clearly still fresh in the minds of the Brighton supporters, who are roaring with rage at every perceived delay by the visitors, despite the fact that Arsenal are losing. The bad blood is adding to the intensity of the occasion.

Ipswich don’t play like a team that is short of confidence and quality. You might assume, if you haven’t seen much of them, that they are destined for a season of toil but there is definite quality with Gary O’Neill’s ranks, including Abdul Fatawu, who has been magnetic in drawing your eye to him. They might be a goal down but they are playing as if they are a goal in front.

Arsenal had just enjoyed a spell of control, but trail to a goal from one of the league’s in-form players. Gross whips a shot from just outside the box around Raya and in off the post.

Brighton have the lead at the Amex and it’s their captain, Pascal Gross, who has provided it. Superb long-range effort, in off the near post. On the overall balance of play, Brighton deserve that. It’s reward for their courage and willingness to go after Arsenal, rather than sitting back.

It took almost 20 minutes but Arsenal have found their feet in this game now. They are starting to find avenues through Brighton’s aggressive pressing and have made a few promising runs in behind, through Havertz and Saka. This is a high quality match.

No goals at the Amex, but Brighton are the team making the running, Arsenal struggling to play out from their own half and are yet to register a shot on goal.

Barry kept himself onside and turned the ball into the back of the net with his stomach. He did well to avoid a handball.

Bright start from Everton and they have the goal they deserve, albeit it came in fortuitous circumstances. James Tarkowski’s volley clattered into Thierno Barry and the deflection took it away from Christian Walton in Ipswich’s goal. Barry now has five goals for the season and, while he is raw, it’s an invaluable contribution.

A storming response to a bad night at Leeds from Newcastle, and it looks like being a long afternoon for Hull. Two down in seven minutes.

What a start for Newcastle United and what will really please manager Matthias Jaissle is the way both goals have come from his players winning important tackles.

The German was incensed by the lack of physicality and intensity in the heavy defeat to Leeds on Monday but the first goal for Joe Wilock came when Lewis Miley won a tackle on the edge of the Hull penalty box.

The second came when Sven Botman came away with the ball just inside his own half. On both occasions Harvey Barnes provided the assist. A short, intricate pass to Willock inside the box and then a surging, twisting run from the halfway line and the perfectly timed pass to Lewis Hall who stroked a first time shot into the bottom corner.

Hull have been outfought so far which is precisely the response Newcastle’s manager had demanded.

The home team are pressing high and all over Arsenal in the early stages. Raya has just made a save to deny Kostoulas.

Brighton have started brilliantly against the champions. They are hunting like wolves, pressing Arsenal with remarkable intensity. We have played seven minutes and I don’t think the ball has left Arsenal’s half.

Big chance for Everton to take the lead, but after great skill to turn his man at the edge of the box Brennan Johnson shoots wide with only the goalkeeper to beat.

The perfect start for Newcastle with all their injuries: Joe Willock has put the home side in a strong position against Hull with a clean strike inside three minutes.

We are under way at the Amex, St James’ Park and the Hill Dickinson.

Another famous face in the stands at Hill Dickinson Stadium today but this time it’s not about politicians. Wayne Rooney is here to watch his boyhood club and he will be hoping Everton can go into the international break unbeaten. An extra special cheer too before kick-off for Jarrad Branthwaite, who has just been called up for England duty. Plenty of Premier League clubs would like to sign Branthwaite, if they were given half a chance, but David Moyes has made it quite clear that Branthwaite: “Isn’t for sale - I want to keep my best players.”

He was not part of the match-day squad at Sunderland but Ben White’s injury has opened up a place, and Dowman fully deserves it after his two goals against Ipswich in the League Cup. Sam Dean has the story of his rise to stardom as well as what Arsenal are doing to nurture such a special talent.

Brighton are wearing a special “125 anniversary” kit today, to mark 125 years since the club was formed in 1901. It’s inspired by the colours of their first ever kit, which means an all-blue shirt, pale gold shorts and dark socks. Personally I would not allow such nonsense. But I don’t make the rules.

Spurs scored two late goals to salvage some pride against Aston Villa, but it is another defeat for Roberto De Zerbi’s team who have two points from five games. This Emi Buendia screamer put the game out of reach.

Emi Buendia, that is a BEAUTIFUL strike 😮‍💨📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nNplbL7mpd

It has been a term tossed around liberally at Newcastle United since Matthias Jaissle arrived as manager, but what does “vertical football” actually mean?

It is the new buzzword in football analysis, the latest fashionable phrase to describe a “new” style of football, and it has been referenced multiple times by both Jaissle and Ross Wilson, the sporting director, since the German coach’s appointment last month.

For some of us of a certain age, vertical football just seems like clever new terminology to describe an old idea.

We are getting to the stage where we really need to start asking questions about Tino Livramento’s injury record.

The right back was due to start for Newcastle against Hull City this afternoon – his first start since April – but has picked up another injury.

That will surely mean he is out of the England squad for the Nations League having also picked up a tournament-ending injury at the World Cup in the summer before the first group game.

Livramento only played 17 Premier League games for Newcastle last season, scuppering his chances of a summer move to Arsenal, missing huge chunks of the season with groin and hamstring issues.

Injuries are already cutting deep into the Newcastle squad, with four teenagers on the bench for the visit of Hull. None have played in the first team before and three of them – Michael Mills, Mason Miley and Kyrian Thompson are just 17–years-old.

Newcastle wanted a younger team this season but not this young. It was interesting to hear Matthias Jaissle talk before the game. He knows how tough this season could be with so little experience in the side.

Lewis Dunk is a surprise absentee for Brighton, it can only be because of injury, and Hurzeler has preferred Diego Gomez to the lively Yalcouye who was very threatening at Old Trafford and Coventry. He could be a handful off the bench.

Good news for Arsenal: Jurrien Timber is finally fit enough to start a match again. This is his first start since mid-March and his return is timely, given the absence of Ben White through injury. Very excited for this one today. Arsenal have won all seven of their matches so far. Only once before in their history have they won their first eight games of a season - that was in 1903, when they were playing in the Second Division as Woolwich Arsenal. pic.twitter.com/iNBxoHl4Gc

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of today’s Premier League 3pm kick-offs, with Brighton vs Arsenal the pick of the three matches.

Brighton are the league’s top goalscorers so far this season and have amassed the most expected goals, but the champions have the league’s best defence and are seeking five wins from five to start their title defence. There is some welcome needle between Fabian Hurzeler and Mikel Arteta, dating back to Declan Rice’s contentious second yellow for delaying the restart two years ago, as well as the Brighton manager’s comments about Arsenal’s style of play in March.

That 1-0 Arsenal victory at the Amex coincided with Man City dropping points at home to Nottingham Forest on a pivotal night in the title race. Bukayo Saka scored a deflected shot in the ninth minute, and Arsenal held on from there in an ugly but resolute display.

With Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz fit and firing, as well as the introduction of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes to Arteta’s midfield stable, Arsenal’s football has been more technical and enterprising so far this season. Brighton are one of the few teams who will back themselves to play through Arsenal’s press, which should make for an absorbing game.

Elsewhere, Newcastle are looking to bounce back from their shellacking at Leeds at home to surprise package Hull City. Mattias Jaissle’s team took four points from Liverpool and Spurs but there is concern about how many shots they are conceding. Hull remain unbeaten and continue to confound the odds and underlying data, but that surely cannot last forever.

Everton are also one of the division’s unbeaten teams, but will be targeting three points from a home game against Ipswich after three consecutive draws. Ipswich are sitting comfortably on six points after their win at Crystal Palace, though they did have the extra man for the majority at Selhurst Park.

#1507. The 6 players Liverpool let go in the summer – & how they’re faring elsewhere

There was a lot of focus on new arrivals, but Liverpool let six players leave in the summer and how are they getting on?

Two club legends, one free transfer and two academy prospects were part of the six players to depart Anfield in the summer.

Here’s how they have fared at their new clubs so far.

Jones left for Inter in the summer, but his start to life in Italy has been disrupted by an abdominal injury.

He was being slowly phased into Cristian Chivu’s side, starting half of the six games he was available, but he picked up an injury following Inter’s 2-2 draw with Roma in September.

Inter confirmed he had a myofascial strain in the adductor muscles of his right thigh and he has been out since then.

The fans do appear to have taken to him though, if this video is anything to go by. We don’t know why either.

— ScoutZone (@ScoutZ0ne) October 10, 2026

Spanish defensive midfielder Bajcetic was a youth prospect that Liverpool took from Celta Vigo in 2013 but he never truly managed to break into the first team.

He made just 12 league appearances for the club over two seasons before being loaned to Red Bull Salzburg and Las Palmas last season.

In the summer, Liverpool cut ties permanently and sold him back to Celta Vigo.

Since moving back to Spain, the 22-year-old has been placed in Celta’s reserve team in the Segunda, where they are currently 16th.

He’s played just 24 minutes of football so far this season after he returned from injury.

Konate was the latest Liverpool product to leave for Madrid on a free but it has worked out better for him than it has for Trent Alexander-Arnold.

The Frenchman is the starting centre-back for Madrid alongside Dean Huijsen and has over 1,000 minutes of football so far this season.

However, Madrid’s defence has not exactly been rock solid as is usually typical for a Jose Mourinho side. The team have kept just four clean sheets this season, one of which Konate spent on the bench.

Despite this, Konate has been one of the better defenders for the team this season.

Trabzonspor pulled off quite the coup when they convinced Salah he should join them rather than their wealthier neighbours or Saudi Arabia.

Club president Ertugrul Dogan told the BBC what he said when he was asked by Salah ‘Why should I choose Trabzonspor now?’ And he was sold a romantic dream of being an idol in the city.

Of course, a £14.6m-a-year salary helps as well as 20% of the merchandise sold with his name on it but Salah was convinced to be part of a project and the star of that.

The Super Lig is a step down from the Premier League but Salah has hit back at suggestions he was a busted flush and is in fine goalscoring form.

In the league, he’s got eight in 10, including a man of the match performance against Galatasaray that saw him score a hat-trick as well as register an assist and he is one off the league’s top scorers Gift Orban and Victor Osimhen.

Salah has been producing in Europe too with two goals and two assists in the three Conference League games he has played so far.

Trabzonspor sit third in the Super Lig, three points off Galatasaray and the only team that have inflicted defeat on the league leaders so far.

After a move in January failed to materialise, Robertson finally joined Spurs in the summer, looking to add a winning mentality to a very shaky backline.

It certainly was not the easiest of starts. Robertson played the full 90 of Spurs’ 3-0 hammering away at Brentford and also started the 2-0 loss to Newcastle.

But since the international break, things have turned around for both player and club. They beat Coventry 3-1 with Robertson getting an assist. He then started the away fixture at Chelsea which resulted in a first win for Spurs at Stamford Bridge since 2018.

Elliott’s various loan moves have just not worked out well for him.

After being contractually frozen out of playing at Villa, he is now not having much luck at Valencia.

He has yet to start a game and has played more than 30 minutes of football on just two occasions so far.

He also has not endeared himself to the fans after he picked up the rarely seen double yellow card, the second of which was for arguing with the referee about his first one.

Valencia have changed manager since and according to AS, new coach Javier Aguirre doesn’t much fancy Elliott.

#1506. It’s fire in Naples!

In Naples, the crisis is now more visible than ever. Traveling to Porto on Wednesday in the Champions League, the Azzurri conceded their seventh defeat of the season in all competitions (4-1), but also displayed worrying nervousness. The image of the heated altercation between Kevin De Bruyne and Lorenzo Lucca at the end of the game illustrated the tensions currently running through the Neapolitan locker room. In the process, Scott McTominay did not hide his annoyance at the situation. “ We have to play better in both areas, we can’t continue like this. We lost 4-1, obviously I’m angry. We have a lot of injuries, but that can’t be an excuse, even if it’s always the same players who come on the pitch. Everyone needs to go home and think about what they can do to improve tomorrow “, explained the Scottish community.

An annoyance which is justified by the worrying sporting situation of the Neapolitan club. Naples is in eighth place in Serie A, is already 14 points behind the leader, Lazio, and is nine points from fourth qualifying place for the C1. On the European scene, Massimiliano Allegri’s squad is the only Italian team not to appear among the top 24. Further proof of the division within the locker room, the exit of Matteo Politano from Sky Italiacriticizing foreign players in particular for not speaking out about the situation. “ Everyone needs to examine their conscience. I put myself forward: I would like others to do it too. Not just us Italians… »

Faced with this critical situation, Massimiliano Allegri is being singled out more than ever. Last night, the transalpine coach did not want to blame his players, mainly citing the lack of solutions on his bench. “ We would have liked to bring in fresh and athletic players, but I only had attackers on the bench. To play matches that require such an expenditure of energy, you have to be able to make changes. Otherwise, we can’t do it, it’s simple. You can only maintain such a rhythm if you have eight or nine changes “. To try to escape this negative spiral, Naples is preparing to carry out a ritiro, according to La Repubblica.

A decision which would have been taken even before the new rout on the Dragão pitch, but which Allegri’s group seems to greatly need. The players should therefore remain together until the reception of Lazio (Sunday, 12:30 p.m.), with the objective of closing ranks and preparing as best as possible for the arrival of the championship leader. Facing the Romans, Massimiliano Allegri himself spoke of a “ final », as the urgency is felt. While the European markets are moving dangerously apart and internal tensions are accumulating, the Italian technician is more threatened than ever. In the event of another defeat, he could leave Napoli, only four months after his arrival.

#1505. Long balls are NOT banned at Newcastle! Matthias Jaissle insists his criticism after Everton defeat was lost in translation - having said stars were failing to follow tactics

Published: 11:50 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 12:02 EDT, 5 November 2026

Matthias Jaissle says his criticism of Newcastle’s players was lost in translation and has clarified that long balls are not forbidden under his management.

The head coach also believes that his squad understands what is being asked of them, although he says his door remains open to any player seeking clarity over his instructions.

In the wake of Monday’s 1-0 home defeat by Everton, Jaissle said that the players had failed to follow his instruction and bemoaned their use of long balls when the plan was to keep it on the floor.

Asked if those comments had been addressed with the squad this week, Jaissle said: ‘I don't know if it's a misinterpretation or a language barrier, but there is an element of that when I explained that in the press conference.

‘But it is indeed (something) we address, because we talked sometimes about the no-risk zone, where we had previously critical-ball losses leading to goals. Of course, if there is a clear risk for ball loss, then I prefer playing a long ball to our striker and protecting the ball and develop the game from there.

‘It (my comments) are not to point any fingers, not at all. Sometimes you are willing to do something, but on that day it just did not work and you make the wrong decisions. It comes also with confidence.

Matthias Jaissle, pictured giving instructions during Newcastle's defeat by Everton, has insisted long balls are not banned

'If you have scenarios where you can find easily your team-mate on the ground and we build up from there with our patterns, then you should for sure also prefer that.

‘But it's not easy, it's easier said from outside. If the confidence is missing, then you prefer to be really safe and shooting maybe even more the long ball.’

Daily Mail Sport was told this week that some players are ‘confused’ by exactly what it is Jaissle wants from them, but the head coach said: ‘The fundamental thing is that we can count on unity and togetherness.

'The door is always open if ever there is anything unclear. If you see the training then I’m pretty sure everyone understands and is fully committed. There was never a question, at least I’m not aware of it.

‘It’s important we listen to the players. If there is anything unclear, they will drop in.’

Meanwhile, Jaissle says he retains the support of the club’s hierarchy after a run of four defeats in five matches.

‘The nice part is that I got even more the feeling from within the club how committed they are (this week),’ he said.

‘That just shows me that everyone believes in the long-term project and that everyone is also aware and realistic about the journey and where we are right now.’

#1503. 12 of the most universally liked players in Premier League history: Zola, Alonso, Crouch…

Football rivalry is such that one person’s hero is another person’s villain – but players occasionally manage to be loved by not just their own club’s supporters but everybody.

There are very few players who have managed to avoid being disliked by at least one set of supporters in the Premier League era, but humility, honesty and humour can go a long way – not to mention being ace at football.

Here are some players we reckon everybody likes. Don’t hate us…

It’s actually quite staggering that it has become so difficult to find a bad word said against Alonso. He played for Liverpool for a start, which doesn’t exactly lend itself to universal popularity.

To make matters worse, Alonso has always seemed one of those annoying people who just has everything: the classy playing style, the trophies, the good looks, the beard just the right shade of ginger. It’s enough to make you sick.

He even came close to f*cking up the miracle of Istanbul when his penalty was saved by Dida. But he didn’t. Because he’s Xabi Alonso. And he’s brilliant.

One of the most unlikely-looking footballers in history, Crouch never took himself to seriously in an era when the game has often lacked a sense of humour.

From the robot celebration to crowd surfing at Kasabian, we don’t think Crouch has ever done anything we didn’t love.

He was also a consistently excellent striker, which too often goes overlooked. His England record is f*cking ace.

Juninho joining Middlesbrough once was weird. Juninho joining Middlesbrough for a second time was endearing. Juninho joining Middlesbrough for a third time was heroic.

He may have won a World Cup with Brazil, but helping Boro to their one and only honour, the 2004 League Cup, was just as significant.

READ: A tribute to the fantastic but flawed Middlesbrough side of 96-97

Mata was already considered one of the loveliest footballers around, but then he announced his Common Goal initiative, which sees players donate 1% of their salaries to charity.

That, combined with his weekly blog, means we could pretty much forgive him for anything. Which explains how he managed to play for Chelsea and Manchester United – under Jose Mourinho at both clubs – and still manage to have everyone love him.

Okocha and Sam Allardyce could hardly have been more different in their approach to football, but if their combination was wrong then we don’t want to be right.

Okocha made everyone want to watch Bolton. Bolton. That’s how much everyone loved him.

Goalkeepers are strange creatures. Solitary and all alone in a team sport but lacking the single-minded glory of a goalscorer.

A career lasting over 20 years saw Van der Sar become one of the most decorated goalkeepers of all time, and he also just seems like a really nice bloke.

Tragically, it took Speed’s suicide in 2011 to make it abundantly clear just how loved the Welshman was in the footballing world.

It speaks volumes that despite playing for clubs with big traditional rivalries – Leeds, Everton, Newcastle and Sheffield United – nobody had a bad word to say about the midfielder, who remains sorely missed.

Before Birmingham fans pipe up, we did say the most popular Premier League players. As a manager, sure, some people might have reason to dislike him, but we just remember his smile and lovely free-kicks. How could you not love him?

He’s also clearly still a really, really nice man. When reporters were outside his house after he was sacked by West Ham, he wouldn’t answer any questions but did make them all cups of tea and coffee. An absolute gent.

The former Newcastle and Aston Villa winger was always a very good, very popular player in the Premier League, but there’s one thing in particular for which he will be forever remembered.

As a keen trumpet player, Solano made a habit of ringing Sir Bobby Robson and tooting his horn down the line at his bemused manager, who remained unaware of the culprit for some time before eventually being informed of the musical talent within his squad.

“I’m not sure he was too amused,” Solano later told FourFourTwo. Bet he still loved you, though, mate.

Peter Beardsley probably best summed Asprilla up when he said: “He was mad – but nice mad. He was different with the ball – a skill that no one else has.”

Asprilla is often blamed as the reason Newcastle failed to win the title 1996, but the Colombian was utterly befitting of Kevin Keegan’s ‘Entertainers’ – admittedly after he lost the deposit on his house due to gunshot holes in the wall.

And since retiring, he’s still kept us all amused on social media, posting videos such as him dressed as a dinosaur while riding a horse playing football.

A player who stole the hearts of a nation both for his talents and his flaws.

For all of Gazza’s exhilarating skill on the pitch and his cheeky charm off it, his vulnerability and struggles with addiction mean you just want to help him. He’s made countless mistakes – and the fact everyone still cares for him says it all.

The man Nelson Mandela called his “hero”.

The man who recovered from being shot in his native South Africa.

The man who rejected Sir Alex Ferguson and Manchester United to stay at Leeds because he would wear “only the white rose, not the red rose”.

The man who played 73 minutes in goal at Old Trafford, conceding just once and making impressive stops to deny Andy Cole, Ryan Giggs and Brian McClair, a month after having to do the same at Middlesbrough and keeping a clean sheet.

The man who, after Leeds were beaten at Cardiff a couple of years ago, tweeted a video of himself singing and dancing to Marching On Together for no apparent reason.

#1502. Mario Hermoso: “This Roma always wants to win.”

Roma beat Sassuolo 3-0 thanks in part to Mario Hermoso who scored the opening goal.

The Spanish defender spoke to Sky Sport after the game.

“The disappointment in Manchester? When these things happen that you can’t win, football doesn’t leave you thinking. The team wants to win, to stay at the top. For us, it was too important, and we did it.”

“The coach prepares you physically, on the pitch, to find these situations. We go there to make a nice pass or a shot on goal. We continue to work in the same way we work on defense. We do the same to help the attackers score.”

#1500. A celebration of peak Joe Cole: ‘A special player, full of fantasy’

Every English football fan of a certain age should have a special place in their hearts for Joe Cole. Once upon a time, he was the nation’s greatest hope.

No matter how many people warn against heaping too much pressure on young players’ shoulders, in England we just can’t help it. The country is constantly looking for a new hero.

Even in the digital age of constant hyperbole, however, few players have had to handle the intense fever which surrounded Joe Cole’s embryonic days as a burgeoning professional footballer.

At the age of 15, Cole was earning rave reviews in the national press thanks to his performances for England schoolboys, attracting interest from the likes of Arsenal and Manchester United.

By 17, he was being invited by Kevin Keegan to train with the senior England squad after inspiring West Ham to a 9-0 thrashing of Coventry City over two legs in the final of the FA Youth Cup.

And just to temper expectations, he was one of the first teenagers to be dubbed ‘The Next Gazza‘.

When Cole was paraded at Upton Park during half-time of a league match against Chelsea to sign his first pro contract, the stadium announcer declared: “You can tell your grandchildren you were here when Joe Cole signed.”

Cole’s career since the end of the noughties created the perception that he failed to live up to his immense potential, but that’s unfair. If not necessarily ever the best English footballer, for a period between 2004-09, Cole was undoubtedly one of the most fun. That alone makes him worthy of celebration.

One of the things which always made Cole so alluring is that he was so obviously mad about football. He always seemed most at home on the pitch, with the ball at his feet and a defender stood in his way, primed to be embarrassed.

By the time he had broken into West Ham’s first team, Cole was already asking Harry Redknapp if he could avoid giving interviews. The boy from Camden only ever had one thing on his mind: football.

He went on to make 150 appearances for the Hammers and became renowned for his flair and trickery. Those sort of players are few and far between in England, and Cole was a welcome breath of fresh air; a footballer seemingly born to entertain.

As a child he had paid particularly close attention to Italian and African football, making a note of the latest piece of skill and honing it himself at the next available opportunity.

Rather than be overawed by the seriousness of top-flight football, Cole carried the same attitude against his senior pros, with the advice of his coach at Camden and Islington Boys, Terry Howard, ringing in his ears: “Do what you like from now on, son.”

“I’ve been coaching for 20 years and have never seen such a combination of flair, pace and commitment,” Howard said of his first impressions of the youngster in an interview with The Independent in 1999. “He was also the most modest.”

Come 2002-03, and still at the tender age of 21, Cole was made West Ham captain by Glenn Roeder and flourished with the added responsibility.

West Ham may have been unable to avoid relegation, but Cole’s valiant displays in midfield earned him the club’s Player of the Year award and a £6.6million move to Chelsea, where he was labelled the “new Gianfranco Zola” by Claudio Ranieri. The unrelenting expectation continued to increase.

However, handed the No.10 shirt, his debut season with the Blues was somewhat underwhelming. While he made 50 appearances in all competitions, exactly half of those were from the bench, and he did not score in the league until April as he struggled to find a suitable role in the team.

It would be a theme which continued throughout his career. Cole played at a time when English football transitioned from 4-4-2 to 4-3-3, neither formation particularly allowing for the indulgence of a free-spirited No.10.

It was the arrival of Jose Mourinho at Chelsea which prompted the best football of Cole’s career. If the game was unwilling to adapt to his talents, he could at least adapt himself under the guidance of one of the most tactically astute managers in modern football.

Two things helped Cole rediscover his verve at Chelsea.

First, John Terry, who Cole has described as “like an older brother” at the time, asked one of the video analysts to pull together a compilation of all the midfielder’s highlights to remind him of his unique ability.

But the main turning point came in October 2004. Cole walked off the pitch at Stamford Bridge having scored an excellent winner against Liverpool, only to be publicly criticised by Mourinho for a lack of defensive application.

“He has two faces – one beautiful and one I don’t like,” Mourinho said. “He must keep one and change the other one.”

﻿

Rather than take the criticism to heart, Cole had the belief in his own game to go out and prove his manager wrong. After all, even though he was still only 22, it was all part and parcel of being Joe Cole.

“We are on the same page,” he said. “He wants Chelsea to win games and I want Chelsea to win games. He wants Joe Cole to be a better player than he already is – and so do I. I have always taken criticism well and it wasn’t massive criticism in my eyes.

“We both want to make me a better player for Chelsea and if that is the end result then that is all that matters. It hurt when people said I was showing off. All I like to do is put a smile on fans’ faces as part of the side.

“What people must appreciate is I have had this attention since I was 16 at West Ham. The expectancy was enormous then and hasn’t changed.”

From that moment on, Cole established himself as one of Mourinho’s go-to men on the wing, starting the League Cup final victory over Liverpool and both legs of the Champions League semi-final defeat to the same opponents.

He ended the season with nine goals in 46 appearances, with only 12 of those outings coming from the bench. Most importantly, he also had a Premier League winner’s medal.

The following season continued in much the same manner. With the fully-earned trust of Mourinho, Cole went one better in terms of both appearances and goals, despite the added competition from Shaun Wright-Phillips alongside Damien Duff and Arjen Robben.

And at the end of that 2005-06 campaign, Cole produced one of his finest moments in a blue shirt.

With Manchester United arriving at Stamford Bridge in April, Chelsea had the chance to clinch the title against their nearest rivals. Fittingly, it was Cole who produced the piece of skill worthy of winning a championship.

Receiving the ball with his back to goal and three United defenders around him just outside the box, Cole somehow left all three for dead with the deception of the world’s greatest conman before firing the ball home with an emphatic finish.

It's Matchday!Manchester United vs Chelsea FCOld Trafford5.30pm (UK Time)#COYB 💙 pic.twitter.com/DYJ0IfjjrZ

— ChelseaFC News & Vids (@CFCclips) December 28, 2015

In one moment Cole showed both the absurd talent which first attracted him so much hype at West Ham and the refinement of his game at Chelsea which made him the country’s best attacking midfielder.

Later that summer, Cole also produced the highlight of his England career with his stunning, dipping volley against Sweden at the World Cup.

It was another example of him attempting something most other players wouldn’t even dream of.

“Joe Cole has always been a special player, full of fantasy,” Sven-Goran Eriksson had commented four years previous. Finally, he was proving it on a regular basis.

#OnThisDay in 2006, Joe Cole scored THAT volley from 35 yards out against Sweden. pic.twitter.com/gDHF4keQDd

— Planet Football (@planetfutebol) June 20, 2020

In the following three seasons Cole cemented his status as one of English football’s favourite sons, collecting the FA Cup twice, another League Cup and coming a John Terry slip away from winning the Champions League.

But in January 2009, Cole ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament playing in an FA Cup replay at Southend, and his career would never be the same.

Upon his return, nine months later, he never fully established himself in what was then Carlo Ancelotti’s side before his contract expired in the summer.

“Ever since I did my knee at Chelsea, it was an uphill struggle,” he told the Daily Mail in 2017.

Cole’s last appearance for Chelsea came in the FA Cup final victory over Portsmouth which secured the club’s first ever Double, and there were still enough flashes of inspiration – namely his back-heeled opener in a win at Old Trafford – to convince Fabio Capello to name him in England’s squad for the 2010 World Cup.

Joe Cole v Manchester United in PL 2009/10

— CFC SAUDI FANS ™ (@CFCSAUDIFANS) August 6, 2019

It speaks volumes about how he was regarded that Terry tried to lead a mutiny against the manager to ensure Cole was selected after a dismal display against Algeria devoid of any spark.

“Listen, Joe is one of the best players in our country,” he said. “He has come back from an injury and showed great form for Chelsea. It still amazes me how the club have come to the conclusion of letting Joe go.”

But Cole was only granted two substitute appearances, and his club career similarly failed to take off thereafter.

A move to Liverpool never recovered after a red card on his debut and a missed penalty in his second appearance.

Though he did impress at Lille alongside Dimitri Payet and Eden Hazard – we’re not ashamed to admit that resembles something close to our wet dream – a return to West Ham and short spell at Aston Villa also fell flat.

To his credit, Cole continued to battle against his body, and dropped down two divisions to rekindle his love for the game at Coventry City before heading west for an Indian Summer with the Tampa Bay Rowdies.

While many are tempted to label Cole a waste of potential, that would be unfair. He is one of only 11 Englishmen to have won three Premier League titles, three FA Cups and played in three World Cups.

“Once you stop learning, there’s no point playing,” he told The Guardian in 2011. “You’d have mastered it. And no one’s mastered football yet.”

Joe Cole shouldn’t be used as a warning to young footballers, he should be used as an example.

#1496. Liverpool Confidential: Billionaires' investment set to beat deadline, new deal for Trey Nyoni, the academy kids who shone in Istanbul and Mor Talla Ndiaye's visa issues

Published: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 12:04 EDT, 5 November 2026

The deal for a group of billionaires to buy a minority stake in Liverpool remains on track to pass a deadline set by the new independent football regulator.

The consortium led by Amit Bhatia, known as 1892 Holdings, agreed to purchase a 38 per cent stake in Fenway Sports Group’s controlling interest in the club earlier this season. And despite some anxieties externally and in the fanbase about a lack of updates, I have been told this week that everything is moving in the right direction.

Sources close to Bhatia and his consortium insist the process takes time but there are no hitches and it is still expected to beat the deadline. It is understood the date in question is in December and in accordance with the new regulator, who must take within 90 days to issue a final suitability determination for prospective new owners or senior executives.

Indeed, this week brought the news that FSG are in exploratory talks to buy a significant stake in Formula One team Cadillac. Both FSG and Cadillac were contacted for comment around that story – and insisted it is an ongoing process.

One source pointed to the fact that FSG clearly expect to have some ‘spare pennies lying around’ – hinting the Liverpool investment will go through.

Senior FSG staff have constantly stressed that selling 38 per cent of the club does not mean they are losing interest and that they are as committed as ever, though the potential for the buy-in to become a full-scale takeover at some point in the future remains.

Bhatia is backed by his billionaire father-in-law Lakshmi Mittal, plus Jeff Bezos and Eduardo Saverin.

Amit Bhatia (second left) is heading up a consortium to buy a stake in Liverpool from John Henry (second right) and his Fenway Sports Group

Liverpool supporters hope the deal will transform the club's fortunes on the pitch

Jeremie Frimpong has had rotten luck with injuries since he joined Liverpool – and Andoni Iraola ruled him out for more than a month with a problem he suffered at Brentford on October 17.

I understand the Dutch international is now all-but fit and could play this weekend if needed – however, given his high number of injuries, a decision has been made to delay his return.

Liverpool were recently punished for bringing back Dominik Szoboszlai too quickly as the Hungarian pulled up shortly after his first start upon his return, which set him back a fortnight.

Frimpong missed only seven Bayer Leverkusen games through injury in four years at the club according to Transfermarkt, but has already sat out nearly 30 Liverpool matches. Most of those absences have been hamstring related, so Frimpong is not being rushed back and will be given the international break to continue working on his recovery.

Jeremie Frimpong has had rotten luck with injuries since he joined Liverpool and went down again against Brentford last month. However, the Dutch international is now close to a return

Trey Nyoni has been offered a bumper new contract to reward him for his fine progress.

The 19-year-old, who scored his first Liverpool goal in the defeat in Istanbul against Fenerbahce on Wednesday night, has had a stellar rise since Iraola took over at Liverpool.

Nyoni, signed from Leicester City in 2023, was in many matchday squads and featured sparingly last season but has come of age this campaign and has already doubled his first-team minutes – with three quarters of the season still to play.

Nottingham Forest made a £30million bid in the summer but Iraola identified him as a key asset and he will be rewarded handsomely for his progress.

Trey Nyoni scored his first Liverpool goal on Wednesday night in the Champions League loss against Fenerbahce

Your question answered: What's the January priority?

One topic fans have asked me about this week is which position is a priority in the January and summer transfer windows.

The first area to mention is midfield. I have reported in the past how Chelsea are currently ahead of Liverpool in the race for Bournemouth's Alex Scott, so let’s keep an eye on that – and the situation of Lamine Camara of Monaco. But I think the priority has to be a left-back.

Are Milos Kerkez and Kostas Tsimikas good enough? Neither have performed at the required level so far this season and bringing Tsimikas back from a loan at Roma – where he barely played – felt like a bit of a cop-out. It has to be a priority position in the next 12 months.

Liverpool flew straight home from Istanbul after the loss to Fenerbahce and did not land on Merseyside until past 2am. It is a departure from last season, when Arne Slot would often have his squad stay for two nights on European away days.

Players are said to be big fans of the extra night at home with most preferring to sleep in their own beds.

Iraola did not hold a post-match team talk after Fenerbahce but will debrief the squad when back in training, having branded the defeat ‘cheap’ and ‘messy’.

Another UEFA Youth League game, another hat-trick for Will Wright.

I was in place on the outskirts of Istanbul on Wednesday afternoon to watch the 18-year-old bag his second treble in four European matches this term, making it 13 goals for the season in all competitions.

Wright had a heated exchange with Josh Sonni-Lambie over who would take a penalty but the pair have smoothed things over now after Wright took it and scored. The striker’s assist for Finn Inglethorpe was also a notable moment that showed he is a team player and not a greedy No9.

Liverpool's Will Wright scored another hat-trick in the UEFA Youth League on Wednesday, against Fenerbahce Under 19s

I was also impressed by right back Oliver O’Connor, who looks like a real athlete. He aced every physical pre-season test for the academy and is versatile, with a quality delivery into the penalty area.

The Scouser joined the club aged six and has been a midfielder for most of his career. Boss Rob Page does not necessarily see him as a right back long-term but he caught the eye up and down that flank.

Those who did watch the academy game – and the first-team later on – would have been wondering where defender Mor Talla Ndiaye was. He is a mainstay in the Youth League XI and has been on the seniors’ bench several times.

It is believed the Senegalese defender had a visa issue and could not feature in the game in Turkey, though next month’s away match in Bruges is not expected to pose the same problem.

Liverpool's Mor Talla Ndiaye (centre) was nowhere to be seen in Istanbul due to visa issues

Also in academy news, young midfielder Michael Laffey has signed with the OmniSports agency who represent the likes of Wright and Crystal Palace midfielder Adam Wharton. Under 21s captain Laffey, whose dad owns the Glenbuck pub in Anfield, made the first-team bench a fortnight ago.

Liverpool supporters have drawn the short straw and will pay more than any of their English counterparts for a pint while following their team in Europe this season.

That’s according to data from LiveScore, who have worked out that Reds will pay an average of £4.91 per pint on their travels.

Still, £4.91 for a pint? Better than most places at home. You might need one after watching Liverpool’s defending this week!
