For the period 920–420 Ma, the main continental blocks in cluster GU-F (Great Unconformity—formation) were Laurentia, Baltica, northeastern North China, most of South America, Western Australia, the Kalahari Craton and parts of Antarctica. Cluster GU-NF (Great Unconformity—no formation) spanned most of Africa, Asia, parts of Antarctica and the São Francisco Craton (Fig. 3a). Cluster GU-F captured positive dynamic topography (Fig. 3d), mainly above whole-mantle upwelling (Supplementary Video 1). Dynamic topography was relatively stable between 900 Ma and 800 Ma, increased rapidly between 800 Ma and 720 Ma, followed by a gradual increase between 720 Ma and 600 Ma, and a rapid decrease between 600 Ma and 420 Ma (Fig. 3d). The predicted uplift would have promoted glacial erosion1,13 during the proposed Sturtian and Marinoan global glaciations (Fig. 3d). The GU-F pattern of prolonged dynamic uplift during Neoproterozoic times (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2), followed by dynamic subsidence during Cambrian times (Fig. 3d) was consistent across all mantle convection models (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3a,c,e). Cluster GU-NF captured dynamic topography on average negative throughout 920–420 Ma with gradual increase between 900 Ma and 760 Ma, a rapid decline between 760 Ma and 520 Ma, and renewed increase between 520 Ma and 420 Ma (Fig. 3d). In cluster GU-NF, Siberia and the Congo and West African cratons were in a dynamic topography low surrounded by subduction zones (Fig. 2a,c and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2).

For the period 420–0 Ma, cluster GU-HPP (Great Unconformity—high preservation potential) spanned Western Laurentia, Baltica, North China and Siberia, and cluster GU-LPP (Great Unconformity—low preservation potential) spanned Eastern Laurentia, Africa, Australia, Antarctica and India (Fig. 3b). The dynamic topography for GU-HPP, which was generally negative because of subduction (Supplementary Video 1), remained relatively stable between 420 Ma and 240 Ma, before gradually declining until 0 Ma (Fig. 3e). By contrast, in GU-LPP dynamic topography increased between 420 Ma and 240 Ma, was stable between 240 Ma and 120 Ma, then gradually declined until 0 Ma (Fig. 3e).

We derived a map highlighting the areas in which the Great Unconformity was predicted to have formed and to have a high preservation potential, which consisted of Laurentia, Baltica and northeastern North China for model M1 (Fig. 3c) and included areas around Laurentia and Baltica in all six models (Extended Data Figs. 3 and 4). We analysed the sensitivity of these results to the number of clusters (either two or three) for each period (formation 920–420 Ma, preservation from 420 Ma) from vote maps (Methods) of areas in which the Great Unconformity was predicted to exist across the six models (Extended Data Fig. 5). This confirmed that Laurentia, Baltica and North China were the main continental blocks in which the Great Unconformity was predicted to have formed and to be preserved, with northern South America emerging as a possible additional region (Extended Data Fig. 5).

The dynamic topography evolution predicted by our models was consistent with the preserved sediment flux for each continent except Africa1,14 (Fig. 4 and Methods). Predicted prolonged Precambrian uplift, followed by rapid Cambrian subsidence, generally matched increased sediment flux across the Precambrian–Cambrian boundary (Fig. 4a–e). A shift from erosion to sedimentation reflecting decreasing dynamic topography (Fig. 4) and flooded continents (Extended Data Fig. 6a) was predicted for all continents except for Eurasia and Africa, which consisted of tectonic blocks with contrasting Neoproterozoic histories. In Eurasia, dynamic uplift was predicted for Baltica and North China, and dynamic subsidence for Siberia40 (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Figs. 7d and 8b,g,l,q,v,aa). In Africa, dynamic uplift was predicted for the Kalahari Craton, and dynamic subsidence for the Congo and West African cratons (Extended Data Figs. 7e and 8e,j,o,t,y,ad) was consistent with their sedimentary record of long-lived depocentres41,42. Extensive Precambrian orogens within Africa enhanced erosion and sedimentation (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6), leading to a landscape in which negative dynamic topography did not result in increased sediment flux at the base of the Cambrian (Extended Data Fig. 6a,c,e,g).

a–e, Evolution of the preserved volume of sediment per year and per unit continental area (increasing down) (left y axis, coloured bar charts) and dynamic topography (right y axis, grey bar charts and coloured lines) for each continent averaged at time steps corresponding to the sediment preservation data1,14. Coloured solid and dotted lines represent the evolution of dynamic topography for Laurentia and continental blocks in Eurasia. f–j, Data in a–e temporally averaged for dynamic topography cycles in each continent. In each panel, the vertical dashed line represents the start of Cambrian times, and the horizontal dashed line represents the datum for dynamic topography.

The evolution of predicted Phanerozoic dynamic topography differed across continental blocks. Laurentia, Baltica and North China were characterized by sustained dynamic subsidence, which aligned with increased preserved sediment flux across North America and Eurasia (Fig. 4). Conversely, predicted renewed dynamic uplift of South America and of Australia, which would have eroded earlier unconformities11,31 and formed new ones, corresponded to decreased preserved sediment flux (Fig. 4).

Importantly, the number of dynamic topography uplift–subsidence cycles governed the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. A single cycle of Precambrian uplift followed by Phanerozoic subsidence was the ideal scenario for forming and preserving the Great Unconformity. This scenario, which is in first-order agreement with thermochronology studies3,4,7,10,18, was predicted for Laurentia for all models except M3 (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 8a,f,k,p,v,z). Although Laurentia was in cluster GU-F for model M3 (Extended Data Fig. 2), it was not predicted to have experienced notable uplift and was subsiding above a mantle downwelling at 640 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 9). Together with a poor match of the present-day mantle structure for M3 (Extended Data Fig. 1d), this confirmed that NNR was an appropriate reference frame to model mantle flow33, but not PMAG in which lithospheric net rotation was large. Precambrian uplift was predicted for four out of six models for Baltica and North China, with marked variations in amplitude and duration between models (Extended Data Fig. 8b,g,l,q,v,aa), possibly reflecting particularly uncertain subduction history (Supplementary Discussion and Supplementary Table 1). All models predicted dynamic uplift of Baltica as it moved from the southern hemisphere to the northern hemisphere between 540 Ma and 520 Ma (Supplementary Videos 1 and 2), followed by rapid subsidence consistent with a sub-Cambrian unconformity linked to epeirogenic uplift22,43.

By contrast, most models predicted two cycles of dynamic uplift followed by dynamic subsidence for South America and Australia and long-lived dynamic subsidence followed by dynamic uplift then renewed dynamic subsidence for Africa (Fig. 4h–j and Extended Data Fig. 8c–ad), consistent with thermochronological and geochronological evidence for these regions44,45,46,47,48. The predicted dynamic uplift of South America and Australia coincided with preserved sediment flux on these continents, as expected (Fig. 4h,i and Extended Data Fig. 8c–ac). However, the dynamic uplift of Africa coincided with increased sediment preservation because Africa was positioned centrally in Gondwana (Extended Data Fig. 6b) and orogens in Antarctica and South America (Fig. 3f) restricted drainage from Africa to the oceans, leading to endorheic (inland) sedimentation49.

The solution of the presented flow models depends strongly on the tectonic reconstruction, for which the uncertainty is large and increases back in time (Supplementary Discussion and Supplementary Table 1). Testing the sensitivity of the flow model to the tectonic scenario is a challenge that could be addressed by developing alternative tectonic reconstructions with continuously closing plate polygons or by developing a different approach to predict past mantle flow.

Comparing dynamic topography cycles to preserved sediment flux confirmed Laurentia, Baltica and North China as continental blocks on which the Great Unconformity was predicted to have formed and to be preserved (Fig. 4). The Great Unconformity surface is exposed and extensively studied in Laurentia1,3,5,6,7,9,10,15,18 and in North China8,25,26,27,28, whereas it is mostly inferred to occur beneath younger sediments in Baltica19,20,21,22,23,24. This largely stems from the tectonic and geodynamic evolution of each of these continental blocks. In the considered tectonic scenario, no subduction occurred directly along the margins of Laurentia between about 930 Ma and 510 Ma, Baltica between about 750 Ma and 520 Ma, and North China between about 720 Ma and 540 Ma (Supplementary Discussion, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). Subduction beneath northeast Laurentia from approximately 470 Ma resulted in its amalgamation with Baltica into Laurussia by around 420 Ma, associated with continent-wide Cambrian transgression (Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). North China was on the periphery of Gondwana during Cambrian times with the Qinling subduction zone system at its western margin from 540 Ma (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Discussion, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). During the assembly of Pangea, collisions occurred along some margins of all three continental blocks (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6b), promoting the deformation and erosion of rocks potentially preserving the Great Unconformity, or their burial in foreland basins. The large continental area of Laurentia and limited reworking at its margins were favourable to recording the formation of the continental-scale Great Unconformity. The prominent exposure of the Great Unconformity in the Grand Canyon15,16,17 has been linked to the Laramide uplift event from Farallon flat-slab subduction and subsequent Colorado River incision50,51. Repeated orogeny along the eastern margin of Baltica (Fig. 3f) could explain why the Great Unconformity is generally inferred to occur at depth on that smaller continental block. Early Cretaceous lithospheric delamination52 could explain the exposure of the Great Unconformity in North China, which is unexpected given its comparatively small area and four episodes of orogenesis between about 500 Ma and 200 Ma (Fig. 3f).

Our models predict changes in dynamic topography that when averaged in time and space by k-means clustering occur over approximately 20 Myr and about 5,000 km, suggesting that the motion of continents over the convecting mantle provided the large-scale geodynamic environments that favoured the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity in Laurentia, Baltica and North China. The geologic record of uplift4,5,6,7,10,53 and subsidence4,5,6,7,9,10,20 indicates that the timing of erosion and deposition54 varied between locations, which probably reflects the effect of processes, such as tectonic deformation, elastic flexure or shorter wavelength dynamic topography, that would affect relative sea level over shorter spatial and temporal scales.

The amplitude of long-wavelength dynamic topography is thought to be about a tenth of the amplitude of tectonic topography37, and continental tilting would not result in the formation of slopes that would lead to sufficient fluvial erosion to explain the magnitude of denudation associated with the Great Unconformity1,4,7. We propose that sustained positive dynamic topography throughout Cryogenian times (Fig. 3d) would have resulted in substantial erosion because glacial erosion rates exceed fluvial erosion rates by an order of magnitude and can operate at lower elevations13. The rarity of extensive unconformities in the history of Earth could be due to the very long timescale (>900 Myr) of the proposed continental-scale uplift and subsidence to form such an unconformity, combined with rare extensive glaciations and decreasing preservation potential back in geological time.

Our models explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved in North America and show that it is a first-order surface expression of deep geodynamic processes that transformed global landscapes and sediment fluxes. In turn, these landscape dynamics would have altered seawater chemistry and catalysed the Cambrian explosion of life2. Future work could investigate the effects of continental-scale dynamic uplift and subsidence on erosion, sedimentation, seawater chemistry and their consequences for the diversification of life forms.

Macrostrat is an open, relational geospatial database that enables large-scale, quantitative analysis of 33,903 lithologically and chronologically defined rock units across 1,474 regions in the Americas, New Zealand and the deep sea55.

We accessed lithostratigraphic data from the Macrostrat (https://macrostrat.org/api/units/?lith_class=sedimentary&lith_type=metasedimentary) database through theAPI (v.2). We downloaded sedimentary units and associated stratigraphic columns as GeoJSON files in June 2025. We created a map of transgressive sequences and erosional remnants across North America and northern South America (Fig. 1) spanning late Neoproterozoic to early Ordovician times.

We used the code CitcomS57 to model mantle convection for a billion years (1,000–0 Ma). In CitcomS, the mantle structure is represented with finite-element nodes in 3D spherical geometry. We considered six model cases (Extended Data Table 1), three of which have been presented in previous work (M4 was MF in ref. 58; M5 was C3 in ref. 59, C20 in ref. 33 and C3 in ref. 60; and M6 was C1 in ref. 59).

We discretized the mantle into about 13 million nodes (129 × 129 × 65 × 12), with radial mesh refinements at the surface (about 50 × 50 × 15 km) and core–mantle boundary (CMB; about 28 × 28 × 27 km) and relatively lower resolution in the mid-mantle (approximately 40 × 40 × 100 km). We reconstructed mantle flow in a modified version of CitcomS57,61 in which plate kinematics and the thermal structure of the oceanic lithosphere and subducting slabs down to 350 km depth were derived from tectonic reconstructions62 with continuously closing plate polygons63 and imposed as time-dependent boundary conditions in 1 million-year increments. We used the extended Boussinesq approximation that assumed the mantle to be an incompressible fluid to account for viscous dissipation, internal heating, depth-dependent thermal expansion coefficient and an adiabatic temperature gradient64.

For initial boundary conditions and time-progressive model simulation, we created a lithospheric thermal structure from reconstructed seafloor ages and half-space cooling with a maximum seafloor age set as 80 Myr to obtain a maximum thickness of oceanic lithosphere consistent with observations for the present day. We used the method in ref. 65 to reconstruct synthetic seafloor ages, whereas the continental lithosphere adopted simplified tectonothermal ages from ref. 66. The global thermal regime of continental lithosphere and subducting slabs, reconstructed using seafloor ages and location of subduction zones61, was imposed in the flow models in increments of 1 million years.

The initial conditions included an adiabatic temperature profile between two boundary layers: the lithosphere at the surface, and a 225 km thick laterally uniform basal layer containing a 113 km thick layer with excess density. The density contrast δρb between the basal layer and the ambient mantle was defined by the buoyancy ratio \(B=\frac{{\rm{\delta }}{\rho }_{{\rm{b}}}}{\rho \alpha \Delta T}\) where ΔT = 4,300 K was the temperature change across mantle for M1–M3 (ΔT = 3,600 K for M4 and ΔT = 2,800 K for M5 and M6), ρ = 5,546 kg m−3 was the average density67 and α = 1.32 × 10−5 K−1 was thermal expansivity68 in the 100 km layer above the CMB. The initial condition consisted of slabs inserted down to 1,000 km depth for models M1–M4 (1,200 km for models M5 and 550 km for M6) with dip angles of 45° dip down to 425 km depth and 90° descent below. To incorporate the advective thickening of more viscous lower mantle, lower mantle slabs were twice as thick as upper mantle slabs in the initial condition. Models were initialized with differing warm-up phases lasting 250 Myr for models M1 and M4, 200 Myr for models M6 and 0 Myr for other models (Extended Data Table 1) using the 1 Ga configuration for tectonic velocities, subduction zone positions and lithospheric age. Boundary conditions were isothermal at the surface and at the CMB, imposed plate kinematics (velocities) at the surface and a free-slip kinematic condition at the CMB.

The convective vigour in models was governed by the Rayleigh number \({\rm{R}}{\rm{a}}=\frac{{\alpha }_{0}\rho g\Delta T{h}_{{\rm{M}}}^{3}}{\kappa {\eta }_{0}}\), where α0 = 3 × 10−5 K−1 was the coefficient of thermal expansion at the surface, ρ = 4,000 kg m−3 was the density, g = 9.81 m s−2 was the gravitational acceleration, hM = 2,867 km was the thickness of the mantle, κ = 1 × 10−6 m2 s−1 was the thermal diffusivity, η0 = 1 × 1021 Pa s was the reference viscosity. The subscript ‘0’ indicated reference values. The coefficient of thermal expansion was depth-dependent, decreasing by a factor of about 2 over the thickness of the mantle (see refs. 68,69). Based on these values, we obtained Ra = 1.2 × 108 for M1–M3. The Rayleigh number was varied across model cases (Extended Data Table 1).

Likewise, the dissipation number governed heat dissipation generated by shear heating. It was given by \({\rm{D}}{\rm{i}}=\frac{{\alpha }_{0}g{h}_{{\rm{M}}}}{{C}_{p}}\), where 2867 Cp = 1,200 J kg−1 K−1 was the heat capacity. The total rate of internal heating was equal to 33.6 TW, accounting for contributions from both radioactive decay (about 9–17 TW; ref. 70) and primordial heat dissipated through secular cooling of the interior of Earth (around 8–29 TW; ref. 70).

Depth-, composition-, temperature- and pressure-dependent viscosity was computed as

The depth-dependent viscosity pre-factor η(r) was equal to 2 × 1019 Pa s above 160 km depth and between 310 km and 660 km depth (upper mantle), to 6 × 1017 Pa s in the asthenosphere between 60 km and 310 km depth for models M1–M3 (2 × 1018 Pa s for models M4–M6), and 6 × 1020 Pa s in the lower mantle below 660 km depth for models M1–M3 (2 × 1020 Pa s for models M4–M6; Extended Data Table 1). The compositional viscosity pre-factors ηC were equal to 1 for ambient mantle, to 100 for continental lithosphere (modelled as in ref. 66), and to 10 for the basal layer. The term r was the radius, Rc = 3,504 km was the radius of the core, Eη = 284 kJ mol−1 was the activation energy, Zη = 2.1 × 10−6 m3 mol−1 was the activation volume, Ru = 8.31 J mol−1 K−1 was the universal gas constant, T was the dimensional temperature, Toff = 694 K was a temperature offset and TCMB = 4,300 K was the temperature at the core–mantle boundary. The viscosity structure, defined by the viscosity pre-factors, activation volume, activation energy and temperature offset produced viscosity variations varying over three orders of magnitude across the model33. Although these contrasts were smaller than expected for the solid Earth71, these lateral viscosity variations could be resolved at a spatial resolution that allows time-dependent mantle flow to be computed using up to about 15,000 CPU hours per 100 million years on supercomputer Gadi.

We derived boundary conditions from the global tectonic reconstructions in ref. 62 (which merges with tectonic reconstructions in refs. 72,73,74,75), which was the only tectonic reconstruction extending back to 1 billion years ago with continuously closing plate polygons that are necessary in models based on the approach in ref. 61. We considered two reference frames for the tectonic reconstruction in ref. 62: the original palaeomagnetic reference frame (PMAG, model M3) and a no-net-rotation reference frame (NNR), which was suitable to model mantle convection33,76. We analysed model results, including dynamic topography, mantle temperature and composition fields in increments of 20 million years.

We computed air-loaded dynamic topography at the surface of Earth as \(h=\frac{{\sigma }_{\mathrm{rr}}}{\Delta \rho g}\), where g = 9.81 m s−2 was the acceleration of gravity and Δρ was the difference in densities between air (ρA = 0 kg m−3) and the shallow upper mantle (ρUM = 3,320 kg m−3). We considered free-slip boundary conditions, contributions from sources of buoyancy deeper than 350 km depth, and lateral viscosity variations deeper than 350 km depth.

As in refs. 32,33,77, we first classified the present-day lower mantle structure as mapped by 10 independent S-wave tomographic models78,79,80,81,82,83,84,85,86,87 and predicted by six mantle flow models (M1–M6). To achieve this, we generated 196,965 evenly spaced points (about 0.45°) on the surface and sampled mantle temperature (seismic velocity) approximately every 58 km between 1,000 km and 2,800 km depths. We then used k-means88 clustering to group these points into user-specified k clusters such that the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS), that is, the squared Euclidean distances between points and the centroid of the group was minimized.

As in previous studies32,33, we examined model success by computing three metrics (Extended Data Fig. 1): (1) the predicted fractional area fa of the surface of Earth covered by clusters for hot BLOBSs (for mantle flow models) and slow LLSVPs (for tomographic models), (2) the global accuracy (\(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}\)), which was a measure of the spatial match between the present-day mantle structure (clusters) predicted by mantle convection models and that averaged across 10 independent tomographic models given by \(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{TN}}{A}\), where TP was the area of true positives representing spatial match between hot BLOBSs and LLSVPs, TN the area of the true negatives measuring the spatial extent of cold basal mantle structure and high seismic velocity profiles and A was the total surface area of Earth. For each model, the mean accuracy \(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}\) represented the average across 10 tomographic models, whereas for each tomographic model, \(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}\) was computed as an average across the nine independent tomographic models; and (3) the time-averaged median angular distance \(\widetilde{\theta }\) between reconstructed volcanic eruption locations (LIPs and kimberlites as in ref. 33) from 320 Ma and the edge of hot BLOBSs. The distance was taken as zero for eruption locations above a BLOBS or LLSVP. Smaller distances indicated a close spatial match between BLOBSs or LLSVPs and volcanic eruptions, which was thought to be favourable32,33,89. Mantle flow models were deemed to perform better if all three metrics were within the range or close to the range for tomographic models (Extended Data Fig. 1, grey areas).

We generated a set of evenly spaced (about 0.45°) points entirely covering present-day continents. We extracted dynamic topography at the reconstructed location of these points in 20 Myr intervals and rotated the results back into the present-day plate configuration. We used the continental blocks that continuously existed from 920 Ma to mask data for all other times so that the considered locations existed for all considered times. We used k-means clustering88 as in ref. 90 to classify geographic regions that share a similar evolution of predicted dynamic topography.

We used the silhouette91 score, Davies–Bouldin index92 (DBI) and elbow method93to determine the appropriate number of clusters to consider (Supplementary Fig. 1). The silhouette score measured how similar a point was to its own cluster compared with other clusters. It combined intra-cluster cohesion and inter-cluster separation. Silhouette scores ranged from −1 to 1, with larger values indicating better-defined clusters. The DBI evaluated intra-cluster similarity and inter-cluster differences based on intra-cluster dispersion and inter-cluster distance. Lower scores indicated better clustering. It was computationally efficient but assumed compact, spherical clusters, making it less reliable for irregular shapes. The heuristic elbow method consisted of plotting the number of clusters (k) against the clustering cost (for example, WCSS) and identifying the ‘elbow’ point, at which the rate of improvement (decrease in WCSS) decreased sharply, suggesting the most appropriate k.

We identified the ideal number of clusters for all six model cases for both the Great Unconformity formation (920–420 Ma) and preservation (420–0 Ma) periods to be equal to either two or three (Supplementary Fig. 1). We produced cluster maps for each model case and each cluster combination (either two or three) and combined them in maps indicating model agreement with a score between zero and six out of six models. These ‘vote’ maps highlighted regions showing both formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity across model and cluster combinations (Extended Data Fig. 5).

We obtained the preserved sediment flux (sediment volume divided by time) from Neoproterozoic times (1.6 Ga) to the present for North America, South America, Africa, Eurasia and Australia from ref. 1. For the period 920–0 Ma, we scaled sediment flux by the present-day area of each considered continent as in ref. 1. We averaged continental dynamic topography for each continental block that continuously existed between 920 Ma and 0 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 8a) using the time periods at which sediment volume data were defined (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8).

To focus on long-term, long-wavelength processes, we filtered the preserved sediment data using time windows that corresponded to the periods of dynamic uplift and dynamic subsidence predicted for each continent. We then averaged the preserved sediment volume to represent the sediment accumulation associated with each phase of dynamic topography (Fig. 4f–j).

The subduction convergence rates at trench segments were computed using plate-kinematic workflow of GPlately (v.2.0.0), built atop PyGPlates94, a Python interface for GPlates95 and PlateTectonicTools. The process consisted of resolving the topological plate model and extracting subduction zones from the network of dynamic plate boundaries reconstructed at a specified age using the NNR model. Each subduction zone was then tessellated, that is, discretized into a series of evenly spaced points using the ‘tessellation_subduction_zone’ module in GPlately. At each tessellated point, subduction convergence rate, obliquity and trench migration rate were calculated from the relative motion of the down-going and overriding plates at each reconstruction time step. Negative convergence-rate values, which indicated infrequent inconsistencies in the model with divergence occurring at a convergent boundary72, were set to zero before computing the range of convergence rates for each subduction zone listed in Supplementary Table 1.

The code used to run mantle models is available at GitHub (https://github.com/EarthByte/citcoms). Figures 1–3 and Extended Data Figs. 2–6 and 9 were created using the open-source Python library PyGMT (v.0.13.0), a Pythonic interface for the Generic Mapping Tools (GMT)97, and Fig. 4, Extended Data Figs. 1, 7 and 8 and Supplementary Fig. 1 were created using the open-source Python library Matplotlib98 (v.3.8.3).

#1441. Man United's secret plot to poach Sir Alex Ferguson from Aberdeen, 40 years on - from phone calls with a fake Scottish accent to clandestine meetings at M74 services on Bonfire Night

Published: 04:53 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 08:07 EDT, 6 November 2026

It is 40 years ago today since Manchester United appointed Sir Alex Ferguson as manager and ushered in the most successful era in the history of the club.

The parallels with the current situation at Old Trafford are striking. United have made their worst start to a league season since then, with just one win from their opening nine games, and Michael Carrick is fighting to save his job, just as Ron Atkinson was on the brink in November 1986.

United had rejected Big Ron’s offer to resign towards the end of the previous season. However, with the team only staying out of the relegation zone on goal difference, the club decided to sack him following a 4-1 League Cup defeat by Southampton.

Atkinson felt the seeds of a decision that would change the course of United’s history had been sown a few months earlier when he was working as a TV pundit at the World Cup in Mexico and Aberdeen boss Ferguson was in temporary charge of Scotland, following the sudden death of Jock Stein.

‘Lawrie McMenemy, also on the World Cup beat as a TV pundit, revealed he had heard Alex Ferguson had already been tapped up for my job,’ Atkinson later wrote in his autobiography.

‘I haven’t lost any sleep about the shenanigans surrounding my premature departure. I don’t blame Alex one bit. It’s all part of the management game. Somebody is inevitably waiting to nick your boots in this business.’

It is 40 years since Manchester United secretively lured Sir Alex Ferguson from Aberdeen

Club director Mike Edelson put on a fake Scottish accent to get through to Ferguson's office at Aberdeen, posing as Gordon Strachan's assistant

Atkinson’s suspicions were founded on a conversation between Ferguson and United director Sir Bobby Charlton in Mexico. Ferguson confirmed the chat, but disputes its significance.

‘That’s not true,’ Ferguson wrote, addressing Atkinson’s claim in his book Managing My Life. ‘Although Bobby did speak to me at the side of the pitch before Scotland’s fiasco of a game in Uruguay, the furthest he went was to ask that if I ever decided to move to England, I should let him know. I don’t think that could be considered an offer.

‘Apart from the brief contact with Bobby, there was nothing but rumour to link me with Old Trafford before November 5.’

Charlton’s recollection also suggests it was incidental. ‘I was working for the BBC and I went to watch Scotland train,’ he told Daily Mail Sport in 2011. ‘He saw me through the fence and came over to say hello. We only spoke for a minute or so, but I liked him.

‘I also recall going to Aberdeen once, to open a garage of all things. The people there were panicking. “You’re not here to take our manager, are you?” The whole city seemed to be in love with him. I stored that away, too.’

Atkinson viewed Charlton as an adversary in the boardroom. When he returned from Mexico keen to complete the signing of England centre back Terry Butcher from Ipswich, using money earmarked from the £2.3million sale of Mark Hughes to Barcelona, Charlton was the main opponent to the move.

Chairman Martin Edwards pulled the plug citing a lack of funds due, in part, to building a new museum at Old Trafford. ‘We’ll bring the museum up for a corner then!’ Atkinson replied.

Having decided a change of manager was needed, United favoured Ferguson over Terry Venables, but were anxious to make sure the 44-year-old wanted the job having drawn a blank with McMenemy, Bobby Robson and Ron Saunders before appointing Atkinson five years earlier.

Club director Martin Edwards spoke with Fergson and met him with a secret delegation at M74 services in Lanarkshire

Ferguson pictured with Graham Hogg (right) in his first week of training at Man United

Edwards, Charlton and fellow directors Mike Edelson and Maurice Watkins hatched a bold plan to get through to Ferguson’s office at Aberdeen by posing as Gordon Strachan’s accountant.

Edelson, who put on a Scottish accent to make the call, said: ‘It suddenly got very embarrassing when the receptionist started asking me personal questions about how my wife was. The other three were rolling around. But she put me through, Alex answered, I quickly explained who I really was and then put him on to Martin.’

Ferguson recalled taking the call in his office. ‘Martin Edwards gave me his number so I could ring him back and thus be assured of the authenticity of the call. I could scarcely contain myself as I dialled the Manchester number. Would I be interested in the job at Man United? Yes, I told him without hesitation.’

Ferguson immediately told his No 2 Archie Knox, but admitted that when he told his wife Cathy she was ‘devastated’ because the family were happy in Aberdeen.

It was her reluctance to move to London that had previously persuaded him to reject Arsenal and Tottenham but this time the opportunity was too good to refuse.

Ferguson arranged to meet the four-man delegation from United at 7pm that night at Hamilton Services on the M74 in Lanarkshire, where they would recognise each other using their car registrations. ‘It really was a case of flashing headlights,’ said Edelson.

Edwards got into Ferguson’s car and the others followed to the home of Cathy’s sister Bridget in the Bishopbriggs suburb of Glasgow.

Ferguson revealed he was offered a ‘disappointing’ salary that was less than he earned in Scotland and had no transfer budget. United also refused his request to buy the family home to ensure a quick sale, or pay back a £40,000 loan from Aberdeen, but he accepted the job anyway.

Ferguson surrounded by photographers in his first game in charge - they lost 2-0 against Oxford United at the Manor Ground

He became the most successful manager in English football history, winning 13 Premier League titles

United’s directors drove back to Manchester that night and Edwards sacked Atkinson at 10.30am on the morning of November 6. Edwards then caught a 2pm flight to Aberdeen with Watkins, who was also United’s solicitor, to conclude the deal with Aberdeen chairman Dick Donald.

Meanwhile, Atkinson was clearing his desk and saying his goodbyes at United before organising a farewell drinks party at his home in Rochdale which was attended by a number of United stars and went on a lot longer than planned.

‘It turned into an all-night rave with more than a hundred people packed into the house and lasted until 5am,’ Atkinson recalled.

There were a few sore heads when a nervous Ferguson gathered the players together on November 7. He was well aware of the drinking culture at Old Trafford and what he felt was Atkinson’s liberal attitude, based on information fed to him by Strachan, who had left Aberdeen for United two years earlier.

‘He cited all sorts of problems with the team, particularly the drinking and the alleged indifference of Big Ron to its damaging effects,’ Ferguson wrote.

‘The training, Gordon suggested, was a shambles, with nothing done until Ron had a session on his sunbed as a preliminary to joining in a small-sided practice game.’

Clamping down on the boozing was one of the first items on Ferguson’s agenda, but not before he banished bus driver Derek Sutton from sitting on the bench following his first game at Oxford 48 hours after being appointed.

It ended with a 2-0 defeat followed by a goalless draw at Norwich as Ferguson made an inauspicious start to a glittering career spanning 26-and-a-half years. His first game at Old Trafford brought a first win, beating QPR 1-0.

In a new book, Fergie: The Lost Tapes, author Wayne Barton has gone through 400 hours of recordings and unearthed a long-forgotten address by the new manager to United fans that day which has echoes of the farewell speech he made on the pitch in 2013.

‘Hello, Alex Ferguson here. I don’t need to tell you how important this day is to me. This is the greatest experience of my life, to be in front of this platform and this stage.

‘Since I’ve arrived here, I’ve been so aware of the traditions and success of this great club. My job is to make sure that success continues and to make us the greatest club in Britain.

‘The real supporters of Manchester United are the greatest in the world - don’t let anyone forget it.’

#1440. Leeds have the longest unbeaten home run in the Premier League - from new transfer strategy and napping to choosing 'rough and ready' over 'comfy and nice', this is how they turned Elland Road into a fortress again

Published: 06:59 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 09:23 EDT, 6 November 2026

We will know a great deal more about the strength of Tottenham’s revival by mid-afternoon on Saturday. If Roberto De Zerbi’s men can escape one of the toughest venues in English football without too much damage, perhaps he really is on to something.

The Elland Road factor is no myth – Leeds United are currently on the longest unbeaten home run of any Premier League side, dating back eight games to a 1-0 reverse against Sunderland on March 3. Since Daniel Farke took over in 2023, only Arsenal, Manchester City and Liverpool have more points per game at home.

Farke's Leeds have won 44 of 69 games at Elland Road, losing only eight and scoring a whopping 141 goals.

After collecting a single point from matches at Sunderland and Bournemouth and failing to score in either, Leeds are desperate to be back in front of their own supporters.

Here, Daily Mail Sport looks at how one of England’s most evocative stadiums is baring its teeth again.

The last time Leeds were in the top flight, their home form was a huge part in their downfall. From 2021-23, Leeds lost nearly half of their home games (16 of 38) and won only nine.

The Elland Road factor is no myth. Since Daniel Farke became Leeds United boss in 2023, only Arsenal, Manchester City and Liverpool have more points per game at home

Farke's Leeds have won 44 of 69 games at Elland Road, losing only eight and scoring a whopping 141 goals. They are unbeaten there this season, and recently thrashed Newcastle 4-1

Farke and the players were able to set it right in the Championship, where Leeds won 35 of 47 in the following two campaigns including the play-off semi-final against Norwich. In the Premier League, it was always going to be a different story but Farke, his players and the supporters have responded to the challenge.

‘Since we’ve come back up, people realise how important the home record is and how we need to drive the team on,’ says Dan Moylan, co-owner of the Square Ball fan channel who has been going to Elland Road since 1982.

‘We know what we need to do to help the team. A lot of players will come to Elland Road and not fancy it. So many stadiums are too comfy and nice. We need it a bit rough and ready to get behind our team.

’Daniel Farke has galvanised the fanbase in a steady way. It’s not been spectacular, more of a steady building of momentum. There has been a lot of jeopardy with Leeds in recent seasons as they’ve gone through the divisions. There was a lot of anxiety in the Championship years but when the nerves were shredded, fans seemed to get behind the team more.’

Elland Road has always provoked strong reactions. Leeds supporters will always be hostile towards Gary Neville but the former Manchester United defender and Sky Sports pundit knows the value of these old-school sporting cathedrals.

‘Elland Road was unbelievable,’ Neville has said. 'There was a real nastiness and hostility to it, but it’s a proper football club with an incredible crowd. You always knew you were in for a brutal afternoon.’

Pep Guardiola saw the other side of the same coin. The 2021-22 campaign had few joys for Leeds, as they stayed up on the final day of the season.

‘Since I arrived, I heard many times about what Elland Road means,’ he said after Manchester City won 4-0 there in April 2022. 'At the end, 4-0 down, fighting to stay in the Premier League and singing, chanting, showing support. I can imagine how the people feel.’

Leeds prioritised top-flight experience after coming up in 2025, signing players such as Dominic Calvert-Lewin (centre) who can handle a rough atmosphere

Calvert-Lewin has scored 12 times at Elland Road since joining in summer 2025

To thrive at Elland Road you need players who can handle it when Leeds are struggling – and this was a significant part of their recruitment plan for the Premier League. Mindful of the failures at Elland Road between 2021 and 2023, Leeds took a different approach to recruitment after returning to the Premier League in 2025.

To make the most of their home, Leeds decided that top-flight experience was needed. In came players like Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Sean Longstaff and James Justin – battle-hardened Premier League footballers who know what it is to play in spicy atmospheres. These were men who would not wilt when Elland Road was at its most exacting.

The groundwork was laid in the Championship. For any home match outside the top flight, Leeds will always be heavy favourites – but this is double-edged. If a match against a low-profile club is still goalless after half an hour, fans start to groan. A couple of misplaced passes later and those groans turn to jeers.

It takes a certain kind of character to override those difficulties and in the second tier Leeds found it, racking up 190 points across the two seasons.

Before home games, Leeds have followed the same routine under Farke. They will meet at a hotel in the city on the morning of the match and travel by coach to Elland Road.

The pre-match meal and final tactical briefings will take place at the hotel and for later kick-offs, players are encouraged to have an afternoon nap. Sleep-deprived players with very young children may opt to stay in the hotel the night before the game. They will arrive at the ground 90 minutes before kick-off.

Elland Road is in the initial phase of a major redevelopment project that is designed to take the capacity from around 37,000 to 53,000. That means players now enter the stadium via a different route and can no longer be greeted by fans on their way in.

The mystique remains, though. Harry Wilson and Jayden Bogle were in the Derby side who won a spectacular play-off semi-final at Elland Road in May 2019. Both regard it as the best atmosphere they had ever played in and it played a part in their decision to join Leeds.

Harry Wilson and Jayden Bogle won a play-off semi-final at Elland Road with Derby in May 2019. Both regard it the best atmosphere they've played in

While stadium improvement is crucial, it is just as important that the essence of Elland Road does not slip away

Leeds lean heavily on their fanbase when recruiting. About 150,000 turned out in Leeds city centre to celebrate promotion 18 months ago and the club show videos of those scenes to transfer targets.

It is all part of the Leeds brand and while stadium improvement is crucial, it is just as important that the essence of Elland Road does not slip away.

‘It depends who can afford to get in,’ adds Moylan. ‘The club need to be careful not to price out supporters and they have to make sure young working-class fans can afford it.

‘I’ve seen the ground pretty raucous and animalistic, going back to the 1990s. Football has changed a lot over the years and the moving of kick-off times doesn’t help but on its day Elland Road now is as good as it’s ever been.’ Tottenham have been warned.

#1439. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

When asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”

3 - Manchester United have failed to win any of their last three Premier League games against sides that have received a red card (D1 L2). Disadvantage? https://t.co/DuSpvymZfu

The Tottenham boss told Sky Sports: “I think we played very well against a great team. We had many chances to score in the first half. Three or four. The second half is normal to suffer against this quality. I am very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character.

“We suffered in the game but every situation of the game. I like the situation we were in with the red card. We need this situation. We have not accepted the defeat. We have to react in all ways we can. It is a bad way, it is not the right way. I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character.

“We win the game if we play as a team. We didn’t win this game playing as a team. Every game like today, we will win many games.”

When asked about Solanke, he replied: “He is a good player for Tottenham. There for not too many strikers better than Solanke. Today he was captain because he deserved it, especially in this moment because he suffer because Tottenham didn’t score or win any games. He is a great guy, great player and we are behind him.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League game between Manchester United and Tottenham at Old Trafford.

If Manchester City had not entered a legal battle with the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching 114 charges relating to financial regulations by an independent panel, then surely there would be more pressure on the two head coaches in the dugout this evening?

Man Utd and Tottenham have undoubtedly both endured extremely disappointing starts to their respective top-flight campaigns. The hosts sit just inside the bottom half of the table after picking up just five points from their opening five matches. It’s going even worse for Tottenham, who languish in 20th with zero wins and just two points.

The perilous landscape leaves only one reasonable conclusion: this has all the ingredients for an early season six-pointer.

The strain is perhaps less intense on Michael Carrick, with the Englishman having built up a bundle of goodwill after cleaning up the mess left by Ruben Amorim last season as Man Utd eventually finished third, qualifying for the Champions League. Fans were left slightly underwhelmed by the club’s transfer window, with the players at Carrick’s disposal having not forged any momentum so far in this campaign.

The spotlight is definitely shining more intensely upon Roberto De Zerbi after big-spending Tottenham splashed over £300m in the summer on the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Savio. However, the Italian boss is yet to strike the correct rhythm with his newly-formed squad. An encouraging performance backed up by a positive result here at Old Trafford could be the perfect antidote to ease the worries of fans fearing that Tottenham could be embroiled in another relegation battle.

All eyes are on this one. Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1438. Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD1,2,3. Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge4. Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals5, and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts6,7; however, the biological basis of this ‘female protective effect’ (FPE) has remained unknown8,9. Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST. Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals10, emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

Large-scale genetic studies have implicated hundreds of genes in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), with many identified through rare mutations that result in loss of function of one allele1,2,3. This suggests that gene dosage plays an important part in ASD11 and makes it critical to determine how appropriate expression levels of ASD genes are maintained. Characterization of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) could provide important insights into mechanisms mediating the proper transcriptional dosage of these ASD genes. In addition, ASD is significantly male-biased in prevalence, and although some ASD genes have been identified on the X chromosome12, X-linked mutations alone cannot fully explain this sex bias8,13. Moreover, it has been consistently demonstrated that female individuals require greater autosomal genetic risk to manifest ASD compared with male individuals6,7, but the genetic mechanisms of this female protective effect (FPE) are unknown8,9.

Here we use GRN reconstruction to identify key drivers of expression of ASD genes, including CHD8 and REST. These analyses also identify female-biased transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and inactive X chromosome in female individuals10, as a key regulator of ASD genes, suggesting a direct transcriptional mechanism that could contribute to the FPE. This study provides a crucial framework for determining how variants in diverse genes can cause convergent molecular effects that ultimately result in ASD.

Functional interrogation of ASD genes revealed strongly overlapping effects on downstream targets in human neural progenitor cells (NPCs). Knockdown (KD) studies were performed for 20 ASD genes, including 18 genes from the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) gene database14 and two long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) previously implicated in ASD (NR2F1-AS1 (ref. 15) and SOX2-OT16). RNA-degrading CRISPR enzyme CasRx17 and an array of three guide RNAs (gRNAs) per target (Supplementary Table 1) were used to induce individual KD of each target gene relative to non-targeting controls (NTCs) in NPC cultures from a control human male (XY) induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell line (Fig. 1a,b and Extended Data Fig. 1). RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis after 24 h of KD demonstrated that nearly all perturbations led to substantial numbers of significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs; adjusted P (Padj) < 0.05), with a median of 920 DEGs per perturbation (25th percentile: 644, 75th percentile: 1,485) (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 2). To ensure sufficient statistical power for downstream analyses of these DEGs, we focused on the 18 perturbations (18 of 20, 90%) that resulted in more than 20 DEGs, excluding the ARHGAP5 and ARID2 KD samples from further analysis. The remaining perturbations each led to a minimum of 287 DEGs, which enabled robust characterization of these samples.

a, Experimental design schematic showing CasRx-based KD in NPCs. b, Immunocytochemistry of iPS cell-derived human NPC cultures, representative of three independent analyses with similar results. c, Bar plot depicting enrichment of SFARI genes or intellectual-disability-only genes among the DEGs for each KD condition, excluding the targeted gene itself. Bars indicate the OR from a one-sided Fisher’s exact test; error bars indicate the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval on the OR. P values were adjusted using Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing. d, Circos plot depicting transcriptomic convergence of HC-SFARI DEGs shared between different KD conditions (Extended Data Fig. 3a). e, Heatmap showing the relative expression of HC-SFARI genes that were DEGs in at least ten KD conditions (recurrent dysregulation) (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Statistically significant DEGs were identified using DESeq2 (Wald test) with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing and are indicated by an asterisk. Top ASD risk genes from ref. 1 are shown in bold. f, Relative CytoTrack dye intensity (−log2) over time. Only KD conditions that exhibited statistically significant effects on NPC proliferation that were consistent over time are displayed. Plot depicts mean ± s.e.m. Statistical significance was determined using ordinary two-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test. At least three biologically independent samples per condition were analysed for each time point. See Supplementary Table 10 for full statistical results. Scale bar, 50 μm. ID, intellectual disability; NS, not significant.

Transcriptome-wide analyses showed that ASD gene KDs caused remarkably widespread disruption of other ASD genes. Most sets of DEGs exhibited significant enrichment for known ASD genes in the SFARI Gene database (15 of 18, 83.3%) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 3). By contrast, there was no significant enrichment for genes implicated in intellectual disability but not ASD (intellectual-disability-only genes) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 3) (Methods), despite their comparable expression in NPCs (intellectual-disability-only genes: 1,062 of 1,242, 85.5% expressed; SFARI genes: 797 of 1230, 64.8% expressed). This suggests that perturbation of ASD genes particularly affects other ASD genes, as opposed to neurodevelopmental genes more broadly.

We observed a striking pattern of transcriptomic convergence across perturbations, which we defined as statistically significant overlap of the same DEGs (Extended Data Fig. 3). This was particularly evident for high-confidence SFARI (HC-SFARI) genes, the SFARI genes in the highest evidentiary tier for association with ASD (Fig. 1d). Moreover, HC-SFARI genes tended to shift in a concordant direction as a result of different perturbations even when they were not significant DEGs within a particular KD sample (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Such genes included prominent ASD risk gene CHD8 (ref. 18), which was significantly downregulated by most (11 of 18, 61.1%) of the KDs. Notably, 27 HC-SFARI genes were DEGs in at least 10 of the KDs (27 of 183, 14.8%, P = 4.1 × 10−9), and all were consistently downregulated (Fig. 1e), indicating convergent dysregulation of many of the strongest risk genes for ASD.

High levels of CasRx have been reported to cause non-specific RNA degradation of a magnitude that is correlated with the expression level of the KD target, whereas use of lower CasRx levels avoids this problem19. In our NPC transcriptomic studies, CasRx was expressed from only a single safe-harbour locus (AAVS1), which limited its expression. We also performed several further experiments to confirm that non-specific RNA degradation did not affect our results. First, we found no relationship between expression levels of KD targets and numbers of resulting DEGs when considering either the whole transcriptome (P = 0.990, R2 = 8 × 10−6, linear regression) or SFARI genes specifically (P = 0.784, R2 = 0.0043, linear regression) (Extended Data Fig. 4a). We next generated NPCs expressing fluorophores mKO2, mScarlet and iRFP670 and targeted each individually with CasRx (Supplementary Table 4); flow cytometry showed no collateral effects on the fluorescence intensity of non-targeted fluorophores (Extended Data Fig. 4b and Supplementary Table 5). Finally, we confirmed strong transcriptomic convergence on shared downregulated DEGs by performing further KD studies of a subset of our target genes using short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) in NPCs (Extended Data Figs. 4c,d and 5 and Supplementary Table 6). Re-analysis of data from a study that used Cas9 to knock out ASD genes in iPS cells and iPS cell-derived excitatory neurons (ExNs)20 similarly demonstrated strong transcriptomic convergence on shared downregulated DEGs both within each cell type and between cell types (Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 6). Recent studies published since our work was submitted have also noted convergence across diverse ASD models21,22. Together, these data confirm that disruption of ASD genes results in transcriptomic convergence across various cell types and experimental contexts.

The marked transcriptomic convergence we observed in our KD studies suggested that candidate ASD risk genes could be nominated by the following features: (1) consistent downregulation following ASD gene KDs; and (2) dosage sensitivity, as indicated by high genic constraint scores (Supplementary Table 7 and Methods). This approach yielded 397 genes (Supplementary Table 8), including 113 SFARI genes (odds ratio (OR) = 5.87, Padj = 1.85 × 10−39) and 49 HC-SFARI genes (OR = 11.17, Padj = 1.11 × 10−29), demonstrating that these criteria effectively prioritize known ASD genes. Notably, this set of genes showed no enrichment for intellectual-disability-only genes (OR = 1.01, Padj = 0.509). All of the remaining 284 non-SFARI genes exhibited significant co-expression with SFARI genes (all Padj < 0.05), which has previously been shown to help prioritize novel ASD risk genes4, further supporting their relevance to ASD. Moreover, at least 40 of these genes showed some association with ASD in at least 1 major sequencing study (Supplementary Table 9). For example, mutations in AKT3, although classically associated with brain overgrowth disorders such as megalencephaly, have recently been associated with ASD; other genes including KIF11, KIF2A and SOS1 have also been associated with ASD in multiple studies (see references in Supplementary Table 9). Therefore, the remaining genes merit consideration as candidate ASD risk genes.

Many ASD gene perturbations also caused similar phenotypic effects in NPCs. Proliferation analysis using heritable dye (CytoTrack) showed that 9 of 18 (50%) of the KDs led to a statistically significant decrease in proliferation (Fig. 1f, Extended Data Fig. 6a, Supplementary Table 10 and Supplementary Fig. 1), including several genes that have been implicated in microcephaly (SETD1B23, SETD2 (ref. 24), SETD5 (ref. 25), KMT2E26 and WAC27). By contrast, only 1 of 18 (5.6%) of the KDs led to a significant increase in NPC proliferation rate. This suggests that reduced NPC proliferation is a common phenotype that results from disruption of several different ASD genes, consistent with previous findings28. Deciphering the specific relationships between these molecular phenotypes and abnormal head size in ASD is complex, as reports implicate increased rates of both microcephaly and macrocephaly across individuals with autism29,30. Indeed, two KD targets that we found to decrease proliferation in NPCs, SETD2 (ref. 24) and KMT2E26, have been reported to be associated with either microcephaly or macrocephaly depending on the specific variants studied in these genes. Thus, although disruption of NPC proliferation is a convergent phenotype observed across many of our perturbations, how this relates to downstream changes in head size remains to be determined.

Inducible KD in cerebral organoids also revealed shared neurodevelopmental phenotypes. For these organoid studies, we created the FLEx-based inducible CRISPR knockdown (FLICK) construct. FLICK enables control over the timing of KD through doxycycline-inducible genetic recombination that results in constitutive expression of CasRx and an EGFP reporter (Fig. 2a), providing robust KD (Extended Data Fig. 7a). The FLICK constructs also contain identifying sequences that can be captured during single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and used to determine the KD target in a given cell; this enables analysis of mosaic cerebral organoids.

a, Design of FLICK constructs for doxycycline-inducible CasRx KD. FLICK constructs also express gRNAs (not shown). b, FLICK organoid after 2 months of development, representative of 3 independent analyses with similar results. Immunohistochemistry was performed to visualize expression of the following markers: EGFP (FLICK construct), DAPI (nuclei), PAX6 (NPCs), TBR2 (intermediate progenitor cells) and CTIP2 (ExNs). c, Expression (expr.) of canonical brain marker genes used to identify cell types by scRNA-seq. d, UMAP showing organoid cell clustering from integrated long-term organoid scRNA-seq data collected at 1 month and 2 months. e, Relative abundance of cells for each KD target from mosaic organoids at 1 month or 2 months. Results were normalized to the starting proportion for each sample at day 0 and are displayed relative to NTCs from the same time point. The plot depicts mean ± s.e.m. The FLICK constructs were induced by treatment with doxycycline on days 14–15. Statistical significance was assessed using repeated measures one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test. n = 3 biologically independent samples per condition. f, Cell type composition per KD target in 1-month organoids. Dotted lines indicate the NTC proportions of main cell types (radial glia, intermediate progenitors and neurons). Samples for which the ExN/RG proportion was significantly different from the NTC are indicated with an asterisk (Padj < 0.05). Statistical analysis was performed using ordinary one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test, considering all long-term samples from 1 month (shown here) and 2 months (see Extended Data Fig. 7f). Scale bar, 1 mm. Avg., average; Dox., doxycycline; ExN-Early, early ExN; ExN-Imm, immature ExN; ExN-Mat; mature ExN; IPC, intermediate progenitor cell; IPC-Div, dividing IPC; IN, inhibitory neuron; RG, radial glia; RG-Div, dividing RG.

For long-term studies, we targeted ASD genes whose KDs were not found to impair NPC proliferation in our CytoTrack experiments (Supplementary Table 10). FLICK constructs targeting these genes or expressing NTC gRNAs were each separately transposed into iPS cells. We then used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to isolate cells that had integrated the FLICK constructs on the basis of their expression of fluorescent reporter TagBFP. Following FACS, we pooled an equal number of FLICK+ iPS cells for each KD target and for the NTCs, and cultured this mixed iPS cell population for 4 days to allow the cells to recover before generating mosaic organoids (day 0). Recombination of the FLICK construct, which leads to constitutive expression of CasRx and an EGFP reporter, was induced in a subset of the cells (approximately 10%) by treatment with doxycycline from days 14–15, when the organoids predominantly consisted of PAX6+ NPCs (Extended Data Fig. 7b). These organoids were subsequently grown until either 1 or 2 months of development (Fig. 2b) and analysed by scRNA-seq; this analysis identified all expected cell types (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 7c,d) including radial glia, intermediate progenitor cells, inhibitory neurons and ExNs. Further scRNA-seq analysis confirmed that the FLICK construct could produce efficient KD (Extended Data Fig. 7e).

Long-term organoid KDs revealed shared phenotypes across several perturbations. Several KDs, particularly those targeting BAZ2B, CLASP1 and EHMT1, were depleted from the organoids compared with NTCs (Fig. 2e), even though these KDs did not impair proliferation in NPC cultures (Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Table 10). This discrepancy between our NPC cultures and organoids suggests that long-term organoids, which support progenitor proliferation as well as differentiation, can be used to identify neurodevelopmental phenotypes that are not apparent in short-term NPC cultures. Notably, microcephaly has been associated with pathogenic variants in these genes31,32,33, consistent with the organoid phenotypes. Furthermore, these KDs also altered cell type proportions in organoids, producing relatively greater numbers of ExNs and fewer radial glia (Padj = 0.021 for BAZ2B, 0.018 for CLASP1 and 0.012 for EHMT1; ordinary one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test) (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 7f). Together, these results indicate that disruption of these genes may result in increased ExN differentiation at the expense of self-renewal of radial glial progenitors. Most of the other KDs also resulted in a trend towards an increased proportion of ExNs by the 2-month time point, suggesting that this is a convergent neurodevelopmental phenotype, in line with previous observations34,35.

Depletion of ASD genes also resulted in prominent transcriptomic convergence in cerebral organoids (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 7g). Radial glia with different KDs exhibited highly overlapping DEGs, further supporting our findings from NPC cultures. Indeed, the DEGs identified in organoid radial glial progenitors strongly overlapped with the DEGs identified from KD of the same target in NPC cultures (Extended Data Fig. 7h), suggesting that these effects on gene expression are not specific to a particular experimental context. Transcriptomic convergence was also observed in other cell types, including intermediate progenitor cells and ExNs (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 7g), demonstrating that the convergence of ASD genes on shared downstream effects is not unique to neural progenitors. This was consistent with findings of studies that identified shared ASD DEGs in postmortem brain tissue from individuals with distinct causes of ASD36,37,38, as well as with widespread observations of convergent ExN phenotypes such as disordered synaptic structure or activity upon disruption of distinct ASD genes20, suggesting that convergence does not reflect merely a shared alteration of cell type or fate of progenitor cells. Furthermore, we found that detection of overlapping DEGs using scRNA-seq was heavily dependent on the number of cells sequenced for each perturbation, as demonstrated by downsampling analysis (Fig. 3b). This sample-size dependence may partially explain the lack of robust transcriptomic convergence observed at the individual gene level in some previous studies with smaller sample sizes34,39. Our use of an isogenic background is also likely to have contributed to our detection of transcriptomic convergence, as different genetic backgrounds have been found to significantly affect neurodevelopmental phenotypes resulting from the disruption of ASD genes in organoids34. Finally, although some convergently disrupted genes were cell-type specific, many genes were consistently disrupted across several cell types, including SFARI DEGs (Fig. 3c). This suggests that although cell-type-specific features affect the transcriptomic consequences of ASD gene perturbations, certain effects could be broadly shared by diverse cell types.

Downsampling of the number of cells per condition to the number indicated above each pie chart decreased the transcriptomic convergence observed. c, Network visualization of SFARI DEGs in long-term organoids shared among different KDs conditions and cell types. The thickness of edges represents the number of shared DEGs. Nodes were plotted on the basis of clustering with the Fruchterman–Reingold algorithm (igraph). Nodes that are closer together had more shared DEGs on average. d, Proportions of cells with each KD target from scRNA-seq of mosaic organoids with acute KD. e, UMAP showing clustering of cells from acute KD mosaic organoids from scRNA-seq. f, Heatmap of cross-enrichment between different KD samples showing transcriptomic convergence in acute KD organoids.

Acute disruption of ASD genes in 2-month organoids revealed even greater convergence on shared DEGs. A further set of mosaic FLICK organoids was grown for 2 months before induction of KD with doxycycline treatment from days 61–62; this was followed by scRNA-seq 2 days later, to determine the acute effects of disruption of these genes in organoids that had developed normally. This approach resulted in similar numbers of cells per KD (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 7i), enabling deeper analysis of the KDs that had been depleted from the organoids with long-term KD (Fig. 2e). As expected, these organoids contained a mixture of cell types (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 7j), with ExNs by far the most abundant cell type at this developmental time point (Extended Data Fig. 7k). Many KDs resulted in ExN DEGs that were enriched for the DEGs identified from NPC cultures (Extended Data Fig. 7l), again suggesting shared changes in gene expression across cell types upon KD of ASD genes. Furthermore, acute KD of the target genes that had been depleted from organoids over the course of long-term KD (Fig. 2e) allowed us to obtain much greater cell numbers for these perturbations, which showed that these KDs also resulted in strong transcriptomic convergence (Fig. 3f).

Transcriptional regulators that could mediate transcriptomic convergence in ASD were identified through MAGIC analysis (Methods), which uses chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) data from ENCODE to identify transcription factors and cofactors whose binding targets are enriched within a gene set of interest. This identified transcriptional regulators whose target genes were recurrently differentially expressed across many of the ASD gene KDs in NPCs (Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 11), including HC-SFARI genes such as CHD2 and SIN3A. Of the recurrent MAGIC regulators not previously implicated in ASD, several were both highly constrained (Supplementary Table 7) and co-expressed with known ASD genes (Extended Data Fig. 8a), features that have been demonstrated to be predictive of novel ASD risk genes4.

MAGIC analysis also identified consistent drivers of convergence in organoids (Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 11). Of the top recurrent transcriptional regulators identified in NPCs, half (13 of 26, 50%) were also identified in organoid radial glial progenitors (Extended Data Fig. 8b). MAGIC also identified recurrent ExN regulators shared across developmental stages and across long-term versus acute KD timescales, including many SFARI genes. Nine of these genes were also identified as top transcriptional regulators in neural progenitors, indicating that they may be key drivers of convergence in various cellular contexts.

Of particular interest, the RE1 silencing transcription factor (REST) was significant according to MAGIC analysis in 17 of 18 (94.4%) NPC perturbations (Extended Data Fig. 8a) and consistently emerged as a top MAGIC regulator across all tested conditions (Extended Data Fig. 8b). Although direct mutations in REST have not previously been associated with ASD, REST has critical neurodevelopmental roles and functions as a master negative regulator of neurogenesis40,41. Dysregulation of REST has also been reported following disruption of ASD genes including CHD8 (ref. 42) and Rett syndrome gene MECP2 (refs. 43,44). Re-analysis of human and mouse REST ChIP–seq binding sites (Methods) identified strong enrichment of SFARI genes (Padj = 3.6 × 10−67 and 7.7 × 10−50, respectively), including HC-SFARI genes (Padj = 2.2 × 10−13 and 3.7 × 10−8, respectively), among REST targets (Extended Data Fig. 8c), supporting a key role for REST in regulation of ASD-relevant gene expression.

De novo GRN reconstruction from our NPC RNA-seq data using ARACNe enabled association of further transcription factors and chromatin modifiers (together referred to as ‘regulators’) with their downstream targets (regulons) (Methods). We validated this approach by separately constructing ‘held-out’ GRNs that excluded data from samples in which the KD target itself was a potential regulator, thereby preventing circularity in regulon inference. Regulons predicted from these held-out GRNs strongly overlapped with the DEGs observed following KD of the corresponding target genes in NPCs (Padj < 3.98 × 10−116 for each, combined P = 4.08 × 10−937) (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 9a). Thus, ARACNe effectively captures bona fide regulatory relationships.
