#1424. The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Animals learn about the external world in part through interoceptive signals1,2. For example, the nutrient content of food is first estimated in the mouth, in the form of flavour, and then it is measured again through slower signals from the gut. How these signals from the mouth and gut are integrated to drive learning is unclear. Here we identify a dopamine (DA) pathway that enables learning about the nutrient content of food. We show that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area are necessary for associating nutrients with flavours, and that post-ingestive nutrients trigger DA release selectively in a small region of the anterior basolateral amygdala (BLA) but not in canonical DA targets in striatum. This nutrient-triggered DA release occurs preferentially in the left BLA in mice, and this same structure is preferentially activated by post-ingestive nutrients in humans. We identify the gut sensors that are responsible for nutrient-triggered DA release; show that they activate BLA-projecting DA neurons defined by expression of cholecystokinin; and demonstrate that stimulation of DA axon terminals in the anterior BLA drives flavour–nutrient learning but not other aspects of feeding behaviour. Two-photon imaging of neurons in the left anterior BLA reveals that they integrate gustatory and post-ingestive cues, and silencing these neurons prevents flavour–nutrient learning. These findings establish a neural basis for how animals learn about the nutrient content of their food.

a, Fibre placement in VTA, shown with median slice along anteroposterior (AP) axis (black=littermate controls, red=GtACR). b, Mice with fibres above posterior VTA showed greater inhibition of flavour learning, consistent with the location of the BLA projecting population (Lammel et al.,2008). c, Fibre placement along the mediolateral (ML) axis did not affect learning, as deviations would cancel within animals due to the fixed bilateral spacing of implants. d, Fibre placement along the dorsoventral (DV) axis did not affect learning. ns P > 0.05; *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01; ***P < 0.001. a–e, Two-step normalization procedure. Step 1: fluorescence traces normalized to activity-independent signal (420 nm), removing movement artefacts. Step 2: traces during IG or IP manipulations further normalized to sham infusion or saline injection, correcting for bleaching and long-term drift. Outside this figure, only step 1 normalization was applied to activity traces, and step 2 was applied only to summary plots. a, Example raw fluorescence traces from a single mBLA GRAB-DA site during Ensure IG (top) or sham (bottom). b, Dopamine-dependent signal after 470 nm traces were normalized to 420 nm. c, Further normalization by subtracting sham traces. d, Summary of mBLA dopamine release during Ensure IG vs sham after step 1. e, Summary of the same data after both steps. f, GRAB-DA recordings in mBLA; dotted lines mark external capsule (scale bar, 0.5 mm). g, Mean traces (left) and summary plots (middle, right) showing greater mBLA DA release during and after Ensure infusion. h, No sex differences in mBLA DA release during (left) or after (right) Ensure infusion. i, Glucose, but not mannitol, increases mBLA DA release. j, Transit times for IG infusions: water 12 ± 1 s; Ensure 21 ± 1 s. k, Example traces with sigmoid fits to estimate T5% (orange) and T3σ (blue). l, Summary rise times relative to infusion onset, corrected for transit time (from e): T5% = 54 ± 9 s; T3σ = 41 ± 12 s; mean = 48 ± 11 s. m, Example traces with sigmoid fits to estimate T95% (orange) and T3σ (blue). n, Summary decay times relative to infusion end: T95% = 749 ± 51 s; T3σ = 388 ± 100 s; mean = 569 ± 79 s. o, GRAB-DA recordings in NAc core; dotted lines mark anterior commissure (scale bar, 0.5 mm). p, No change in NAc DA release with Ensure or water. q, GRAB-DA recordings in DLS; dotted lines mark corpus callosum (scale bar, 0.5 mm). r, No change in DLS DA release with Ensure or water. s, Reconstructed fibre placements in BLA (colour scale = ∆F/F during Ensure IG), showing greater DA release in magnocellular vs parvocellular BLA. t, GRAB-DA recordings in lateral BLA; dotted lines mark external capsule (scale bar, 0.5 mm). u, Lateral BLA shows increased DA release during Ensure infusion, but not after. v, Both glucose and mannitol increase DA release in lateral BLA. ns P > 0.05; a, Protocol for delayed flavour–nutrient conditioning. Mice received 10 min access to a flavoured saccharin solution followed by IG infusion of water or glucose. Averaged aBLA neuron dynamics during sucrose bouts (z-score) and distributions of activity compared to sham (p = 6.7 × 10-15, KS test) or mock lick bouts (p = 0.005, KS test). c, Peak (magenta) and 5% rise times (mint) with example cells (left) and summary plots (right). d, Lick count across trials and during the first 0.5 s of bouts. e, Activity of all cells (left) and sucrose-activated cells (right) across trials and during the first 0.5 s of bouts. f, Correlation of activity and lick count during first 0.5 s of sucrose vs mock bouts (sucrose: R² = 0.030, p = 0.0017; mock: R² = 0.00014, p = 0.95). g, Cross-registered neuron dynamics during sucrose (left) and sucralose (right) bouts. h, Mean traces (left) and activity (right) of sucrose-activated neurons during sucrose vs sucralose and sucrose vs water bouts. Minor differences in sucrose activity reflect cross-registration. i, Correlation of activity and lick count during mock, sucrose, sucralose, and water bouts (mock: R² = 0.062, p = 0.21; sucrose: R² = 0.018, p = 0.016; sucralose: R² = 0.17, p = 1 × 10-7; water: R² = 0.076, p = 0.0089). j, PCA of cross-registered neurons across sucrose, sucralose, and water sessions: scree plot (left) and first three PCs during each bout (right). k, Single-neuron dynamics (left) and distribution of activity (right) during and after sucrose IG infusion (both: p = 0.002, KS test). l, Population-weighted z-score activity during IG infusions, averaged by mouse. m, Nutrient specific activation during IG infusion of sucrose, but not water or mannitol. n, Activity after IG infusions. o, Unlike early activation, post-IG activity is not nutrient-selective. p, Population-weighted z-score activity after IG infusions, averaged by mouse. q, Distribution of neurons activated (red), inhibited (blue), or unchanged (black) during early (bouts 2–6) vs late (last five) sucrose bouts. Legends and additional references for Supplementary Tables 1–6.

Behaviour statistics. Summary information for all behavioural tests for each manipulation. Values are reported to 1 decimal place. Number of animals is reported as n. P values are reported for all statistical tests, and are shown in bold if below standard significance level (α = 0.05). In cases in which a Benjamini–Hochberg correction was made for multiple comparisons, an adjusted P value (p′) is shown (where p′ = P × m/i, where i is rank and m is number of cohorts tested; Methods). X′ corresponds to the normalized value of X. For self-stimulation, ‘presses’ means the number of inactive lever presses has been subtracted from the number of active lever presses. In flavour conditioning experiments in which mice began the test with >90% preference for one flavour, statistics are also provided (in parentheses) with these mice excluded. Permutation (perm.) tests use an exact test (or 100,000 iterations if n > 9) and are unpaired, unless otherwise mentioned (note: this means the lowest calculable P value is 1 × 10−5).

Dopamine imaging statistics. Summary information for all recordings of dopamine release in each brain region. Values are reported to 2 decimal places. Number of animals is reported as n. P values are reported for all statistical tests, and are shown in bold if below standard significance level (α = 0.05). X′ corresponds to the normalized value of X. For photometry traces, dF′/F′ means the dF/F values seen during sham infusion have been subtracted. For rise times, s′ means that the time is relative to approximate entry of liquid into the stomach. For fall times, s′ means that the time is relative to the end of the infusion. For peak times during licking, s′ means that the time is relative to the start of the first licking bout. The baseline is defined as the first 10 min of the recording for GI and post-GI measurements, or 0–20 s before the start of the first licking bout for oral measurements. Permutation tests use an exact test (or 100,000 iterations if n >9) and are unpaired, unless otherwise mentioned (note that this means the lowest calculable P value is 1 × 10−5).

Single-cell imaging statistics. Summary information for all 1- and 2-photon miniscope recordings. Values are reported to 2 decimal places. The number (n) of animals and number of cells are reported separately. P values are reported for all statistical tests, and are shown in bold if below standard significance level (α = 0.05). X′ corresponds to the normalized value of X. For rise times, s′ means that the time is relative to either the onset of the licking bout or to the approximate entry of liquid into the stomach. Population-weighted activity (pop-z) is calculated for a group of neurons (for example, activated or inhibited neurons) by multiplying activity by the fraction of neurons belonging to that group. Linear-mixed models (LME) treat mouse differences as both a fixed random effect and covariate (Methods). The relative contribution of mouse differences to total variance is reported by ICCs. Note that, for PCA, the number of PCs is equal to the number of cells. Permutation tests use an exact test (or 100,000 iterations if n > 9) and are unpaired, unless otherwise mentioned (note that this means that the lowest calculable P value for those tests is 1 × 10−5).

fMRI imaging statistics (n = 38). Activity from left and right BLA clusters binned every 2 min (20 min total), as shown in Extended Data Figs. 10f and 11n. For PET statistics, see ref. 56. Each of the ten time bins after glucose intake was contrasted against the baseline (2 min before glucose intake), representing the change in brain activity after glucose intake relative to the baseline. The contrast for the first effect was [ones(1,10)], and for the following contrasts [1], corresponding to the different time bins. The significance threshold was P < 0.05, FWE-corrected for multiple comparisons at the voxel level within the left or right BLA mask, respectively, with initial peak-level threshold set to P < 0.05 uncorrected.

Pseudorabies statistics. Regional labelling (load) was normalized to VTA load to control for injection efficiency. From the 1,328 annotated CCFv3 regions, only grey-matter areas were retained (372 total), with cortical layers collapsed into single structures. Regions smaller than 100 × 100 × 100 pixels were excluded to remove small nuclei with high variance from few labelled cells, yielding 131 analysed regions.

Brain connectivity tables. Connectivity matrices were generated manually, with each pair given a number indicating bidirectional projection strength from 0 (no known direct connection) to 5 (strongest projection known from this area). The connectivity strength between an area and itself was assigned a value of 5. For deciding what strength to assign a projection, large databases like the Allan Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (ref. 1 of the Supplementary References) were preferred, supplemented by additional sources comprising reviews and anatomical tracing studies (refs. 2–32 of the Supplementary References).

#1423. Carrick’s United are in crisis and now spotlight is on Wilcox

Michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he launched a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

ATLETICO ARE AHEAD IN JUST 53 SECONDS! ⚡️ A nightmare start for United at the Metropolitano Stadium 😬 https://t.co/TdOwoXxopn

They certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Ademola Lookman scored Atlético’s second soon after and Carrick was staring at another defeat. And so they now move on to a big game at Leeds on Sunday. This was not the result Carrick would have wanted – and that is before what happened off the pitch.

Ademola Lookman PUNISHES a 10-man Man United 💥 https://t.co/GHKYIHGhNC

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

On the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring issues to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the company man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

It now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

That Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

United cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

[The performance] was a little bit mixed. It’s a tough enough place to come and the start we had put us in a difficult situation. I thought we grew into the game, had four big chances and [score one or more] and the game looks really different. They were really good chances.

And then the red card which I thought was a really poor one. It’s difficult after that. Disappointed that with the chances we had we didn’t [get] more [out of the game].

I haven’t seen [Martinez’s interview]. After a game like this you come here to try and get something from the game and you are disappointed and can be a little bit emotional. I have not seen it so I don’t think it is the right time for me to comment on it.

I fully know we all care and show that in different ways but now is the time to be together and work through. We have a big game on Sunday.

[What do you make of Lisandro’s comments?] I have no comment about that.

The only thing that’s going to get us back into it is to get a few wins.

It is very hard to say after a defeat that there are positives. We just have to work hard to keep working and keep trusting in our structure.

We have to keep working, keep trusting each other and be together on this.

I always wanted to be outspoken as a player but I think he’s gone too far. You can clearly see he cares and wants the club to invest more in new players but his performances have not been good enough. In some ways he’s right, the club needs to invest more. It looks like a bit of an agenda because it wasn’t a poor performance.

[How do you sum up the performance?] Really poor, Really poor. I have to control myself a lot. Sometimes it’s a mirror of the reflection of how our club is. We had a fantastic season last season but in order to compete we needed to buy more players. Many teams buy many players and Atletico Madrid did. They have an amazing team and deserved to win today.

I expected more. [Are you saying you expected more investment in the squad this summer?] Yes 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director. I have to be honest. As players we have to do more but it is important to make a strong squad to be ready for for this kind of night.

In general, in general [should you have invested more in defence and attack given all the midfielders]. Last season we made a strong base to build an amazing team. It’s annoying and disappointing coming here and trying to get a result.

I don’t think so [was the manager backed?] He does his best. You can’t [live on] what you did last season. Every season is different. You can’t stay with what you did last season. The teams knows how you play, they know every detail, if you don’t change next season is a big problem.

It’s changing, changing, changing the manager [after a poor run]. But what about other areas? I can’t say more.

Tonight is it easy to say the coach, easy to say the players [are at fault]. But we have to look at other areas.

So far this season there have been more times when the performances have been worse than the results. This was the other way round but there is a sizeable quality gap between Carrick’s squad and the company they are keeping. They can point to a soft red card but they still shot themselves in the foot with their doziness in the first minute and squandering the good chances they created.

This feels a big moment for Carrick and United’s players to answer some of their critics. They have been getting battered from all sides in the last couple of days. Nicky Butt suggested on his podcast that Carrick told him before he got the United job that management “not for me” and “my head’s all over the shop” and that United was the only job he would take. At the very least, those comments are unhelpful and they are thought to have been dimly received internally.

Jamie Carragher offered a lacerating analysis of United’s performance against Spurs on Saturday on Sky Sports on Monday night and suggested things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved if there is not marked improvement. Steven Gerrard questioned why United opted to invest £50m of their summer budget in Andrey Santos, an unused substitute in the last three league games, insisted the back four was not good enough and questioned the work ethic.

And it was interesting to see Carrick alongside his mate Wayne Rooney just now pitchside. Rooney told the Stick to United podcast that captain Bruno Fernandes looks “fed up” and ready to explode at any moment.

It would have been pretty unthinkable for Carrick not to run with a three-man midfield here, not just because of the wide open spaces opponents have exploited this season but when you look at the back line United are fielding. Dalot at left back, two youngsters in Lenny Yoro and Ayden Heaven and a horribly out of form Lisandro Maríinez.

Nor has Senne Lammens looked convincing this term. Matheus Cunha has been dropped – not before time – and I expect to see Fernandes playing off the right. There’s going to a big onus on Rashford on the left. I’m not sure if he is fully fit but he’s going to be important.

It’s fantastic. It’s where we want to be, these games, these competitions. It’s as tough a place as you can come to. They’ve got a really good history in this competition and it’s where we want to come to challenge and test ourselves. We have put ourselves in this position, got a good start at home and now this is our first away game.

We want a reaction, of course. A positive reaction [to Saturday’s poor performance]. It hasn’t gone how we wanted, how we expected so far but it’s been fine margins in some of those games. It can go both ways but the reality is where we are at now.

It’s a fresh night and we’ve got to adapt, we’ve got to adjust in a positive way.

We want a little more control in the game [with three central midfielders]. At times we have been too open. We wanted to make a difference in that way. We’ve made other changes, certain spaces, certain positions.

To be honest it’s not really a big change of shape, personnel maybe but a lot of it is similar. We want more control, a little bit without the ball and a lot more with it. We’re happy with the way we set up.

Look at the last three goals we’ve conceded. They’re a mixed bag, simple goals you can something about. We need to defend better as a whole team .

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

The one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.

#1422. Embattled FIFA chief Gianni Infantino 'used Trump adviser to get work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper'

By ISABEL BALDWIN, US ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 15:01 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 13:36 EDT, 6 November 2026

FIFA President Gianni Infantino allegedly influenced Trump administration officials to fast-track a work permit for his undocumented Nicaraguan housekeeper after she lost her legal status, according to bombshell documents.

The global soccer chief is alleged to have turned to politically-connected contacts to secure a new work permit for Yajarlin del Socorro Fernandez after the White House revoked her legal permission to work in the United States, according to documents reviewed by the Daily Mail.

The Nicaraguan-born Fernandez was reportedly employed by the soccer governing body to work as a housekeeper for the FIFA boss and his family in August 2024. Despite being on FIFA's payroll, she performed no services for the organization.

However, she reportedly continued illegally working in her role and living in the Infantino household for months after the Trump administration terminated the immigration agreement that granted her permission to stay in the United States.

Fernandez is then said to have secured a new work authorization under Kristi Noem's Department of Homeland Security following an intervention by a Trump adviser, documents show.

Infantino allegedly tapped Carlos Cordeiro, the former US Soccer chief who served as a senior World Cup adviser to Donald Trump, to orchestrate the new work permit.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino (right) reportedly enlisted the help of a Trump adviser to secure a work permit for his family's Nicaraguan housekeeper

Infantino allegedly tapped Carlos Cordeiro (pictured) to orchestrate a new work permit for Yajarlin del Socorro Fernandez

In January, Infantino reportedly asked Cordeiro, who in May 2025 was appointed to the White House's World Cup task force alongside Noem, to use his connections at the state department to smooth the path to getting Fernandez's new work visa approved, according to the documents.

Cordeiro also allegedly first helped to secure Fernandez's right to work in the US under Infantino's orders in 2024.

Fernandez was reportedly already living and working at Infantino's residence in Miami, Florida, in early 2024.

However, until May 2024, she had not yet filed or received an approved work permit and was therefore working at the residence illegally, per the documents.

During a January 2024 meeting at Infantino's home, Cordeiro, at the FIFA boss's request, is said to have instructed a subordinate to submit their own Miami rental address on Fernandez's immigration filing rather than that of the Infantino family home.

While Fernandez's work visa was initially approved, it came to an abrupt end last year when the Department of Homeland Security terminated the Humanitarian Parole Program for Cuba, Haiti, Venezuela and her native Nicaragua.

On May 30, 2025, the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to scrap the four-country scheme, which had permitted Fernandez and other Nicaraguans to secure permission to work in the US.

Fernandez's contract with FIFA was terminated in October 2025, but she was paid a three-month salary as a bonus and remained illegally working as Infantino's housekeeper for the remainder of the year, according to the documents.

Cordeiro (left) was appointed to Trump's White House's World Cup task force in 2025

Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem worked in connection with the task force

In January 2026, Infantino allegedly asked Cordeiro, who was now working on the World Cup task force which operated directly out of Homeland Security, to leverage his new government contacts to secure Fernandez a new permit. That same month, Fernandez was granted a new work visa.

There is no suggestion that Fernandez personally is accused of any wrongdoing.

FIFA strongly denied the allegations that it had 'employed an individual in the US without the necessary authorisation.'

'FIFA verifies the employment status of each employee and ensures compliance with U.S. immigration and employment requirements,' a FIFA spokesperson told The Daily Mail.

'Matters related to the FIFA President's personal and home life are private; however, for the avoidance of any doubt, the costs of any domestic staff are met by the FIFA President personally.

The organization added: 'As FIFA stated in August, it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President. FIFA welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a license to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading FIFA will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously.'

Cordeiro did not immediately respond to The Daily Mail's requests for comment. However, he declined to address his alleged role to The New York Post, claiming he was 'not aware of the story.'

In a statement to the Daily Mail, a spokesperson for the DHS said: 'On December 16, 2023, Yajarlin del Socor Fernandez, an alien from Nicaragua, was permitted entry into the United States through the now-defunct Biden-era CHNV parole program.

'Del Socor Fernandez re-applied for lawful status in December 2025 and was approved to remain in the United States until January 2027.'

Infantino, who is standing for reelection in 2027, has faced months of scrutiny

The bombshell report comes after months of scrutiny for Infantino, who faces reelection in 2027.

Infantino faced mutiny earlier this year over his secret plans – later scrapped – to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity investors including Joshua Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

It sparked uncertainty around Infantino's future after three confederations rejected his plan, which was then abandoned.

Among them was UEFA, which said it has lost confidence in Infantino and threatened to boycott future World Cups.

Cordeiro also recently quit FIFA over Infantino's commercial deals with Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital.

Infantino faced further scrutiny last month when it was alleged that Infantino personally intervened to suspend USA Folarin Balogun's World Cup red card following a call with President Trump.

In a saga that sparked condemnation from across the world, the striker was originally barred from the USA's last-16 match against Belgium, only for his ban to be sensationally suspended by the FIFA disciplinary committee following a protest by the White House. The New York Post claimed in October that Infantino told Trump in a call on July 1 that 'he would take care of it. One call and it was done.'

FIFA did not comment on the claims at the time but pointed to a July statement from Infantino, when he insisted the decision was made by 'independent' bodies acting 'autonomously.'

Despite mounting pressure over recent months, Infantino intends to stand for a fourth consecutive term next March at the FIFA Congress.

#1421. Exiled Jack Grealish RETURNS to Everton training after being dropped following boozy nights at pubs and karaoke: Ex-England star could be back in team after international break

Published: 12:34 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 14:16 EDT, 6 November 2026

Jack Grealish will return to Everton training after being dropped and exiled by David Moyes.

The 31-year-old was axed for back-to-back matches against Newcastle following a 'breach of club discipline' and is not part of the Toffees' matchday squad for the third game on the spin when they host Coventry tonight.

Grealish, who has made seven appearances since re-joining Everton for a second season-long loan spell from Man City in the summer, had been banished since failing to show up for a training session on Monday last week. It is understood staff struggled to make contact with the winger.

Grealish will now be reintegrated on a tailored training programme to regain match fitness and could be included in first-team sessions during the international break from next week.

Grealish had made four successive starts before he missed Everton's 2-0 defeat by Arsenal on October 24 due to illness.

Grealish was reported to have had back-to-back nights out prior to the Toffees' defeat in north London.

Jack Grealish, previously pictured out with a friend, was exiled by Everton but is now set to return to training with the team

David Moyes could start Grealish against Brentford after the international break

The three-time Premier League winner attended the Pride of Britain awards at the Grosvenor House hotel in London on October 19 where he presented the Child of Courage award to 12-year-old Zac Howells.

He is then reported to have finished the night of celebration off at Bam Karaoke Box, a karaoke hotspot in Victoria, central London.

According to the Sun, he stayed up until the early hours of the morning singing with his friends and enjoying the drinks on offer.

The next day, Grealish is believed to have returned to Cheshire, where he and many of his footballer friends live, to meet team-mates Jordan Pickford and Tyler Dibling at The Mauldeth pub in Wilmslow.

The trio, joined by Grealish's former City team-mate and captain Kyle Walker, where they watched Paris Saint-Germain's thrilling Champions League victory over Barcelona. A witness claimed to the Sun that they enjoyed a few drinks.

Moyes had been coy on the situation when asked about it on Thursday. He said: 'You probably know I'm not going to give any details, it is a club decision and I support that decision (for him to be punished). It is something I don't want to speak too much about.

'The one thing about Everton is that we have got really good values behind it. All the players stand up to the values and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch. From that point of view, I think the players did a brilliant job.'

Without Grealish once again, Everton are seeking to secure a third win in a row when they come up against former Toffees boss Frank Lampard and his Coventry team.

Grealish is reported to have gone on consecutive nights out after attending the Pride of Britain Awards on October 19

After the Coventry clash, Everton are next in Premier League action at Gtech Community Stadium against Brentford on November 23.

Grealish will be targeting a return in that fixture and hope he can begin to rebuild his relationship with Moyes over the next three weeks.

He has played for England 39 times and turned out for Everton on 22 occasions, scoring twice and providing six assists, with a nasty foot injury cut short his campaign last term.

#1420. Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival1. Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells2,3. The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported4,5. Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe–HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. These Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs. Vegfr2KO ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF, Vegfr2KO ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs. This work has implications for our understanding of the role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and demonstrates venousization as a mechanism of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss during angiogenesis.

VEGF is frequently targeted in clinical settings to suppress tumour angiogenesis, metastasis and retina disease6. However, resistance to VEGF-blocking antibodies arises over time, which limits the effectiveness of such treatments4,5,7,8. By contrast, resistance to loss of VEGF signalling has not been reported during physiological vascular development.

Embryos or postnatal tissues lacking activity of the VEGF signalling pathway in all cells fail to develop vessels3. VEGFR2 (encoded by the Kdr (also known as Vegfr2) gene in mice) is the most important VEGF receptor and has been shown to be essential for angiogenesis in all vascular development contexts studied so far1,9. Germline mutants for this gene completely lack blood vessels and die very early during embryonic development2, and mouse embryos chimeras formed by wild-type and Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) progenitor cells cannot form endothelial cells (ECs)10. Conditional deletion of Vegfr2 with Tie2–Cre after endothelial differentiation11, or in postnatal tissues with Cdh5–CreERT2, also strongly impairs angiogenesis12, without any evidence of genetic compensation or resistance.

Despite a large body of literature showing that VEGFR2 is essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, migration and survival, previous studies involving deletion of Vegfr2 in all ECs (Vegfr2iDEC) during embryonic or postnatal organ development could only analyse its effect on angiogenesis for a relatively short period of time. Its essential role in vascular development and hence in tissue development and organ function causes severe impairment of angiogenesis and premature lethality of Vegfr2iDEC embryos and postnatal animals; thus, such studies have been unable to determine whether ECs can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 over time or make certain organ vascular beds in the complete absence of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling.

Here we used iFlpMosaics13 and iSuRe–HadCre14 to mosaically induce and longitudinally track Vegfr2KO ECs, enabling us to assess the role of this gene during the entire embryonic and postnatal vascular development of different organs. We found that despite its essential role during the initial wave of embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is dispensable for many subsequent angiogenic processes originating from veins. Vegfr2KO ECs expand and out-compete wild-type ECs in venous vessels, which serve as a continuous source of these mutant cells for angiogenesis in most organs. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) showed that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time through upregulation of ligands for other VEGF receptors and through increased expression of venous-specific genes, particularly Nr2f2. Targeting these adaptive and resistance-associated molecular mechanisms prevents expansion of ECs following prolonged loss of VEGFR2 signalling.

Given the essential role of VEGFR2 in early angiogenesis and embryonic development, we induced mosaic loss of VEGFR2 with iFlpMosaics13 to investigate whether mutant cells could adapt and form new vessels over time. This technology enables FlpO-dependent ratiometric induction and tracking over long periods of time of cells expressing MTomato-2A-Cre (knockout for any floxed gene) or MYFP (wild type). To induce these mosaics, we used the Apln-FlpO allele, which is expressed in the first angiogenic and sprouting ECs at embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) and throughout vascular development. In female embryos, the X-chromosome-located Apln–FlpO allele is mosaically silenced15 and expressed only in a fraction (23–50%) of ECs, generating relatively few mutant and wild-type cells, which we found to be compatible with embryonic development (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a). Analysis of major organs of Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic mice showed that ECs with full loss of VEGFR2 (Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7) were able to survive and proliferate during embryonic development and until postnatal day 7 (P7), with only a relatively minor competitive disadvantage (2–7-fold) compared with wild-type cells (Fig. 1b). This competitive disadvantage was more pronounced in the lung and kidney endothelium and less so in brain ECs (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). As Apln-FlpO is constitutively active and can drive recombination at later stages of embryonic development, we also induced Vegfr2 deletion using 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) at E10.5 and E12.5 in embryos carrying Cdh5-CreERT2, iSuRe-HadCre and an iMb2-Mosaic16 control reporter that recombines independently of Vegfr2 deletion (Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). This resulted in a maximum of 1–6% recombined ECs, as opposed to 23–50% with Apln-FlpO. However, this recapitulated the trend in which brain ECs were least affected by VEGFR2 loss, followed by those in the heart, liver, lung and kidney (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

a, Schematic of iFlpMosaics induced by Apln-FlpO from E8.5 to P7. b, log2 ratio of MTomato+/MYFP+ within CD31+CD45− cells detected by FACS for the indicated organs. The absolute fold change of the ratio of Vegfr2KO ECs versus the ratio of control Tomato+ cells is indicated in red. c, Representative gating scheme for the ratiometric analysis (see also Extended Data Fig. 1a). d, Representative confocal micrographs of control and Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 retinas immunostained for Tomato, YFP and ERG (which labels EC nuclei). Heatmap, XY dot plot and charts showing the zonal distribution and percentage of Tomato+Cre+ cells when equal numbers of randomly selected YFP+ and Tomato+ cells were plotted (see method in Extended Data Fig. 3a). Right, log2 ratio of Tomato+/YFP+ cells detected in whole-mount retina immunostainings, showing an overall competitive disadvantage of Vegfr2KO cells in the mapped retinas. e, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas immunostained for ERG at P7, from pups injected with 4-OHT at P1. Heatmap, XY dot plot and charts showing distribution of MTomato+ERG+ (wild-type, Vegfr2HET or Vegfr2KO) cells in space in relation to MTomato−ERG+ (wild-type) cells. f, Bar plot contrasting the relative frequency of the indicated cells in the indicated areas and genotypes. g, log2 fold change of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 and Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 cells relative to the respective control wild-type cells. Numbers indicate fold change (×) between the two groups. Data are presented as the mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm. A, arteries; AF, angiogenic front; dist., distance; freq., frequency; IntCap, intermediate capillaries; LE, leading edge; MA, mature area; V, veins; WT, wild type.

VEGFR2 activity is essential for NOTCH activation and the development of arteries17,18,19. Arteries are formed by tip ECs20, which have the highest level of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling and guide vascular growth. Our high-resolution spatial zonation data with long-term iFlpMosaics showed that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were significantly enriched in veins and surrounding capillaries, and avoided angiogenic front capillaries or tip ECs, but were able to form arteries (Fig. 1d; see also Extended Data Fig. 3a for the heatmapping method).

To complement these results, we intercrossed the Vegfr2 floxed allele with Cdh5-CreERT2 and iSuRe-HadCre14 alleles to ensure fast (24 h; Extended Data Fig. 3b,c) and effective mosaic genetic deletion and full loss of VEGFR2 protein and downstream targets in ECs (Cdh5 expressing), after a single injection of 4-OHT. Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs were located mainly in veins and surrounding capillaries, as well as in the more proximal and mature segments of retina arteries (Fig. 1e). This indicates that when Vegfr2KO ECs are induced in the initial retina sprouting plexus at P1, they can make arteries forming from P1 to P3. However, owing to their inability to continue to sprout and form tip cells at the leading edge, they cannot participate in the subsequent arterial development process occurring from P3 to P7, which in the retina is dependent on incorporation of new tip cells21.

Notably, compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1−P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front capillaries (Fig. 1f,g) and were still able to make arteries. This suggests that embryonic Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs can adapt to long-term loss of VEGFR2 and contribute to venous vascular growth, tip cells and arteries at postnatal stages.

We next investigated how Vegfr2KO ECs could compete with wild-type cells and contribute to growing vascular networks over long periods of time, given the proposed important role of this pathway in EC proliferation1,22. During angiogenesis, there are two main locations for EC proliferation: the capillary angiogenic front and veins (Fig. 2a). We found that the surviving Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs proliferated (as determined by Ki-67 detection) as well as wild-type cells in postnatal brain, heart and lung vessels (Fig. 2b).

a, Representative confocal micrograph of a control P7 retina immunostained for the proliferation marker Ki-67 and the EC nuclear marker ERG. The chart shows the frequency of Ki-67+ERG+ (pink pseudocolored) nuclei in different vascular zones. b, Representative confocal micrographs of the indicated organs of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 mice at P7, immunostained for YFP, Tomato, ERG and Ki-67. Yellow arrows indicate YFP+Ki-67+ cells and magenta arrows Tomato+Ki-67+ ECs. c, Representative confocal micrographs of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20 retinas induced at P1 and analysed at P20. Heatmap, XY dot plot and chart showing that Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20 ECs grow in veins and surrounding capillaries. d,e, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas immunostained for cleaved caspase 3 and respective quantification charts, showing increased apoptosis of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 but not Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs. f, Representative confocal micrographs of the indicated organs of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 mice induced at P4 and analysed at P7. Arrows indicate recombined ECs (Tomato+) that are Ki-67+ (yellow) and Ki-67− (white), respectively. Chart shows the percentage of Tomato+ ECs positive for Ki-67. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm (a,c–e), 50 μm (b,f). Cap., capillaries; CC3, cleaved caspase 3; Ctrl, control; DCap, distal capillaries; IntCap, intermediate capillaries; PCap, proximal capillaries. *Adjusted P < 0.05.

Venous ECs provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis and these migrate against the blood flow to capillaries and then towards arterial vessels20,23,24. When we induced Vegfr2KO ECs for longer periods of time, from P1 to P20 (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20), we observed that mutant cells stayed in the vein stem, where they proliferated and gradually outcompeted wild-type cells, which moved outwards towards the VEGF-rich leading edge and adjacent capillaries (Fig. 2c). This preferential occupation of the venous stem niche by Vegfr2KO ECs allowed them to continue proliferating for longer periods of time and later to form most of the perivenous capillary vessels and the deeper vascular plexus that developed during a second wave of VEGF-independent angiogenesis from P7 to P20 (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). This was consistent with previous findings showing that the tip cells that dive to form the deeper vascular plexus in the retina lack expression of the VEGFR2 signalling target gene Esm1; instead, their migration is dependent on other pathways such as Alk or TGFβ and WNT signalling25,26,27.

Together, these data show that VEGFR2 function is essential for the initial sprouting angiogenesis driven by high VEGF levels in hypoxic embryos and organs but not for the development of veins and perivenous capillaries or the subsequent steps of capillary angiogenesis and remodelling that occur after the first vascular plexus is formed in various organs. Thus, by forming veins, which are known to provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis23, Vegfr2KO ECs can continue to proliferate and participate in subsequent steps of vascular development for long periods of time.

We previously observed that the distribution of Vegfr2KO ECs in the retina plexus at P7 differed between animals with long-term (Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7) and short-term (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7) mosaic deletion of Vegfr2. Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front than Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs (Fig. 1f,g). Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs also proliferated normally (Fig. 2b). Therefore, we hypothesized that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs might be genetically rewired and adapt over time to loss of the most important receptor for VEGF.

To assess the early response of ECs to loss of VEGFR2, we first analysed apoptosis markers in growing retina vessels, as VEGFR2 has been shown to regulate EC survival. Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 mice showed a very significant increase in the number of apoptotic (cleaved caspase 3 positive) ECs (Fig. 2d). This apoptosis was a reaction to the acute loss of VEGFR2, as Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 or even Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 mice did not show any apoptotic ECs (Fig. 2e), suggesting adaptation of the surviving cells over time. When the acute loss of Vegfr2 was induced in all ECs, we observed an immediate depletion of Vegfr2KO ECs from the VEGF-high angiogenic front, but not from veins or more mature vessels (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Therefore, even though many ECs in the retina plexus showed upregulation of the apoptosis marker in the first days after Vegfr2 loss (Fig. 2d), only the angiogenic ECs that were exposed to high VEGF levels at the time of Vegfr2 deletion died (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

We also found that Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs were significantly less proliferative than control cells only in the heart and kidney (Fig. 2f), whereas the proliferation of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs was similar to that of controls (Fig. 2b). This suggests that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time and are later able to proliferate in these organs. In the newborn retina, deletion of Vegfr2 did not affect the proliferation of surviving ECs in any segment (Extended Data Fig. 4d), indicating that in this organ VEGFR2 mainly controls EC migration and survival, not proliferation.

Together, our data suggest that ECs lacking VEGF signalling during active angiogenesis suffer an acute VEGFR2 withdrawal effect, followed by a period of adaptation to the loss, after which they can form new vessels. ECs that are more distant from the VEGF source, and therefore have less VEGF signalling, adapt better to the loss and can expand over time, particularly in veins and perivenous vessels.

To further confirm the insensitivity of more mature ECs to loss of VEGFR2 signalling, we deleted Vegfr2 in several adult quiescent vascular beds for 2 weeks. Only the quiescent sinusoidal liver endothelium showed a strong sensitivity and loss of Vegfr2KO ECs, whereas only the kidney endothelium showed significantly lower proliferation (Extended Data Fig. 5), suggesting that only fenestrated or discontinuous mature endothelial vessels present in these organs remain sensitive to VEGFR2 loss.

Given the observed differences in the biology of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 and Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs, we performed scRNA-seq of these cells and respective control Tomato+ cells to identify possible differences in their transcriptional profiles and potential mechanisms of adaptation to loss of VEGFR2 signalling in distinct organ vascular beds.

Although VEGFR2 is a central regulator of angiogenesis and widely regarded as essential for EC biology, Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs showed only modest changes in their transcriptome (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 6), even though VEGFR2 protein and downstream signalling were lost already within the first 24 h following 4-OHT administration (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). In general, the expression of genes related to sprouting or tip cell biology was decreased, whereas that of genes related to apoptosis and vascular permeability was increased in all organs analysed (Fig. 3a,b). However, considerable differences were observed among organs.

In the brain, clusters of proliferating (S–G2–M) ECs expressing venous capillaries markers were increased after Vegfr2 deletion for 3 days (Fig. 3c–f). This was consistent with higher clonal expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs from P1 to P20 in this organ (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Clusters comprising capillary and activated or angiogenic ECs (with high expression of Apln, Adm, Mcam, Lamb1 and Angpt2) were decreased (Fig. 3d–f). In total, only 569 genes were significantly deregulated (Fig. 3g). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed an increase in the expression of E2F and MYC target genes, as well as G2M, DNA repair and mitotic spindle genes, confirming the increase in EC proliferation (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7a). The expression of most tip cell marker genes was decreased in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 brain ECs (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 6a–f).

In contrast to those in the brain, Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 capillary ECs in the heart were significantly less proliferative (Fig. 3j–m and Extended Data Fig. 7b), matching the 54% decrease in Ki-67 percentage observed in sections (Fig. 2f). The proportion of mutant ECs found in bigger vessels (arteries and veins) was increased 2- to 4-fold (Fig. 3k–m), suggesting a proportional fast depletion of Vegfr2KO capillary ECs in only 3 days. Unlike in the brain, GSEA of Vegfr2KO heart ECs showed the expected decrease in expression of E2F and MYC target genes, as well as decreases in expression of G2M, mitotic spindle and tip cell genes (Fig. 3n–p), in accordance with the decrease in proliferation and sprouting of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 heart ECs. Vegfr2KO heart ECs also showed upregulation of genes related to apoptosis and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Fig. 3n–p), as has been shown previously for ECs losing ERK signalling28.

In contrast to the results for brain and heart, we found no significant difference in the proportions of proliferating cells among control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs in lung (Extended Data Fig. 6g–j), as shown by immunostaining for Ki-67 and clonal analysis (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 7c). The proportion of the vein cluster was only slightly increased, and the capillary cluster was slightly decreased. Despite the lack of significant changes in cluster proportions, GSEA showed increased TNF signalling through NF-κB, hypoxia and reactive oxygen species signalling and a decrease in the interferon response (Extended Data Fig. 6k,l). In lung, there was only a small trend of decreased expression of tip cell marker genes (Extended Data Fig. 6m), and several genes related to apoptosis were upregulated (Extended Data Fig. 6l,m).

In the kidney, similar to the heart, Vegfr2 deletion for 3 days led to an increase in the relative proportion of ECs of bigger vessels (arteries and veins), suggesting fast depletion of a fraction of capillary ECs in only 3 days (Extended Data Fig. 6n–q). Proliferation and clonal expansion of kidney capillary ECs were also reduced (Extended Data Figs. 6o,q and 7d), as shown by immunostaining for Ki-67 (Fig. 2f). GSEA showed the expected decrease in expression of E2F, G2M and mitotic spindle genes and an increase in the expression of genes related to p53, xenobiotic metabolism and apoptosis (Extended Data Fig. 6r,s), indicative of cellular stress in kidney ECs after short-term Vegfr2 deletion from P4 to P7. Similar to brain and heart ECs, the expression of tip cell marker genes was also decreased in kidney Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (Extended Data Fig. 6t).

Following our analysis of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, we performed scRNA-seq of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs of distinct organs to identify potential differences in gene expression related to long-term adaptation of cells to loss of VEGFR2 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). In contrast to Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs exhibited predominantly upregulation rather than downregulation of genes, including marked upregulation of several venous-enriched genes (compare Figs. 3a,b and 4a).

In contrast to brain Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had increased frequencies of venous capillaries (Extended Data Fig. 8b–d) and marked upregulation of the key regulator of vein specification Nr2f2 (Extended Data Fig. 8e). Similarly to Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had decreased frequencies of activated and sprouting ECs and lower expression levels of several tip cell genes (Extended Data Fig. 8c–e). The number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), particularly upregulated genes, was much higher (1,621 versus 569 DEGs) in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs; this is likely to represent a long-term adaptation response to loss of VEGFR2 function (compare Extended Data Fig. 8e with Fig. 3g). Whereas in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 brain ECs, genetic pathways related to EC proliferation and cellular activity (E2F targets, MYC, oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis) were paradoxically increased, in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs they were decreased (compare Extended Data Fig. 8e,f with Fig. 3g,h). This suggests that brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs adapt to the long-term loss of VEGFR2 signalling through a decrease in cellular activity and upregulation of Nr2f2, which probably decreases their dependence on VEGF signalling for growth and survival.

In the heart, we confirmed previous histological analysis showing that heart Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs proliferated at levels similar to those of control cells and markedly higher than those of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (compare Fig. 3k,m with Fig. 4b–d). They also had many more DEGs (1,750 DEGs versus 242 DEGs), particularly upregulated genes (compare Fig. 3n with Fig. 4e). GSEA showed increased epithelial–mesenchymal transition, KRAS signalling and angiogenesis, and less expression of metabolic-pathway-related genes (Fig. 4e,f), as seen in the brain. Expression of tip or activated EC genes was not as compromised in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (Fig. 4g), suggesting some adaptation over time to the loss of VEGFR2. Notably, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were four times more frequent in veins (Fig. 4c,d), similar to our observations in the retina (Fig. 1d–f), confirming that mosaic loss of Vegfr2 causes mutant ECs to expand more in veins. In comparison with Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs showed strong upregulation of most venous-specific genes, including Nr2f2, Fbln2, Igf1 and Vwf (Fig. 4e). This was not caused only by the increased proportion of venous ECs in these mutants; capillary and angiogenic ECs also showed much higher expression of these venous marker genes, indicating venousization of mutant Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 capillary ECs over time (Fig. 4h,p).

In the lung, the same adaptation and venousization of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs was observed. Mutant cells were four times more frequent in veins (Fig. 4i–k), and even capillary or CAR4+ ECs showed significantly upregulated expression of lung venous genes including Vegfc, Nr2f2, Vwf and Fbln2 (Fig. 4l,m and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). Similar to findings in the other organs, lung Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had significantly more DEGs than lung Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (3,116 vs 502), particularly upregulated genes (compare Extended Data Fig. 6k with Fig. 4m). Volcano plots and GSEA revealed upregulation of many venous-enriched and epithelial–mesenchymal transition genes, as well as oestrogen response genes. Lung Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had lower expression of E2F targets and metabolism genes, as seen in the other organs (Fig. 4m,n).

Notably, deletion of Vegfr2 for 2 weeks in adult organ blood vessels did not induce venousization of adult Vegfr2KO ECs; instead, it decreased expression of venous genes (Extended Data Fig. 8g–u), indicating that upregulation of Nr2f2 and venousization may represent a long-term adaptative response to VEGFR2 loss that occurs only during active angiogenesis.

The scRNA-seq data indicating venousization of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs over time were confirmed by immunostaining for the master regulator of venous development NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII) (Fig. 4o,p and Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). To understand the venousization requirement for long-term adaptation of Vegfr2KO ECs, we also analysed Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic Vegfr2Flox/Flox, Nr2f2Flox/Flox mice. When ECs lacked both VEGFR2 and NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), their capacity to expand was significantly reduced, particularly in veins (Fig. 4q,r and Extended Data Fig. 9e). This suggests that endothelial venousization is a key mechanism of adaptation to long-term loss of VEGFR2 signalling during angiogenesis that enables mutant cells to expand in veins and derived vessels over time.

In addition to analysing embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, we tested the capacity of Vegfr2KO ECs to form tumour vessels over a period of 2 weeks. When Vegfr2 deletion was induced a few days before tumour implantation, Vegfr2IECKO-day-3–adult ECs formed tumour vessels mainly at the tumour border and failed to penetrate deeper into the tumour, where they were 5.2-fold less frequent than control ECs (Extended Data Fig. 10a). By contrast, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–adult ECs, which had undergone venousization throughout embryonic and postnatal development, could better reach inside the tumour and were only 2.6-fold less frequent than control ECs (Extended Data Fig. 10b). These data show that although VEGFR2 signalling promotes tumour angiogenesis, ECs can progressively adapt to its absence and sustain tumour angiogenesis.

In addition to our findings with respect to venousization, we observed significant upregulation of expression of other VEGF receptor ligands in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs (Extended Data Fig. 11a), including PGF and VEGFC, which bind and activate VEGFR1 and VEGFR3, respectively1. In the absence of VEGFR2, VEGFR1 is the only other receptor that can bind VEGFA. However, all studies so far have shown that VEGFR1 kinase activity is too weak29,30, whereas its extracellular soluble form (sVEGFR1 or sFLT1) acts as a strong VEGF decoy receptor31. Therefore, when VEGFR2 is present, VEGFR1 is considered to mainly antagonize VEGFA–VEGFR2 signalling and angiogenesis. However, we found that Vegfr1 expression was much higher in ECs in the brain, the organ least sensitive to VEGFR2 loss (Extended Data Fig. 11b). We also found that during postnatal angiogenesis, sVegfr1 showed 2–5-fold lower expression than the membrane full-length Vegfr1 (flVegfr1) mRNA form, except in brain ECs (Extended Data Fig. 11c), suggesting a potential signalling role for flVEGFR1.

To evaluate whether VEGFR1 could compensate for loss of VEGFR2, we induced mosaic codeletion of Vegfr1 and Vegfr2 in ECs with iSuRe-HadCre from P1 to P7 (Vegfr1/2IECKO-P1–P7). Compared with Vegfr2KO ECs, Vegfr1/2KO ECs showed a further decrease in ability to migrate and form retina capillaries, but not veins or arteries (Fig. 5a). In veins, Vegfr1/2KO ECs could clonally expand (Extended Data Fig. 11d). Brain and heart Vegfr1/2KO ECs proliferated less than Vegfr2KO ECs at P7 (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). Deletion of both Vegfr2 and Vegfr1 had a stronger effect on endothelial and pup survival (Extended Data Fig. 11g–i), confirming the requirement for VEGFR1 signalling when VEGFR2 is absent in capillaries. Mosaic deletion of Vegfr1 alone also led to a decrease in EC migration towards the VEGF-rich front (Extended Data Fig. 11j). In contrast to deletion of Vegfr1 in all ECs, mosaic loss of Vegfr1 in single ECs did not increase VEGF signalling (as assessed by ESM1 expression), probably owing to normal levels of sFLT1 present in the mostly wild-type microenvironment (Extended Data Fig. 11k).
