In addition to VEGFR1 and VEGFR2, ECs express VEGFR3. Previous studies have shown that VEGFR3 is strongly expressed by capillary and venous ECs; however, this receptor cannot bind VEGF (VEGFA), only VEGFC and VEGFD, which are key molecules for lymphangiogenesis but less relevant to blood vessel angiogenesis. Vegfr2IECKO-E8.5–P7 ECs showed very strong upregulation of VEGFC (Extended Data Fig. 11a), which could signal to VEGFR3 in the absence of VEGFR2. Loss of VEGFR3 in growing retina ECs has been shown to induce angiogenesis, suggesting that VEGFR3 negatively regulates VEGFR2 signalling32. However, single Vegfr3IECKO-P1–P7 ECs also had decreased ability to migrate and reach the leading edge (Extended Data Fig. 11l–n). Arterial ECs and smooth muscle cells express high levels of VEGFC33,34,35 a ligand that can bind both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3. Compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1-P7 ECs, Vegfr2/3IECKO-P1-P7 ECs had a very similar zonal distribution in capillaries and veins (Fig. 5b) but a 3.4-fold lower frequency in arteries (Fig. 5c); this suggests an important role for VEGFC to VEGFR3 signalling in arterial mobilization or survival, but only when VEGFR2 signalling is absent. Loss of both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 did not compromise the proliferation of surviving ECs in any vascular segments (Fig. 5d).

We also observed that Vegfr2KO ECs had decreased VEGFR3 expression only at the angiogenic front, where VEGFA levels are highest. By contrast Vegfr1/2KO ECs showed strong downregulation of VEGFR3 in all vascular segments, except in arteries (Fig. 5e). Vegfr1/2/3IECKO-P1-P7 ECs behaved similarly to Vegfr1/2IECKO-P1-P7 ECs, except for a pronounced decrease in formation of arterial vessels (Fig. 5f–h). Taken together, our findings show that in the absence of VEGFR2 signalling, VEGFR1 is required to sustain VEGFR3 expression and growth and migration of capillary ECs. In arteries, VEGFR3 continues to be expressed after loss of VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 and regulates development of arteries when the other VEGFA receptors are missing. Notably, vein ECs can survive and clonally expand in the complete absence of all VEGF receptor signalling (Fig. 5i).

Our study challenges the longstanding view that VEGFR2 signalling is indispensable for endothelial proliferation, migration and sprouting during angiogenesis1,22. By using iFlpMosaics to induce ratiometric genetic mosaics of wild-type and Vegfr2KO ECs, we demonstrated that these mutant cells are capable of surviving, proliferating and competing with wild-type ECs during the entire embryonic and postnatal organ growth period (Extended Data Fig. 12). Contrary to previous studies suggesting that VEGFR2 is required for all forms of vascular differentiation and development10,12,36, our findings indicate that VEGFR2-independent mechanisms support angiogenesis in certain vascular beds, particularly the long-term development of venous and perivenous capillaries.

We identified significant organ-specific differences in adaptation to acute loss of VEGFR2 signalling (Extended Data Fig. 12a), thereby extending previous findings37,38. Whereas angiogenic retina ECs were strongly affected, brain ECs were the least affected, retaining high angiogenic potential, partially because of VEGFR1 compensation (Extended Data Fig. 12b). By contrast, postnatal heart, kidney and liver ECs were more sensitive to acute withdrawal of VEGFR2, showing partial depletion of Vegfr2KO ECs in capillaries, as well as a partial reduction in proliferation. The postnatal lung showed a distinct response, with no major changes in EC proliferation or cluster composition but instead a shift in transcriptional programs towards inflammation and metabolic adaptations. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of endothelial responses across different vascular beds and suggest that organ-specific factors influence EC resilience to perturbations in VEGF signalling.

The long-term adaptation of Vegfr2KO ECs was a notable observation. Although these cells initially had a competitive disadvantage during early embryonic and postnatal sprouting angiogenesis stages, they ultimately expanded and outcompeted wild-type cells in venous and perivenous regions, indicating that alternative pathways support their survival and proliferation in this niche. Veins are known to provide a continuous source of ECs for capillary angiogenesis and later arterialization20,23, and this venous dominance of Vegfr2KO ECs allows them to compete with wild-type cells over time. Our scRNA-seq analysis of different vascular beds further showed that ECs with prolonged loss of VEGFR2 exhibited a significant shift towards a venous transcriptional signature (venousization), marked by upregulation of many venous genes, including Nr2f2, a master regulator of veins development24,39. Vegfr2KONr2f2KO ECs were significantly less able to expand, particularly in veins, showing that venousization is a key adaptation mechanism that enables Vegfr2KO ECs to persist and contribute to vascular development (Extended Data Fig. 12c,d).

In addition to venousization, our findings demonstrate the compensatory roles of VEGFR1 and VEGFR3 in supporting survival and growth signalling when VEGFR2 is absent (Extended Data Fig. 12b). Previously, VEGFR1 has mainly been reported to negatively regulate VEGFR2 signalling during angiogenesis, because its soluble secreted version sFLT1 or VEGFR1 is a decoy receptor of VEGF1,22. In our mosaic Vegfr1KO and Vegfr1/2KO experiments, sFLT1 levels in the microenvironment were normal; this led us to find that membrane or full-length VEGFR1 acted as a positive regulator of angiogenesis and partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss, supporting both EC survival and migration. The mosaic single loss of VEGFR3 also showed that this receptor was a positive regulator of EC migration towards the leading edge. This was consistent with results obtained using VEGFR3-blocking antibodies40; however, our findings were contrary to results from pan-endothelial Vegfr3KO genetics experiments32 in which the receptor was lost from all ECs. In this case, VEGFC and/or VEGFD bioavailability in the whole body increases, thereby increasing VEGFC–VEGFR2 signalling, whereas in low-frequency Vegfr3KO mosaics this does not occur. In addition, Vegfr2/3KO ECs mobilized less to the angiogenic front and had decreased arterialization when compared with Vegfr2KO ECs. The ability of these alternative VEGF receptors to sustain EC survival, migration and proliferation at the single-cell level indicates potential functional plasticity and compensation within the VEGF signalling network, as suggested previously by studies using classical full-tissue conditional genetics12,32,37.

An important implication of our study is that EC sensitivity to VEGFR2 loss varies depending on the vascular context and the time since the loss. We found that acute loss of VEGFR2 during active angiogenesis resulted in significant EC depletion in the first 3 days, particularly depletion of tip cells and other ECs at the angiogenic front, where VEGF signalling is highest. However, Vegfr2KO ECs in VEGF-low areas and those that had undergone long-term adaptation were able to persist and even contribute to a substantial portion of capillary vessels, particularly those around veins. This suggests that ECs experiencing prolonged VEGFR2 deficiency undergo venousization in VEGF-low areas, enabling them to survive and then grow in the absence of canonical VEGF signalling. Our tumour models showed that Vegfr2KO ECs could form tumour vessels, particularly if they had previously undergone venousization during embryonic angiogenesis. The use of ratiometric and trackable iFlpMosaics was key to obtaining these findings.

Our work may also provide biomarkers and insights into resistance mechanisms to anti-VEGF therapies5,41,42,43. Adaptation of ECs to VEGFR2 loss by engaging alternative venous-related angiogenic pathways may also occur in tumours. If this is confirmed, therapeutic strategies that simultaneously block the compensatory and venous-related pathways identified here may be necessary to overcome resistance to anti-VEGF treatments.

In conclusion, our study reshapes our understanding of VEGFR2-dependent angiogenesis by demonstrating that ECs possess intrinsic mechanisms to adapt to long-term absence of VEGFR2 signalling. The discovery of endothelial venousization and compensatory VEGF receptor signalling provides a new framework for investigation of alternative modes of vascular development and resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

All mouse husbandry and experiments were conducted using protocols approved by local animal ethics committees and authorities (Comunidad Autónoma de Madrid and Universidad Autónoma de Madrid CAM-PROEX 164.8/20, PROEX 293.1/22 and PROEX-288.7/24). The mouse colonies were maintained in racked individual ventilation cages according to current national legislation. The mice had dust- and pathogen-free bedding and sufficient nesting and environmental enrichment material for development of species-specific behaviour. All mice had ad libitum access to food and water in environmental conditions of 45–65% relative humidity, temperatures of 21–24 °C and a 12 h/12 h light–dark cycle. For preservation of animal welfare, mouse health was monitored with an animal health surveillance programme that followed the recommendations of the Federation of European Laboratory Animal Science Associations for specific-pathogen-free facilities

We used Mus musculus lines mostly on the C57BL6 genetic background, with some having a fraction of 129SV, or B6CBAF1 or DBA genetic backgrounds. Mice were backcrossed to C57Bl6 for several generations. To generate mice for analysis, we intercrossed mice aged between 7 weeks and 30 weeks. We did not anticipate any influence of mouse sex on our data, and both female and male mice were analysed. The initial sample size was determined taking into account the ‘3 Rs’ for animal experimentation and the expected experimental variability based on protocols (published and our own; refs. 13 and 14). The final sample size was defined a posteriori after statistical analysis of the data. Sample size and related statistical analysis methods are indicated in the figure legends or source data. No randomization or blinding was used, and the animals or tissues were selected for analysis on the basis of their genotype, the detected Cre- or FlpO-dependent recombination frequency and the quality of multiplex immunostaining.

The following mouse lines were used and intercrossed: Tg(Cdh5–CreERT2)44, Tg(iSuRe–HadCre)14, Vegfr2flox (ref. 45), Vegfr1flox (ref. 46), Vegfr3flox (ref. 47) (for this work, we also generated a new Vegfr3flox allele in the Vegfr1/2flox background, as indicated below), Nr2f2flox (ref. 48), iMb2–Mosaic16, Apln–FlpO15 and the iFlpMosaic lines13 (R26-iFlpMTomato-2A-Cre/MYFP and Tg-iFlpChromatin–Mosaic).

To generate a new Vegfr3flox allele combined with Vegfr1/2flox we injected Cas9, donor DNAs containing LoxP sites and guide RNAs (TGTTAAAGACACGCATACCT/AGG and AGATGGGGTGAATAGCTCCG/TGG) into mouse eggs of the Vegfr1/2flox iSuRe–HadCre Cdh5–CreERT2 line. Founders containing LoxP sites flanking exon 1 in the same chromosome were screened by PCR, and inducible Vegfr3 deletion was confirmed by PCR and immunostaining for the VEGFR3 protein (Extended Data Fig. 11l,m).

For induction of CreERT2 activity in adult mice, 1 g tamoxifen (Sigma-Aldrich, P5648_1G) was dissolved in 50 ml corn oil (stock tamoxifen concentration, 20 mg m−1), and aliquots were stored at −20 °C. Animals received intraperitoneal injections of 100 µl of this stock solution (total dose: 2 mg tamoxifen per animal at 80 mg kg−1), as indicated in the figures. To activate recombination in pups, we injected 4-OHT at the indicated stages at a dose of 40 mg kg−1. For double (VEGFR1/2, VEGFR2/3) or triple (VEGFR1/2/3) mutants, 4-OHT was administered to pups at 15 mg kg−1. For activation of recombination during embryogenesis, pregnant dams were induced with 0.25 mg 4-OHT supplemented with 0.125 mg progesterone at E10.5 and E12.5. All mouse lines and primer sequences required for genotyping are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Lewis carcinoma cells were obtained from ATCC and cultured in DMEM (Gibco) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1× penicillin–streptomycin and 2 mM glutamine at 37 °C, 5% CO2. The cell medium was changed every other day, and cells were passaged every 3–4 days. Cells were routinely screened for mycoplasma contamination. Cells were used for tumour inoculation when they were at 75–80% confluency. Cells were trypsinized and resuspended in Matrigel solution (Biosciences). Age-matched (15–20 weeks) and sex-matched mice were injected subcutaneously with 5 × 105 tumour cells suspended in Matrigel (Corning, 354234). Mice were euthanized after 15 days, and tumours (less than 2 cm3) were extracted, fixed and processed for immunostaining.

For immunostaining of mouse retinas, eyes were dissected from mouse pups and fixed by incubation with agitation for 20 min in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (diluted from a stock of 16% PFA; EMS 15710). After two washes in PBS (5 min each), retinas were microdissected from the eyes; 4 incisions were made to enable later flat mounting, and the retinas were refixed in 4% PFA for 45 min with agitation. After two washes in PBS, retinas were blocked and permeabilized by incubation for 1 h in PBST (0.3% Triton X-100, 3% FBS and 3% donkey serum in PBS). Samples were then incubated with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) diluted in PBST overnight at 4 °C with agitation. The next day, retinas were washed 5 times for 20 min in PBST diluted 1:2. Then, they were incubated in the same solution for 2 h at room temperature with Alexa-conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2). After washing (3 × 15 min) in PBS containing 0.15% Triton X-100, retinas were washed (2 × 15 min) in PBS and flat mounted in Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). For combination of rabbit anti-ERG-647 with other antibodies produced in rabbit, retinas were incubated with the Alexa 594 AffiniPure Fab Fragment Donkey Anti-Rabbit secondary antibody, then with 5% rabbit serum for 30 min at room temperature, and finally with rabbit anti-ERG-647.

For collection of organs and histological analysis, mice were euthanized in CO2 chambers, and 10 ml of PBS was injected into the left ventricles, followed by perfusion with 3.7–4% formaldehyde (ITW Reagents, 252931) at pH 7. The explanted organs were postfixed for 2 h in 4% PFA (Thermo Scientific, 043368.9M) in PBS at 4 °C with gentle rotation. After three washes in PBS for 10 min each, the organs were stored overnight in 30% sucrose (Sigma) in PBS. The organs were then embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound (Sakura) and frozen at −80 °C. Cryosections of 30 µm were cut on a cryostat (Leica), washed three times for 10 min each time in PBS, and blocked and permeabilized in PBS containing 10% donkey serum (Millipore), 10% FBS and 1% Triton X-100. The primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) were diluted in the same buffer and incubated with sections overnight at 4 °C. This step was followed by three 10-min washes in PBS and incubation for 2 h with conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) and 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) in PBS at room temperature. After three washes in PBS, the sections were mounted with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). For combination of rabbit anti-ERG-647 with other antibodies produced in rabbit, retinas were incubated first with the other primary rabbit antibodies, followed by Alexa 594 AffiniPure Fab Fragment Donkey Anti-Rabbit secondary antibody, then rabbit epitopes blocked with 5% rabbit serum for 30 min at room temperature, and finally incubated with rabbit anti-ERG-647.

For confocal scanning, immunostained organ sections or whole-mount retinas were imaged at high resolution with a Leica SP8 Navigator confocal microscope fitted with a ×10 or ×40 objective. Individual fields or tiles of large areas were acquired. All images shown are representative of the results obtained for each group and experiment. Animals were dissected and processed under identical conditions. Phenotypes or signal intensities were compared using images obtained with the same laser excitation and confocal scanner detection settings. We used ImageJ/Fiji v.1.54f to threshold, select and quantify the objects in confocal micrographs.

For arteriovenous mapping of ERG-labelled control and mutant ECs (Extended Data Fig. 3a), a semiautomatic Fiji script (available at https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab) was developed. First, six regions of interest were manually defined by the user: artery, vein, mature capillaries between the established arteries and veins, intermediate capillaries, angiogenic front and leading edge. ERG labelling was used to segment endothelial nuclei and classify each nucleus according to reporter or marker positivity (determined by the percentage of pixels within each nucleus above a given intensity threshold level), and the XY coordinates of nuclei were extracted. Then, arterial, venous, distal and proximal arteriovenous boundaries were defined by the user to determine the relative position of each segmented nucleus to each arteriovenous field boundary; this enabled compilation of data extracted from different arteriovenous fields into a single XY dot plot or heatmap.

The data collected in Fiji were post-analysed in R (v.4.5.2) for generation of graphs representing the spatial distribution of the cells of interest. For the XY plots and heatmaps, samples were randomly subsetted to enable us to display equal numbers of control and mutant cells (MYFP+ versus MTomato+ in the Apln–FlpO, iFlpMosaic background, and MTomato− versus MTomato+ in the Cdh5–CreERT2, iSuRe–HadCre background); this was to make clear the zonation differences between control and mutant cells. For visualization with XY dot plots, 2,000 randomly selected cells of each group were plotted; for the heatmap generation, the maximal number of cells (determined by the cell type (control or mutant) with fewer cells) was used. The percentage of each cell type in each arteriovenous region was calculated given its spatial distribution per field (Extended Data Fig. 3a).

We generated Fiji macro Script_Reporter_MarkerDetection_Mapping.ijm for spatial mapping of ERG and/or quantification of EC colocalization with reporters (MYFP or MTomato) and other markers (Ki-67) as in Figs. 1, 2, 5. R scripts were used for data quantification and heatmapping (Script_Spatial Heatmap; Figs. 1, 2, 5 and Extended Data Figs. 3, 4, 11) and are available at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab). Fiji, Adobe Photoshop CC 24.1.0 and Adobe Illustrator CC v.27.1.1 were used for downstream image processing, analysis and illustration.

To quantify the clonal expansion of single ECs expressing the iSuRe–HadCre and the Tg-iFlpChromatin–Mosaic alleles, we segmented and analysed images with MTomato+H2B-Cherry+, MTomato+H2B-EGFP+ or MTomato+HA-H2B-Cerulean+ signals with the Clone_Identification_Quantification script, deposited at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab/).

Postnatal and adult tissues were dissociated before fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). Enzymatic digestion was carried out at 37 °C for 20 min using a solution containing 2.5 mg ml−1 collagenase type I (Thermo Fisher), 2.5 mg ml−1 dispase II (Thermo Fisher) and 50 μg ml−1 DNase I (Roche). Following dissociation, samples were pelleted by centrifugation (450g, 4 °C, 5 min). Pellets were gently resuspended in 1× blood lysis buffer (BioLegend, 420301) and incubated on ice for 5 min for lysis of erythroid cells. After lysis, cells were passed through a 70-μm cell strainer and centrifuged again (450g, 4 °C, 5 min). Cells were resuspended in antibody incubation solution (PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+, supplemented with 2% dialysed FBS; Biowest, X0515), with primary antibodies (APC rat anti-mouse CD31 and APC-Cy7 anti-CD45; Supplementary Table 2) only or with the addition of Hashtag oligo (HTO) antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) when scRNA-seq was performed. Samples were then incubated at 4 °C with gentle agitation for 20 min.

After immunolabelling, cells were centrifuged (450g, 4 °C, 5 min), washed with antibody incubation solution, centrifuged again and resuspended in sorting buffer (10% FBS in PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+). Stained cells were maintained on ice until acquisition. DAPI (5 mg ml−1) was added immediately before FACS analysis. Cells were analysed using an LSRFortessa cell analyser or sorted using a FACS Aria Cell Sorter (BD Biosciences). For an example of the FACS gating strategy, see Extended Data Fig. 1a. BD FACSDiva v.8.0.1 and FlowJo v.10 were used for data acquisition and analysis.

For RNA-seq analysis, APC rat anti-mouse CD31 (which labels ECs), APC-Cy7 rat anti-CD45 (which labels blood cells) and HTO antibodies (BD Biosciences) (Supplementary Table 2) were used together to hashtag and distinguish the different organ Tomato+CD31+ ECs when loaded on the same 10x Genomics port (Extended Data Figs. 6a and 8a). After antibody incubation, samples were washed twice with antibody incubation solution, centrifuged (450g, 5 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in sorting buffer (10% FBS in PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+). Stained cells were maintained on ice until acquisition. Immediately before FACS analysis, DAPI (5 mg ml−1) was added, and the cell suspension was passed slowly through a 70-µm cell strainer attached to a 1-ml syringe for removal of aggregates. Live, DAPI-negative, CD31+CD45− and endogenous-reporter-positive cells were sorted into cold 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tubes containing 300 µl of sorting buffer. Cells were collected using a 100-µm nozzle at 20 PSI in high-purity mode with a flow rate of fewer than 3,000 events per second to preserve cell viability and minimize contamination. After sorting, cells were pelleted at 500g for 5 min at 4 °C and resuspended in 30–40 µl cell-capture buffer (Ca2+- and Mg2+-free PBS supplemented with 0.04% ultrapure bovine serum albumin; Thermo Fisher, AM2616). Viability and cell concentration were determined using a Countess 3 Automated Cell Counter (Thermo Fisher Scientific) before loading of the 10x Genomics port.

Single-cell suspensions were loaded on to the 10x Genomics Chromium Controller system for encapsulation into emulsion droplets. The 10x Genomics Chromium single-cell 3′ RNA-seq library preparation and sequencing were carried out at the CNIC Genomics Unit according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Each port was loaded with 20,000 to 50,000 cells. Final libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 platform, with software v.1.7.2.

scRNA-seq data were aligned and quality controlled by the CNIC Bioinformatics Unit using Cell Ranger (v.8 and v.9). Clustering, cell type identification and downstream analysis were performed by I.G.-G. The following pipeline was applied for transcript alignment, quantification, quality control and cell type classification.

Reference transcriptomes were generated using the Ensembl GRCm38 mouse genome, build version 98 (sep2019.archive.ensembl.org). Genes metadata were obtained from the corresponding Ensembl BioMart archive. To enable downstream analysis of gene deletion efficiency and soluble versus full-length isoform abundance, we appended Vegfr2 (also known as Kdr) exon 3, Kdr exon 30, Vegfr1 (also known as Flt1) exon 13b and Flt1 exon 30 to the reference transcriptome as custom metadata features. Gene annotations were obtained from the corresponding Ensembl BioMart archive. Raw sequencing reads from gene expression libraries, hashtag oligonucleotides and targeted transcript sequences were aligned and quantified using Cell Ranger (v.8 and v.9).

Downstream analyses were performed using R (v.4.5.0) and the Seurat package (v.5.5.1; https://satijalab.org/seurat/)49. Cells were filtered for removal of low-quality profiles and technical artifacts using the following criteria: 2,000–30,000 total unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), 800–6,000 detected genes, mitochondrial transcript content less than 25%, fewer than 65% of reads mapping to the top 50 expressed genes and fewer than 0.1% haemoglobin transcripts. Cells with fewer than 15 hashtag UMIs were excluded to improve sample assignment accuracy. To enrich for endothelial populations and exclude hematopoietic contamination, we also required cells to express Cdh5 (normalized expression greater than 0.1) and no or very low expression of Ptprc (normalized expression less than 0.1). Cells identified as doublets on the basis of hashtag antibody signals were removed. Demultiplexing by organ was performed using sample-specific hashtag oligonucleotide signals (Supplementary Table 2) and after confirmed by organ-specific EC markers, and all downstream analyses were conducted separately for each organ ECs.

Mitochondrial genes, haemoglobin genes and transgenes were removed before clustering to avoid biasing of normalization and dimensionality reduction. Filtered count data were log-normalized and scaled before analysis. Dimensionality reduction was performed using principal component analysis, and batch effects across independent ports were corrected with the Harmony algorithm50.

We clustered cells by constructing a shared nearest neighbour graph and applying the Louvain community detection algorithm to identify distinct cell populations. The optimal number of principal components for dimensionality reduction was determined using an elbow plot, and clustering resolution parameters were selected on the basis of the EC complexity observed in each organ.

Clusters and cells were classified using the SingleR function from the SingleR package v.2.10.0 (ref. 51). Putative doublets were identified as cell clusters that had high total UMI or gene counts or unusual gene coexpression or were located in principal component analysis outliers. Cells classified as singlets were retained and reclustered. Final cluster identities were manually curated on the basis of known EC subtypes and literature-based markers. The FUNCTION_Dotplot_Markers custom function in R was used to find and plot top marker genes per cluster to determine cell identities.

To assess the rate of exon deletion in Vegfr2flox/flox samples, we computed the number of UMI reads aligned to each exon, including the floxed region and the terminal 3′ exon or untranslated region (which is typically overrepresented in 10x Genomics 3′ libraries). Only reads with valid barcodes, UMIs and matching strand orientation were retained.

Read counts for floxed exons were normalized to total UMI counts per cell. These values were added to the Seurat metadata. Deletion efficiency was visualized using dot plots and violin plots, comparing expression of the whole transcript (including the 3′ untranslated region). These visualizations were generated using the custom R function FUNCTION_violin_dotplot_deletion_FC.R, which combines violin plots of single-cell expression distributions with dot plots displaying total average expression numbers and signed fold change between conditions.

To obtain the ratio between the soluble (sVegfr1) and full-length (flVegfr1) isoforms, the normalized reads from exon 13b (the last exon in the soluble form) were divided by the normalized reads of exon 30 (the last exon in the full-length version).

We quantified differences in cell type composition between control and mutant samples for each organ by comparing relative proportions across conditions. For UMAP visualizations (both split and integrated), equal downsampling of the two conditions was performed to ensure identical cell numbers, thereby avoiding sampling bias in visual comparisons.

Differential gene expression between conditions was visualized using volcano plots. These were generated using R functions (FUNCTION_VolcanoPlot) developed in-house that built on the EnhancedVolcano package (v.1.26.0)52. For volcano plots and heatmaps, statistical analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. GSEA was performed using FGSEA with a custom wrapper function (FUNCTION_Fgsea_TableFgsea) based on the FGSEA package. For hallmark pathways, statistical analyses were performed using the multilevel Monte Carlo approach implemented in fgseaMultilevel (R package fgsea v.1.34.2)53 and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple testing.

Genes used for differential gene expression analysis were prefiltered using FUNCTION_FilterLowExpressionGenes_onlyTable; this removes genes with low and highly heterogeneous expression patterns across cells, which are often inconsistently detected between datasets and potentially reflect technical artefacts such as ambient RNA contamination. The function acts as an empirical, distribution-based filter to improve robustness of downstream differential expression analysis. Differential expression heatmaps were generated using a custom function (FUNCTION_Find_PlotGenesHeatmap_FC_Metadata), implemented in-house and based on the pheatmap package.

Most numerical data shown in charts were first compiled and processed with Microsoft Excel 2019 and 2024 and then analysed and plotted with GraphPad Prism v.10.1.0. All bar graphs show mean ± s.d. Experiments were repeated with independent animals, as stated in the source data file or figure legends. Comparisons between two sample groups with a Gaussian distribution were performed using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. Comparisons among more than two groups were made by one-way or two-way analysis of variance followed by multiple comparison tests. Data points were analysed and plotted with GraphPad Prism. No randomization or blinding was used, and the animals or tissues were selected for analysis on the basis of their genotype, the detected Cre- or FlpO-dependent recombination frequency and the quality of multiplex immunostaining. For mosaic analysis, only samples with less than 50% recombination were selected. The sample sizes were chosen according to the observed statistical variation and published protocols.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

RNA-seq data can be viewed at the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession code GSE331295. Unprocessed FACS raw data files and original microscopy images of the data are available upon request. All other data supporting the findings in this study are included in the main article and associated files. Source data are provided with this paper.

All custom scripts and functions used in this study are available at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab/).

a, Schematic of the iFlpMosaic and iSuRe-HadCre genetic systems used to induce and map genetic mosaics. Flow-chart depicting the main steps in image analysis used for the digital mapping of the identified cells, and the generation of heatmaps or XY dot plots, with an example of the analysis for a control retinal AV field with AplnFlpO, iFlpMTomato-Cre/MYFP or Cdh5-CreERT2, iSure-HadCre genetics. Definition of the 6 regions of interest, ERG-based segmentation (endothelial nuclei), nuclear-classification according to reporter or marker expression and relative distance of each nucleus to the AV limits are determined using a custom made semi-automatic FIJI script (steps i-iv). Once a minimum of 2000 cells per reporter group (Tomato+/−, YFP+) are analysed, data is then post-analysed in RStudio to determine the cell distribution of each reporter group in each region and the contribution of Tomato+ cells to each region when compared to control (YFP+ or Tomato- cells) (step v). XY dot plots (step vi) and heatmaps (step vii) are then generated. Note that dot plots (shown in vi) have a maximum of 2000 + 2000 mapped cells plotted as dots, to allow their spatial visualization, whereas heatmaps (shown in vii) are generated with maximal number of mapped cells (with equal cell number in control and mutant group).b,c, Representative confocal micrographs showing the loss of VEGFR2 protein (b), and its downstream target ESM1 (c), 24 h after 4-OHT administration. Data are presented as mean values +/−SD. For statistics see Source Data File 1. Scale bars are 25 μm.

Red negative values indicate fold changes between conditions. Green and red labels above the dots show the absolute average expression (not log). h, UMAP and accompanying histobar plot illustrating the distribution and proportion of lung endothelial cell clusters within each condition. i, Dot plot showing the expression of key marker genes for the different lung EC clusters. j, UMAP projection of the control and Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 lung ECs. The associated bar plot shows the log2 ratio of the number of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 divided by the number of control cells per cluster. k, Volcano plot of showing top DEGs in lung ECs. Coloured genes correspond to highlighted pathways or processes of biological relevance. l, List of hallmark pathways deregulated in lung Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs. m, Heatmap showing the average log2 fold change of apoptosis-related and tip-cell genes in lung ECs between Vegfr2KO (P4–P7) and control samples. n, Violin plots showing expression of the terminal exon 30 (detected in the 3′10x genomics library sequencing) and the deleted floxed exon 3, used to assess Vegfr2 deletion efficiency from P4 to P7. Note that in some cells there is still some residual Vegfr2 mRNA given the short-term deletion nature of the assay, or some contamination with mRNA from wild-type kidney ECs. Red negative values indicate fold changes between conditions. Green and red labels above the dots show the absolute average expression (not log). o, UMAP and accompanying histobar plot illustrating the distribution and proportion of kidney endothelial cell clusters within each condition. p, Dot plot showing the expression of key marker genes for the different clusters. q, UMAP projection of the control and Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 Kidney ECs. The associated bar plot shows the log2 ratio of the number of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 divided by the number of control cells per cluster. r, Volcano plot of showing top DEGs. Colored genes correspond to highlighted pathways or processes of biological relevance. s, List of hallmark pathways deregulated in kidney Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs. t, Heatmap showing the average log2 fold change of apoptosis-related and tip-cell genes in kidney ECs between Vegfr2KO (P4–P7) and control samples. For volcano plots and heatmaps (k, m, r, t), statistical analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. For hallmark pathways (l, s), statistical analyses were performed using the multilevel Monte Carlo approach implemented in fgseaMultilevel (R package fgsea) and Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) FDR correction for multiple testing.

Heatmap, XY dot plot and chart showing the position and relative % of Tomato+ (KO) and Tomato negative (WT) cells. k, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas from Vegfr1 heterozygous floxed (flox/wt; n = 3 pups) and Vegfr1 homozygous mice, with complete (n = 6 pups) or mosaic deletion (n = 5 pups) in ECs induced at P1 with 4-OHT. Note the presence of VEGFR3 protein in angiogenic front Tomato negative (EC nuclei ERG+) cells. n, Representative confocal micrograph of retinas with mosaic deletion of Vegfr3 in ECs from P1 to P7. Heatmap, XY dot plot and chart showing the position and relative % of Tomato+ (KO) and Tomato negative (WT) cells. Data are presented as mean values +/−SD. For statistics see Source Data File 1. Scale bar 100 microns. Abbreviations: LE – leading edge, AF – angiogenic front, IntCap – intermediate capillaries, MA – mature area, A – artery, V- vein.

a, Single cell RNAseq and histological analysis of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs (gene deletion induced at P4 and analysis at P7) in distinct organs revealed common but also distinct transcriptional programs and functions for VEGFR2. b, Loss of VEGFR2 affects the migration of ECs towards VEGF produced by hypoxic tissues, during the first wave of angiogenesis. This leads to the accumulation of Vegfr2KO ECs in more mature vessels and veins, which provides for a continuous source of mutant ECs during subsequent waves of angiogenesis derived from veins. The additional loss of VEGFR1 compromises capillary angiogenesis, whereas the additional loss of VEGFR3 compromises arterialization. c, The comparison of scRNAseq data from ECs with short-term (P4 to P7) and long-term (embryonic to P7) deletion of Vegfr2 revealed that over time Vegfr2KO ECs undergo significant transcriptional changes and upregulate the expression of many venous genes (venousization), particularly Nr2f2. d, The upregulation of Nr2f2, and venousization, enables Vegfr2KO-E8.5-P7 ECs to compete with wildtype ECs over time, and form veins and many other venous-derived vessels, such as capillaries, tip cells and even arteries. Note that these cells adapt over time to the loss of VEGFR2 and become more capable of angiogenesis than Vegfr2KO-P1-P7 ECs. The additional loss of the master regulator of vein specification Nr2f2, prevents the venousization and growth of Vegfr2KO ECs.

#1419. Barcola starts to justify £123m price tag with hat-trick as Liverpool hit LASK for six

There was no grand gesture as Bradley Barcola walked back to the bench, just a high-five from Andoni Iraola and some of Liverpool’s coaching staff.

It was a similar situation as he left the stadium. Hood up, jacket zipped, baseball cap pulled on tightly, he politely turned down all requests to talk in English. “Not good enough,” he said with a smile, but that was the only thing that had not been up to standard.

The giveaway here was what he held in his right hand – the match ball. On it were the signatures of Liverpool’s squad, congratulating him on a momentous performance that had arrived right on cue.

If you are going end a barren spell, you do not want to just turn on the taps but burst the dam, and that is precisely what Barcola did on a wild night in Austria. He needed one goal to get his Liverpool career up and running, he ended up scoring three.

Iraola had said he was not concerned about Barcola’s numbers when Liverpool arrived in Linz, even if no goals and no assists since his £123m move from Paris St-Germain had caused debate, but those numbers look infinitely better now after his first senior hat-trick.

Bradley Barcola's first ever senior hat-trick ⚽️ He's been unplayable 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/UMhUDmGPo9

“I’m really happy for Bradley, because you were asking me yesterday about him, not making the numbers,” Iraola smiled. “Also Florian [Wirtz], and I think both of them played really, really well. They made a difference. Bradley apart from the hat-trick I thought he was a threat.

“He was always one-on-one, certainly in behind and he helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am happy for both of them, yes. For their confidence for sure, it’s very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. It’s going to be very good for them.”

Barcola should have had the stage to himself on an evening when Liverpool were so obviously better than LASK in Linz but it will have frustrated Iraola immensely that his team scoring six times was tarnished by three daft goals being given up in the final 25 minutes.

We can look at the late switch off in due course but the only place to begin is with Barcola, who looked ready for business as early as the eighth minute when his first touch was a cushioned back heel, taking possession by crossing one leg behind the other, and how he seized his moment.

Liverpool had already taken the lead when Ronald Araújo rose powerfully to head in a Kostas Tsimikas corner but, two minutes after, the Barcola show began, a confident right-footed shot being swept past Lukas Jungwirth from 10 yards after some good build-up play from Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Koumas.

Araujo rises to score his first goal for Liverpool 🔴 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/W1C4iYd89m

Bradley Barcola gets off the mark for Liverpool with an instinctive finish 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/5K7YBB7UyG

He put his fingers in his ears as he celebrated, with every outfield player running to engulf him, and it was clear how much Barcola was aware of the requirement to get up and running, especially with Cody Gakpo, Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai injured.

Liverpool needed Barcola to deliver as much as the player himself needed to prove a little point and there is absolutely nothing wrong with having a cause to light a fire. Like a batsman who has been waiting nervously to get off the mark, soon the France international began playing his shots.

There were cushioned touches, changes of gear and even a stunned pass to Ryan Gravenberch, using his heel, that showed confidence had started surging through him and how obvious that was when Wirtz sent him scampering away in the 37th minute to finish with his left foot.

Partnership building... 👀 Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola link up for Liverpool's third 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/UJC9VW82Q8

That effectively ended the game as a contest, so it was bizarre how it ended up 6-3. Jeremie Frimpong had made it 4-0 and Robert Ljubicic’s reply in the 65th minute looked nothing more than a consolation before Barcola completed his hat-trick.

A brilliant night should have been glossed by Koumas’s first European goal – he matched Steven Gerrard in becoming just the second player aged 21 and under to assist and score for Liverpool in a Champions League game – but LASK kept pushing and exploited spaces to halve the deficit with a double from Florian Flecker, much to Alisson Becker’s obvious disgust.

One novice who certainly deserves his starting spot is Trey Nyoni, the England Under-21 international has impressed in the opportunities he has been given so far this year. Watch out for his calmness on the ball and the efficiency with which he uses it.

He should get more chances in the next 10 days, as it is difficult to see Dominik Szoboszlai being ready at least until the home match against Brighton on Sunday week.

Our team to take on LASK ✊ #UCL https://t.co/8vObg7mgLF

It is early days for Bradley Barcola but is has been an underwhelming start to his Liverpool career. The winger was a rotational player at Paris St-Germain, as he is for France, so Liverpool spending £120m is a gamble on his raw athletic attributes and the hope that he pieces everything together.

As Dominic King writes in this piece: “Barcola had no control over the price that Richard Hughes, Liverpool’s former sporting director, brokered with Paris St-Germain for his release. But something he can control is public perception and, with no goals or assists so far, opinions are starting to form.”

Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are currently third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

#1418. Is Jobe Bellingham England's next big thing who shares his older brother's 'X-Factor' - or a 'problem child' whose dad blows up at his bosses? Inside the rise of the 21-year-old after first call-up

Published: 09:16 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 16:31 EDT, 6 November 2026

For years, Jobe Bellingham has been in the shadows of his older brother Jude.

Now, for the first time since they were children, the duo are poised to perform on the same stage. Only this time it won't be under the lampposts of Stourbridge, but the floodlights at Wembley.

Jobe, 21, has been called up to England's senior squad for the first time and is often described in similar terms to his elder sibling: relentlessly ambitious, focused, and a quick learner who is wise beyond his years.

'You have to have an X-Factor and Jobe does,' said Regis Le Bris, his old manager at Sunderland.

That X-Factor appears to run in the Bellingham blood. Earlier this week Jude was unveiled as the new underwear heart-throb for Calvin Klein, channelling his inner David Beckham in a smouldering photoshoot. No pressure, Jobe.

Their main difference on the pitch is that Jobe, while versatile, tends to occupy a deeper-lying role in midfield – and that actually increases the chances of Thomas Tuchel fielding them together. There is every chance that, against Croatia or Spain next week, we will see just the fourth pair of brothers to feature for England since the Second World War.

Jude and Jobe Bellingham's dream of playing for England together may finally come true

The duo grew up playing together and both joined the Birmingham City academy (Instagram: judebellingham)

The duo visited the Spanish Grand Prix in September with matching shirts and haircuts

They share a close relationship and in September were VIP guests of McLaren for the Spanish Grand Prix, posing for photographs in matching blue shirts and identical haircuts, a mischievous double act.

If you were a few pints deep in the Formula One hospitality area, you'd be forgiven for thinking they were the same bloke – especially when their footballing trajectories are so similar.

Jobe began his career at Birmingham City, like Jude, before moving to Sunderland and now Borussia Dortmund, where his brother also played. Jobe, who is two years younger than his superstar brother, is now in his second full season with the Westphalia giants.

He has previously admitted his trepidation at following in Jude's footsteps, once telling the German club's in-house media channel: 'I was biased against joining Borussia Dortmund for a very long time.

'I had anxieties, fears, and you want to be your own man. But I don't think I should let those stop me from making the right decision.'

The comparisons are inevitable, though, when you share the same name and your potential also happens to be through the ceiling. It is a theme Jobe will simply have to contend with wherever he roams.

In Dortmund's 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich on Saturday, the resemblance was striking as he delivered a standout performance – even having the ball in the back of the net, though his goal was ruled out for a Carney Chukwuemeka foul.

At one stage, Bellingham backheeled the ball over Aleksandar Pavlovic, won the ball back off Dayot Upamecano, drifted past Pavlovic with a skill that left him on one knee, and drove about 30 yards towards goal before firing a shot just over the bar.

They would be just the fourth pair of brother to play for England since the Second World War

Jude and Jobe are pictured together at a Louis Vuitton Paris Fashion Week show in 2023

In that ten-second flash, he displayed the sort of tenacity, ingenuity, and swagger which we have come to associate with Jude.

While not as brazen on the surface as Jude, Jobe perhaps gets some of his confidence from their father Mark.

The brothers were introduced to football by their dad, a retired police sergeant who also scored 700 goals in non-league.

Raising his sons in the West Midlands alongside their mother Denise, Mark gave them tips on how to improve and how to deal with the pressures of football. Jude even describes his father as his first footballing hero.

The crackerjack duo have always competed to see who can be the most precocious. Jude became Birmingham City's youngest-ever player when he debuted for them in 2019. When Jobe made his bow for them in 2022, he did so just 69 days older.

He earned his move to Sunderland after just 26 games and was a hit on Wearside. In his second campaign, he won the Championship Young Player of the Season award and helped them to promotion via the play-offs.

Manager Le Bris was breathless in his praise. 'There are many [qualities], there is a long list,' he said. 'Probably his ambition is one of the first ideas I have when I think about Jobe.

'He is very ambitious but this ambition is not naive. It is connected with what he is doing every day in training and every game on the pitch.

Jude pictured with his brother Jobe, father Mark, and mother Denise upon signing for Borussia Dortmund in 2020

'He has many good qualities as a footballer. He is very powerful and he understands the game very well. He is really interested in the game and, because of that, he is able to improve with experiences. He can learn very quickly.

'He is older than his age. He has more maturity. He is like an exception in the sport. It is not easy to play at the level he is doing so at his age, but he is doing so well.'

In the summer of 2025, Dortmund got on the blower. They were willing to pay £31million – more than they had for Jude – and put him straight in the squad for the Club World Cup. Dortmund's UK scout is Daniel Dodds, the brother of Mike, who had worked with Jobe in Birmingham's academy and at Sunderland.

'I think he can go to the very top,' Mike told the Northern Echo in 2023. 'Both brothers have a very similar mindset in terms of their relentlessness in their pursuit of where they want to get to.'

Despite the extravagant projections, Jobe's time in Germany's industrial belt has not been entirely smooth. Often he has been left to simmer on the bench, unable to nail down a regular starting spot.

In his first Klassiker experience, he came on only to lose the ball and have Michael Olise's shot deflect in off him. One report described him as a man who looked 'completely stripped of confidence'.

On the opening day of last season against St Pauli, he was hauled off at the break, leading to his father going ballistic and allegedly confronting sporting director Sebastian Kehl. That put Jobe in an awkward spot. He was also sent off for a professional foul against Freiburg.

Amid his struggles to adapt to the Bundesliga, he has copped criticism off the ferocious pundit Dietmar Hamann, who blasted him as a 'problem child' in a column for Sky Sport. 'Young, expensive and, so far, not even half as good as Jude Bellingham,' seethed the former Liverpool midfielder.

Jobe has become a more regular starter since the turn of the year and, in any case, has always been highly thought of in English football circles.

Jobe helped Sunderland to promotion from the Championship - manager Regis Le Bris said he had the 'X-factor'

Lee Carsley made Jobe his captain for the Under-21s and waxed lyrical about him: 'I think he will be an all-round box-to-box player. He can be creative, score goals. I still feel he can score more goals.

'His shooting is excellent, especially in training. He can link and receive in tight areas.'

Carsley added: 'He’s a good example to the rest of the group, the way he conducts himself on and off the pitch, the way he prepares, the influence he has on the rest of the team.

'He’s a player who can grow into that role. We just assume that players understand leadership and how that works. It will be good to add another string to his bow and keep improving his game.'

After his U21s debut against Spain in Cadiz, he was ambushed by people who wanted signatures... on their Real Madrid shirts. It was opportune and distasteful, but reflected the bigger picture: the name Bellingham is associated with Jude.

Now Jobe's moment has come. Tuchel picked him partly because of Carsley jabbering on with praise in his ear over recent months. The noise around him has become unavoidable and, with Alex Scott injured and Myles Lewis-Skelly suspended for the first game, the Three Lions are light in midfield.

'To play with my brother for England that would be the biggest dream of my life. Nothing would even get close to that,' Jude said in 2024. That may soon be a reality.

#1417. Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age1,2,3. How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested4, with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts5,6,7,8. Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.

Europe’s present-day linguistic landscape is dominated by Romance, Germanic and Slavic languages, which expanded relatively recently during the Iron Age10,11,12,13. Before these events, Celtic languages were prominent across Europe1,2,3: Lepontic has been documented in northwestern Italy (2600–2100 bp), Celtiberian in central-northeastern Iberia (2200–1900 bp) and Gaulish across present-day France, central Europe, northern Italy and the Balkans (2500–1400 bp)14,15 (Fig. 1a). In the modern era, Celtic languages have retreated to the northwestern Atlantic fringe, where they persist as two groups: the Goidelic languages Irish, Manx and Scottish Gaelic; and the Brittonic languages Welsh, Cornish and Breton.

a, The four proposed source regions for the spread of the Celtic languages (circled) and the approximate pre-Roman and premodern distribution of Celtic languages from roughly 2000 bp (shaded). b, Tree schematic illustrating the position of Proto-Celtic relative to events that bound its emergence: the divergence of its predecessor (Pre-Celtic) from other Indo-European branches and the subsequent divergence into Brittonic and Goidelic (Insular Celtic). The tree structure and branch lengths are shown for illustrative purposes only and remain unresolved. c, Density plot showing the overlap of estimates for the divergence of Pre-Celtic (computational, quantitative), the emergence and dissolution of Proto-Celtic (archaeological and linguistic, qualitative) and the subsequent divergence of Goidelic and Brittonic (computational, quantitative). The linguistic studies from which the estimates come are depicted in Extended Data Fig. 1 and detailed in Supplementary Table 5.1. d,e, Geographical (d) and temporal (e) distributions of ancient samples included in the dataset that overlap with the region and timelines from a and c. In d, a small amount of jitter is added to the geographical coordinates. C. E., central-eastern; N., northern; S., southern; W., western. Base maps in a and d were generated in R (v.4.2.3) using map_data(“world”) in ggplot2 (v.3.5.0.9000); geographic boundary data are derived from the public-domain Natural Earth 1:50 m dataset (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) through the R maps package (v.3.4.2.1).

All Celtic languages diverged from an undocumented ancestral language, Proto-Celtic (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a). This language is defined by a series of linguistic innovations present in all Celtic languages, but absent from the other Indo-European languages, including closely related Italic and Lusitanian (Supplementary Note 5). Whereas there is widespread agreement that Indo-European dialects, including the one ancestral to Proto-Celtic, spread across Europe from the Pontic Steppe after 5000 bp (refs. 16,17,18,19), the centre and timing of the subsequent dispersal of Celtic within Europe remain contentious4. Existing hypotheses generally fall within one of the following four models:

The Bell Beaker model associates the Celtic split and dispersal with the Late Neolithic to Early Bronze Age Bell Beaker Complex (roughly 4750–4500 to 4000–3800 bp)20,21,22,23, which spanned much of western and central Europe. Under this model, Celtic diverged largely in situ over the millennia following the Bell Beaker expansion. By contrast, the following three models place the formation of Proto-Celtic after 4000 bp.

The Celtic-from-the-West model (Fig. 1a) claims that Proto-Celtic emerged from relatively undiversified Indo-European dialects within long-distance maritime networks of the Atlantic Bronze Age Culture (3300–2700 bp)24, connecting Atlantic Iberia, parts of France, Ireland and Britain. It further posits a subsequent eastward expansion of a Gaulish–Brittonic–Goidelic Celtic subgroup into central Europe during the Hallstatt C period (2750–2600 bp), traced archaeologically through the distribution of Gündlingen swords25.

The Celtic-from-the-Centre model, in turn, posits that Proto-Celtic emerged neither along the Atlantic seaboard nor from eastern central Europe (next model). Instead, it situates this ancestral language in inland France and possibly northwestern Italy 4000–3000 bp, with a subsequent spread in many directions, including to Britain, Italy and Spain, after 3000 bp (refs. 26,27,28) (Fig. 1a). This model rejects overly strong archaeological–linguistic correlations and is instead supported by a relative density of Celtic toponyms and personal names in France.

Finally, the longstanding Celtic-from-the-East model places the formation of Proto-Celtic in eastern central Europe (Fig. 1a) and associates its diversification with the Late Bronze Age Urnfield Culture29,30, the subsequent Hallstatt Culture and La Tène archaeological horizon5,6,7,8, or a combination of these. The documentation of Lepontic Celtic inscriptions in the Urnfield-derived Alpine Golasecca Culture (2850–2350 bp) has been taken to support this model30. In addition, under this model (as well as models (2) and (3)), the geographic distribution of the Iron Age La Tène Culture, extending from France to the Balkans, broadly coincides with the distribution of Gaulish and closely related Celtic dialects31.

These models differ in their proposed centres and chronologies for the formation and spread of Celtic and imply conflicting proposals of human mobility. We therefore test to what degree each model is supported by past population genomic data, similar to approaches that have proved to be illuminative in other historical-linguistic debates11,12,16,17,32,33,34,35. We note, in this context, that the terms ‘spread’ and ‘population movements’ are used as purely descriptive terms that do not speak to the social mechanism driving them.

We expand on the results of a parallel study on the Germanic languages32, leveraging a filtered dataset of 4,587 imputed ancient human genomes that temporally and geographically encompasses the regions in which early Celtic languages have been historically documented (Fig. 1d,e and Supplementary Table 1.1). In addition, we assembled an auxiliary dataset including individuals from Urnfield contexts in Iberia, Celtic-associated contexts in Britain and southwest Germany, and Bronze Age northern Italy (Supplementary Table 1.4). We used identity-by-descent (IBD) mixture modelling and qpAdm, as well as an updated version of chromopainter together with Sourcefind (Methods), to distinguish population continuity from directional gene flow and to test whether proposed linguistic dispersals require additional, unsupported demographic events.

Current evidence suggests that the Indo-European dialect ancestral to the Celtic languages entered Europe along with a ‘massive migration’ from the Pontic Steppe16,17. In western Europe, the earliest Steppe ancestry appears in people of the Bell Beaker Complex36, whose cultural package in northwestern Europe includes Maritime Beaker influence from Iberia, and All-Over-Corded and All-Over-Ornamented Beaker influence from the Corded Ware region to the east37. Western and eastern contributions are also represented genetically, with Bell Beaker individuals deriving ancestry in various proportions from western Neolithic and eastern Steppe sources. To test whether their Steppe ancestry persisted in the four proposed formative regions for Proto-Celtic, we performed IBD mixture modelling (Methods). In brief, a palette is created for every ancient individual in the dataset, representing the proportion of IBD segments of DNA shared with all 386 clusters in the dataset. The palette of each ‘target’ individual is then modelled as the best-fitting combination of the palettes of the ‘source’ groups, using non-negative least squares in the R package limSolve (v.1.5.6)38. Full IBD mixture modelling results, including source-set definitions, spatial and temporal distributions, alternative source models and sensitivity analyses, are provided in Supplementary Note 1, Supplementary Figs. 1.1–1.58 and Supplementary Tables 1.1–1.6.

As sources, we included groups of individuals from Bell Beaker-related and Corded Ware-related contexts, together with a series of earlier source groups (Supplementary Figs. 1.1 and 1.2 and Supplementary Note 1). For source individuals, we prioritized early Bell Beaker and Corded Ware individuals to measure the persistence of their ancestry through time. We also prioritized individuals with high Steppe ancestry and minimal Neolithic Farmer ancestries as sources, to allow more Farmer ancestry in later individuals to be detected. As we are interested specifically in the spread of Steppe ancestry, we refer to these ancestry sources as Bell Beaker-related and Corded Ware-related ancestry, while acknowledging that many Neolithic-related sources also contributed to Corded Ware and Bell Beaker populations32,39. When including a single, early Steppe source (Yamnaya-related), we find Steppe ancestry appearing in eastern and northern Europe between 5000 bp and 4500 bp (Supplementary Fig. 1.31a), spreading to western and southern Europe between 4500 bp and 4000 bp, consistent with expectations16,17,39. When including the two other sources with high Steppe ancestry (Bell Beaker-related and Corded Ware-related, Extended Data Fig. 2c), we find that Steppe ancestry of individuals in the Corded Ware region of northern and eastern Europe is now modelled with Corded Ware-related ancestry (Fig. 2, Supplementary Fig. 1.31b). In the Bell Beaker region of western, central and southern Europe between 4500 bp and 4000 bp, we find the Steppe ancestry of individuals modelled as Bell Beaker-related (Fig. 2), as previously demonstrated32. These ancestries remain dominant in the respective regions through to the Iron Age (Fig. 2). We note an influx of Corded Ware-related ancestry 4000–3600 bp in people of the Únětice Culture in central Europe (Extended Data Fig. 3), consistent with expectations40. However, we find that Únětice people genetically contribute little to no ancestry to later people in the region, or to Celtic-speaking regions more broadly (Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1.52). The absence of an influx of Corded Ware-related ancestry from northern Europe or further Yamnaya-related ancestry from eastern Europe, together with the persistence of Bell Beaker-related ancestry, is consistent with a Bell Beaker-mediated entry of the dialects ancestral to Indo-European languages spoken in the region during the Iron Age, including Celtic, and is thus key to evaluating all four models.

The size and fullness of the moons represent the proportion of each ancestry modelled. Whereas only a subset of sources is shown here, the results can be seen for all ancestries as timelines in Supplementary Fig. 1.15 and in ‘ADMIXTURE’ style plots in Supplementary Fig. 1.6. Base maps were generated in R (v.4.2.3) using map_data(“world”) in ggplot2 (v.3.5.0.9000); geographic boundary data are derived from the public-domain Natural Earth 1:50 m dataset (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) through the R maps package (v.3.4.2.1).

Next, we look to the region in which Steppe ancestry was incorporated during the formation of Bell Beaker-related populations. Across the Bell Beaker range, we find individuals with the highest proportions of Steppe ancestry to the northwest and lower proportions to the south, suggestive of a more northern origin (Supplementary Fig. 1.31a). When using the Bell Beaker-related source, we find that most individuals in Britain, Ireland, France and the Netherlands have higher proportions of Bell Beaker-related ancestry than in central Europe (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1.41). This pattern remains even when using alternative Bell Beaker and Corded Ware sources from the Czech Republic (Supplementary Figs. 1.40 and 1.42). The expansion to Britain and Ireland from northwestern mainland Europe is also consistent with a previous study indicating that the Bell Beakers of the Lower Rhine formed through a mixture of Corded Ware and local Rhine–Meuse Neolithic ancestry, before spreading to Britain41. Our results indicate that this expansion also reached central and southern Europe. The linguistic identity of Bell Beaker groups cannot be directly inferred from genomic evidence. However, if Indo-European dialects were introduced to the region by this expansion, as previously proposed, it provides a potential vector for the Indo-European dialect ancestral to Celtic. Further sampling from northern France to Germany will help refine this northwestern region.

Over a millennium separates the presumed arrival of Indo-European language varieties in western Europe (roughly 4300 bp) from Iron Age Celtic-speaking populations (roughly 2500 bp) (Fig. 1a). Although northwestern Bell Beaker-related ancestry persisted, the extent to which the population structure within this region changed remains unclear. Evaluating the four models on Celtic origins therefore requires reconstructing the demographic processes that affected Bell Beaker-derived groups after roughly 4000 bp.

Detecting the movement of people during this time has so far proved difficult, due to the close genetic relation between all individuals postdating the arrival of Steppe ancestry. Here we apply two complementary approaches. First, we refine Farmer ancestry as a proxy for mobility by identifying the specific source region of European Farmer ancestry (set C3). This is informative about where the initial admixture occurred, allowing us to infer the region from which later movements spread. Second, we model the later movements directly, using Bronze Age sources from the southeastern and southwestern ends of the region in which Bell Beaker ancestry spread (set C4). The movement from a specific region should be reflected in both the Neolithic Farmer proxy and the Bronze Age source. Rather than attempting to pinpoint specific source populations, these proxies represent broader regional ancestries, allowing the likely spatiotemporal range of possible source populations to be inferred.

To identify variation in the specific sources of Farmer-related ancestry across the Bell Beaker region, we performed IBD mixture modelling (Supplementary Note 1). We included source individuals from IBD clusters associated with Neolithic Britain and Ireland (British–Irish Neo.-related), France and Iberia (Iberia–France Neo.-related), Italy (Italy Neo.-related) and the Czech Republic (Euro. Neo.-related), encompassing the proposed homelands for Celtic. In addition, we included a series of Neolithic-related groups, Bronze Age Anatolia (Anatolia BA-related), Polish Globular Amphora Culture (GAC-related) and Early Anatolian Farmers (E. Anatolia-related). The geographical distribution of these Neolithic-related clusters is plotted in Extended Data Fig. 2b. For the ancestries persisting after roughly 4000 bp (Supplementary Fig. 1.16), we performed spatiotemporal kriging to identify the regions in which these ancestries are found at the end of the Bell Beaker period. We find British–Irish Neo.-related ancestry in Britain and Ireland, Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry in southern France and Iberia, Italy Neo.-related ancestry around the Adriatic and Anatolia BA-related ancestry in the Balkans (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4). We confirmed the spatiotemporal results by plotting the raw results (Supplementary Fig. 1.32).

To model movements more directly, we included Bronze Age source individuals from around 4000 bp, a point in time that marks the end of the Bell Beaker period and predates almost all linguistic and archaeological estimates for the formation of Proto-Celtic (Extended Data Fig. 1). From southwestern Europe, we included individuals from Bronze Age southern France–northern Iberia (S. France–N. Iberia BA-related, Extended Data Fig. 2d), where Bell Beaker-related and the local Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestries are found (Figs. 2 and 3a). From southeastern Europe, where Bell Beaker-related, Italy Neo.-related and Anatolia BA-related ancestries are found (Figs. 2 and 3a), we included individuals from Bronze Age Hungary and Serbia (Hungary–Serbia BA-related, Extended Data Fig. 2d). On the basis of spatiotemporal kriging and plotting the raw mixture modelling proportions, we find these ancestries restricted to southwestern and southeastern Europe roughly 4000 bp (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 5).
