TdTomato-expressing PDGCs were transduced with Dox-inducible TF OE or empty control vectors, selected with puromycin for at least 7 days and seeded onto day-7 primary cortical cultures at a density of 14,000 cells per cm2. To assess the effects of TF induction, 2 µg ml−1 Dox was added to the growth medium on the day of seeding and replenished every second day with a half-medium change. To assess the effects of TF removal, 2 µg ml−1 Dox was added to PDGC growth medium 3 days before co-seeding to induce TF expression and removed 24 h after co-seeding. In both conditions, cells from three to six co-culture wells were pooled 6 days after, and PDGCs were isolated by FACS (BD FACSAria III, BD FACSymphony S6 or BD FACSDiscover S8) for ATAC and/or RNA sequencing. FACS gating is reported in Supplementary Fig. 1.

To assess the effects of MYT1L OE under therapeutic pressure, tdTomato-expressing S24 PDGCs transduced with Dox-inducible MYT1L or empty control vectors were exposed to standard-of-care chemotherapy or radiotherapy before Dox-mediated induction. For chemotherapy, PDGCs were treated with 300 µM temozolomide (TMZ; Sigma-Aldrich) for 4 days, with TMZ replenished on day 2. For radiotherapy, PDGCs were treated with 2 Gy ionizing radiation (MultiRad Faxitron 225) on two consecutive days. Both treatment regimens were confirmed to be effective against PDGCs, consistent with clinical response90. Surviving PDGCs from each treatment condition, or untreated controls, were cultured for 48 h in normal growth medium and subsequently seeded onto day-7 primary cortical cultures. MYT1L OE was induced after seeding by adding Dox to the medium (2 µg ml) and replenishing every second day with half-medium changes. Cells from three to six co-culture wells were collected after 6 days. PDGCs were isolated by FACS (BD FACSAria III, BD FACSymphony S6 or BD FACSDiscover S8) and processed for ATAC-seq.

ATAC libraries were prepared as described24 from TF-perturbed or control PDGCs after neurospheroid culture or co-culture with primary cortical cells (vectors in Supplementary Table 12). In brief, 50,000 nuclei were isolated from single-cell PDGC suspensions, previously isolated by FACS if co-cultured. DNA was tagmented with in-house-assembled Tn5 (oligos in Supplementary Table 12) and extracted with the MinElute Purification Kit (QIAGEN). After the addition of P5 and P7 indexes to DNA fragments using PCR, amplified libraries were size-selected with AMPure XP beads (100−500 bp, Beckman Coulter), quality-checked on a D1000 High-Sensitivity Tape (Agilent TapeStation) and sequenced paired-end on the NextSeq 2000 platform (Illumina).

Sequenced reads were processed with the nf-core ATAC-seq pipeline (Nextflow v.23.04.3)91. After quality control with FastQC (v.0.11.9)92, reads were trimmed with Trim Galore (v.0.6.7)93 and aligned to hg38 with BWA (v.0.7.17)94. Aligned reads were cleaned and filtered with SAMTools (v.1.17)95, BEDTools (v.2.30.0)96 and Picard (v.3.0.0)97. Peaks were called using MACS2 (v.2.2.7.1)98. Final quality checks were performed with MultiQC (v.1.13)99. Differential peak analysis was performed with DiffBind (v.3.16.0)100, adjusting the summits parameter to 500 bp and treating all differentially accessible (DA) peaks with FDR < 0.05 as significant. DA peaks were annotated to the nearest gene and type of genomic region (enhancer, promoter, exonic, transcription termination site or other) using Homer (v.5.1)101 and can be found in Supplementary Table 8. Differential accessibility of Topics was assessed by testing whether DA peaks in each comparison were significantly enriched for peaks associated with a given Topic (Topic-association score ≥ 0.95 in scDORI Topic–peak matrix; Supplementary Methods 1.9.2). We computed the percentage of Topic-associated peaks represented in opened or closed DA peak sets and tested significance with a one-sided hypergeometric test, using the full scDORI consensus peak set as background. P values were BH-adjusted across Topics, and FDR < 0.05 was considered significant. DAGs were defined as those assigned to at least one DA peak within a 150-kbp window of their TSS. Genes assigned to peaks with conflicting directions of change were excluded. Full DAG sets per condition are reported in Supplementary Table 9. We assessed enrichment of Topic signatures by GSEA, ranking DAGs by the maximum fold change of linked DA peaks and comparing them against Topic signatures, defined as the top 250 genes per Topic in the scDORI Topic–gene matrix (Supplementary Methods 1.9.3). We considered comparisons with 50 or more overlapping genes and P < 0.05 significant. State association of DAG sets was scored with Scanpy’s score_genes() function, averaged across cells of each state and z-scored across states.

Bulk RNA-seq was performed from PDGCs (S24, P3XX or BG5) neurospheroid-monocultured or co-cultured with primary cortical cells, previously transduced with TF OE or knockout (KO) constructs, along with their respective controls (Supplementary Table 12). For each experiment, we took three biological replicates per condition, derived from independent transduction batches, and isolated total RNA using the Direct-zol RNA Miniprep kit (Zymo Research). We prepared RNA libraries for samples with Dox-inducible vectors with the SMART-Seq v4 Ultra Low Input RNA Kit (Takara Bio) and subsequently processed them with the NEBNext ChIP-Seq Library Prep Master Mix Kit. Libraries from all other samples were prepared following the Illumina TruSeq Stranded Total RNA protocol. Final libraries were sequenced on NovaSeq 6000 or NovaSeq X Plus sequencers (Illumina). Sequenced reads were trimmed for adaptor sequences and masked for low-complexity or low-quality sequences. Reads were mapped to the hg38 reference genome using STAR102 and tested for differential expression with DESeq2 (ref. 103), with BH-corrected P < 0.05 considered significant. We assessed differentially enriched pathways with GSEA by ranking all DEGs by fold change and comparing them against gene sets from subcategories H, C2, C5 and C8 in the MSigDB database v2023.1.Hs with at least 15 and at most 500 genes using decoupleR (v.1.6.0). Enrichment of Topic signatures among DEGs was determined as for DAGs, ranking highly deregulated genes by fold change (absolute fold change > 1.5). For PBX1 OE, SOX4 OE and MYT1L KO DEGs, a less stringent threshold of 0.5 was used given the lower number of total DEGs. For MYT1L-perturbed datasets, we assessed the enrichment of state signatures analogously, using all DEGs per condition and comparing them against state marker gene sets defined as the top 250 genes ranked by Scanpy’s rank_genes_groups() function applied to cells of each state in our patient atlas. We considered comparisons with P < 0.05 statistically significant. Full lists of DEGs and significantly enriched gene sets for each TF perturbation are shown in Supplementary Table 10.

CUT&RUN was performed in S24 PDGCs 8 days after transduction with MYT1L OE or control vectors. Single-cell suspensions from three independent transduction batches were strained through a 70-µm filter, 100,000 cells were collected per sample and MYT1L-bound DNA regions were isolated following previously published protocols104. In brief, cells were bound to Concanavalin-A beads (Polysciences), permeabilized and incubated with 1 µg of MYT1L antibody (Millipore, ABE2915) at 4 °C for 1 h. Non-specific binding control experiments were performed for each sample with an IgG antibody (Sigma 12-370; 1:100 dilution). Unbound chromatin was digested with protein A-MNase + CaCl2 treatment, and undigested DNA was isolated by phenol–chloroform extraction. Libraries were prepared with the NEBNext DNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB, E7645) and sequenced paired-end on the NextSeq 2000 platform (Illumina). CUT&RUN data were analysed using the nf-core/cutandrun pipeline v.1.0.0 with Nextflow (v.23.04.3)91. Reads were aligned to hg38. Software versions: BEDTools (v.2.30.0)96, Bowtie 2 (v.2.4.4)105, deepTools (v.3.5.1)106, FastQC (v.0.11.9)92, MultiQC (v.1.14)99, Picard (v.2.27.4)97, SAMTools (v.1.16.1)95 and Trim Galore (v.0.6.6)93. Consensus peaks were defined with Genrich (https://github.com/jsh58/Genrich, v.0.6.6) using BH-adjusted FDR < 0.005. We assessed the signal intensity of consensus MYT1L-bound peaks with deepTools, and annotated the nearest gene and genomic region for each peak using Homer (v.5.1)101. Directly bound DA regions (DARs) and DAGs were identified as those in which the corresponding DA peak region directly overlapped with that of a MYT1L-bound peak. MYT1L-bound regions are listed in Supplementary Table 11.

We define target genes for neuronal-like regulator TFs as those that are differentially regulated at both ATAC and RNA levels after TF overexpression in PDGCs. We exclude genes that change in opposite directions across modalities. For MYT1L, we used CUT&RUN-derived binding data to determine target genes, and defined their direction of regulation on the basis of significant changes in at least one modality. To assess the accuracy of scDORI predictions, we used the union of neuronal-like Topic eGRNs (24, 36, 37, 41 and 49) as the predicted regulon and quantified the overlap between predicted target genes and the experimentally determined target gene set. Prediction accuracy was defined as the percentage of overlapping genes changing in concordant directions. We performed the same analysis using TF eGRNs inferred by SCENIC+ exclusively in neuronal-like cells for comparison.

Proliferation of MYT1L-perturbed PDGCs (S24 and BG5) was determined with the AlamarBlue assay (Invitrogen). Neurospheroids were dissociated with Accutase at day 7 after transduction with MYT1L OE (S24; pLVX-puro_MYT1L), MYT1L KO (BG5; lentiCRISPRv2_gMYT1L) or the respective control constructs. Cells were seeded at 2,000 cells per well in 96-well plates (Corning), pre-coated with Geltrex (1:200 in DMEM/F12, 30 min, 37 °C, Life Technologies) and allowed to attach for 4 h. AlamarBlue reagent was added (10% v/v final) and incubated for 2.5 h at 37 °C and 5% CO2. After incubation, the metabolized medium was collected into a separate 96-well black microplate with clear flat bottom (Corning), and fresh growth medium was added back to the PDGCs. Fluorescence of the collected medium was measured on a Tecan Infinite M1000Pro microplate reader (excitation 535 nm, emission 590 nm). This measurement cycle (AlamarBlue exposure, medium collection, fluorescence reading) was repeated on days 3, 5 and 7, with cells maintained in culture for the full 7-day period. We calculated proliferation at each time point by normalizing fluorescence to the day-0 measurement.

To investigate the tumour microtube (TM)-forming capabilities of control and MYT1L-perturbed PDGCs, we used an established two-dimensional model57,107 in which Matrigel-coated vessels and glucose-supplemented, growth-factor-devoid GB medium (high-glucose medium; HGM) preserve both the transcriptional profile and the characteristic phenotypic features of human primary PDGCs, including infiltrative morphology and TM-network formation108. Imaging plates (96 wells; Greiner Bio-One) were freshly coated with growth-factor-reduced, phenol-red-free Matrigel (Corning) diluted 1:50 in growth-factor-free GB medium. TdTomato-labelled S24 and BG5 PDGC neurospheroids were dissociated with Accutase and resuspended in HGM. S24 PDGCs with or without MYT1L OE were seeded at 5,000 cells per well, and BG5 PDGCs with or without MYT1L knockdown at 7,500 cells per well, then incubated for 3 days to allow TM formation. TMs were visualized by incubating PDGCs with MemGlow560 (4 nM; Cytoskeleton) for 30 min before imaging, followed by three rinses with PBS. Images were acquired on a ZEISS LSM 710 ConfoCor 3 confocal microscope with a 20× (NA 0.8) dry objective using Zen Black v.8.1.0.484 (ZEISS). Nuclei and TM connectivity were quantified using a previously established pipeline57,109. Stained nuclei and cell bodies were segmented with Ilastik v.1.3.2 following extensive training, and the total TM length per region of interest (ROI) was estimated as the summed Euclidean distance divided by the nuclei count, reflecting the mean TM length per viable PDGC. To control for differences in nuclei density across ROIs, only ROIs within ±1 s.d. of the mean nuclei density were retained. Hoechst 33342 and tdTomato signals were oversaturated in displayed maximum intensity projections to improve the visibility of nuclei and TMs. OE, knockdown and respective control vectors can be found in Supplementary Table 12.

Primary hippocampal cultures were prepared as described above, dissecting hippocampi instead of cortical regions. TdTomato-expressing S24 PDGCs were transduced with MYT1L OE or control vectors on the day of hippocampal isolation, then dissociated with Accutase on day 7 and seeded onto the primary hippocampal cultures at a low density (4,500 cells per cm2) to favour PDGC–neuron over PDGC–PDGC interactions. Cultures were fixed 7 days later with 4% paraformaldehyde (15 min, room temperature), washed three times with PBS and imaged at 10× on a Nikon Ti-HCS inverted microscope (NIS-Elements software), capturing five or six images per independent experiment. Experiments were repeated three times, deriving cultures from three mice per experiment. Primary branches per cell were manually quantified by counting projections emerging directly from the cell body across ten cells (or all cells if fewer than ten) per field of view. Total branches per cell were quantified by counting all terminal branches per cell.

Single neurospheroids of tdTomato-expressing S24 PDGCs, previously transduced with Dox-inducible MYT1L vector (pLIX-MYT1L; Supplementary Table 12), were transferred to the centre of a Geltrex-containing well (300 μl, 48-well plate, Corning) on ice and subsequently incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Fresh PDGC growth medium with or without Dox (2 µg ml−1) was added to the embedded neurospheroids, which were maintained for 7 days with medium changes every 2–3 days. All neurospheroids were imaged at day 0 and day 7 on a DM IL LED fluorescence microscope (Leica) using the LAX software (4× magnification). Day-7 fluorescent images were binarized to create a spheroid mask, and raw integrated density was quantified within this area. Spheroid growth was determined by normalizing raw integrated density to day-0 spheroid area. Fold change in growth induced by MYT1L was computed by further normalizing to the average values in uninduced spheroids.

To determine whether MYT1L regulates proliferation and neurospheroid growth mainly through activation or repression, S24 PDGCs were transduced with Dox-inducible constructs encoding the minimal MYT1L DBD (410–623) (ref. 60) fused to either (i) the VP64 activator domain110 (four tandem repeats of the herpes simplex virus VP16 minimal activation domain; amino acids (aa) 437-447) or (ii) the Drosophila melanogaster engrailed (EnR) repressor domain111 (aa 1–298). AlamarBlue proliferation and spheroid growth assays were performed after adding 2 µg ml−1 Dox to PDGC growth medium, as described above. For proliferation assays, eight wells were seeded per condition per batch across three independent transduction batches. For spheroid growth assays, indicated spheroid numbers from three independent transduction batches were analysed, respectively. Proliferation and spheroid growth were determined by normalizing day-7 to day-0 values, as described in the respective assay sections. Values were further normalized to those of the respective non-induced controls to determine OE effects, and were compared with results obtained with full-length MYT1L OE.

Patient-derived xenografts were performed in male NMRI nude mice (8–10 weeks old, Charles River) to monitor tumour growth after MYT1L manipulation. For survival studies, S24 PDGCs, previously transduced with MYT1L OE or control vectors, were stereotactically injected into the cortex of mice (100,000 cells in PBS). For in vivo two-photon imaging, a chronic cranial window and titanium ring were implanted for pain-free head fixation during imaging, as described previously112. Two weeks later, tdTomato-labelled S24 PDGCs transduced with MYT1L OE or control vectors were injected into the cortex at a depth of 500 µm (300,000 cells in PBS). Intravital two-photon microscopy was performed 21 days after injection on anaesthetized mice (4% isoflurane induction, 0.5–2% maintenance) using a ZEISS 7MP microscope with a Coherent Chameleon Ultra II laser and a custom aperture for painless head fixation. Angiograms were obtained by tail-vein injection of FITC–dextran (2,000 kDa, FD2000S, Sigma-Aldrich). Fluorophores were excited at 750 nm (FITC–dextran) and 950 nm (tdTomato), using 500–550 nm and 575–610 nm bandpass filters. Tile scans (around 5,000 × 5,000 µm2) covering the injection site and both hemispheres were acquired at depths of 200 µm and 300 µm. Acquisition was unblinded to avoid mixing treatment groups. Images were analysed in Fiji, and PDGCs were counted manually after segmentation and summed across both depths. All mouse experiments were approved by the local authorities of Regierungspräsidium Karlsruhe. Tumour growth was monitored regularly, and mice were euthanized when tumours reached the maximum permitted tumour size or when humane end-point criteria were met. These limits were defined in accordance with the approved animal protocols and were not exceeded in any experiment. The mice were housed at the DKFZ animal facilities in accordance with the local and latest standards with a 12-h dark and light cycle and a constant temperature (20–24 °C) and humidity (45–65%). They were provided with a rodent-specific diet and water ad libitum.

No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size. Statistical testing was performed in Python or GraphPad Prism v.9.0, and details are provided in the corresponding figure legends and Methods sections. Mice for primary cultures and in vivo experiments were selected randomly before the indicated treatments. The investigators were blinded to the microscopy analysis and quantification. Otherwise, no blinding or randomization was performed. All figures were assembled in Affinity Designer, and Figs. 1a,b, 2a,d, 3a, 4a–e,g–j and 5a,d,f–i and Extended Data Figs. 1f, 2a, 6a, 7a, 8a,d, 9b, 10b,e,i,j and 11a were created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026). Microsoft Excel v.16.0 was used to create and organize Supplementary Tables and Source Data.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

All data are included in the manuscript and its Supplementary Information. The processed GB multiome (snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq) datasets can be explored on our interactive web portal (https://www.gbmspace.org). The processed data objects have been deposited on ArrayExpress under accession number E-MTAB-17183 and include the snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq AnnData objects, as well as the metacell-level aggregated RNA counts and ATAC gene scores used for the epigenetic plasticity analysis. The raw GB multiome sequencing data have been deposited in the European Genome-phenome Archive (EGA) under accession number EGAD00001015526. All remaining NGS data have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under SuperSeries GSE294940. Regulatory outputs from scDORI (Topic-level gene-regulatory networks, per-cell Topic proportions with matched cell-state annotations, Topic–peak matrices and peak-level in silico chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) binding and gene–peak links) together with the SCENIC+ comparison, are available via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21873381 (ref. 73). The hg38 (GRCh38) human reference genome assembly was obtained from UCSC (https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/goldenpath/hg38/bigZips/hg38.fa.gz) or the Illumina iGenomes resource (via nf-core atac and cutandrun pipelines, Homo_sapiens/NCBI/GRCh38; https://ewels.github.io/AWS-iGenomes/). The cisBP TF motif database was downloaded from https://cisbp.ccbr.utoronto.ca/bulk.php and the MSigDB gene-set collection from www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb (v.2023.1.Hs). Source data are provided with this paper.

The scDORI implementation is available at https://github.com/bioFAM/scDORI and via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21937078 (ref. 113). Scripts and Python notebooks for epigenetic plasticity scoring, transition potential computation and TF gain-of-function screen data analysis are available at https://github.com/PMBio/GBM_analysis and via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21873381 (ref. 73).

a, Correspondence between the GB cell-state annotations used in this study and the GB meta-modules defined by Neftel et al.10. Each malignant cell was scored for every Neftel meta-module by signature scoring on log-normalized RNA (excluding the cell-cycle modules G1/S and G2/M), and assigned to its highest-scoring module. Shown is the proportion of cells in each cell state that map to each Neftel et al. meta-module. b, Cell-state prediction accuracy of the classifier in Fig. 1b, trained on gene expression from a random 80% of 16,423 metacells (9,464 GB, 6,959 TME; 12 patients). Accuracy is shown for the held-out 20% (n = 3,285) using gene expression, and for all metacells using gene accessibility. Cell states are predicted less accurately from accessibility than from expression, most pronounced for malignant states, indicating elevated epigenetic plasticity. c, Uncertainty (entropy) of expression-based cell-state predictions per metacell (n = 16,423 metacells). Low uncertainty across all cell states confirms that expression profiles support confident state assignment. d, Evaluation of cell-state prediction accuracy of the cell-state classifier as in b, however trained on human neurodevelopmental cell types of a multi-ome brain atlas (12 donors; early fetal, late fetal and post-natal stages48), evaluated based on gene expression (held-out 20%; n = 512 metacells) and gene accessibility (n = 2,559 metacells). Cell-state predictions show comparable accuracy across modalities, except in progenitor populations. e, Epigenetic plasticity across neurodevelopmental metacells (n = 2,559), analysed as in Fig. 1c,d. Top: Epigenetic plasticity score (prediction entropy) across the cell types in d. Bottom: Percentage of cells from each expression-defined state (columns) assigned to each state from gene accessibility (rows). Off-diagonal values reflect accessibility compatible with several transcriptional states. As expected, radial glia and NPCs show the highest epigenetic plasticity (P = 7.5 × 10−59, two-sided t-test). f, Schematic of the canonical neurodevelopmental lineage relationships among the cell types analysed in d,e. Radial glia sit at the apex and give rise to three differentiation routes: Towards neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, with plasticity decreasing along each route as cells mature. g, Global correlation between gene expression and accessibility in GB metacells (Pearson r across n = 21,369 genes), stratified by cell state. The concordance of correlation levels across GB cell states suggests that state-specific differences in epigenetic plasticity are not driven by differences in the global coupling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility. h, Average epigenetic plasticity per patient (n = 12) for the cell states in b, computed with the linear model of Fig. 1e after downsampling each state to equal cell numbers. Plasticity trends match those in Fig. 1e, indicating that the observed differences are not driven by variation in cell abundance. i, Average epigenetic plasticity score of GB states (n = 9) across patients. Although individual patients exhibit variation in plasticity across states, the average plasticity is comparable across patients (one-way ANOVA, P = 0.53). j, Donor-associated variation in epigenetic plasticity within defined cell neighbourhoods, shown as the ratio of the standard deviation of mean plasticity scores across donors to the standard deviation across all cells. Values were computed using k = 10 or k = 30 neighbours for each metacell (n = 4,813 and n = 11,868 metacells respectively), considering neighbourhoods represented by at least three donors, and stratified by state. Donor-associated variation was lower than overall local variation in plasticity across all malignant states. Box plots in c,e,g–j show median and IQR, 1.5 × IQR (whiskers), and outliers. Illustration in f created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Two-phase training scheme. Phase 1: Topic construction by joint training of the core autoencoder modules. scDORI embeds paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq profiles in a shared latent Topic space, from which three modules reconstruct the data. Module 1 maps Topic proportions to peak accessibility through a linear decoder with batch-specific adjustments. Module 2 predicts gene expression from the denoised Topic-specific accessibility of Module 1, using a learnable gene–peak linkage matrix restricted to a fixed genomic window around each gene. Module 3 reconstructs TF expression through Topic-TF weights. The three modules are trained jointly, minimizing the sum of their reconstruction losses together with regularization terms. Phase 2: Fine-tuning for eGRN inference. A fourth module infers Topic-specific TF–gene-regulatory links. In silico TF–peak binding scores, signed for activation or repression, are weighted by Topic-specific peak accessibility (Module 1) and propagated to target genes through the gene–peak links (Module 2). Learnable TF–gene-Topic weights adjust these links according to TF–target expression co-variation, and activating and repressive contributions are combined into a net regulatory score that predicts gene expression from Topic-level TF expression (Module 3). The encoder, gene–peak links, and Topic–peak decoder are optionally frozen during fine-tuning, with sparsity constraints on the learned TF–gene weights. b, Training runtime of scDORI as a function of dataset size, shown for Phase 1, Phase 2, and both phases combined, measured on subsampled multi-ome data from the GB atlas. Runtime scales to datasets of millions of cells. Empirical runtimes on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU (32 GB). c, Assessment of peak–gene link predictions in three cell lines (IMR90, K562, GM12878) of the published ENCODE dataset76,77, converted to semi-synthetic single-cell multi-ome data as in18 and scored against curated experimentally supported enhancer–gene links from BENGI33 as ground truth. Benchmarks span nine evidence x cell-line combinations available in BENGI, drawn from seven evidence sources derived from chromatin configuration, perturbation, and genomic interaction assays. AUPRC is shown for recovered peak–gene pairs with scDORI and SCENIC+. scDORI achieved higher AUPRC than SCENIC+ in all nine comparisons (P = 2.0 × 10−3, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 9 paired comparisons). Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Average Topic activity in malignant and TME states. Extended version of Fig. 2c showing data for 31 Topics (all Topics with max activation > 0.1 across cells). Key biological functions of each Topic based on GSEA are shown. Raw values and complete pathway analysis are reported in Supplementary Table 2. b, Activity of GB-associated Topics in all cells visualized on the UMAP representation of Fig. 1a. State-specific, inter-state, and pan-state Topics are labelled accordingly. c, Activity of GB-associated Topics across patients. Shown is the number of patients with at least 1% of their cells exhibiting activity (>0.05) for each Topic. All GB Topics are active in at least 4 out of 12 patients, confirming that Topics capture universal regulatory programs of GB.

a, UMAP visualization of ATAC peaks in the patient atlas using Topic–peak scores (from scDORI Module 1) as embedding. (Left) Z-scored accessibility of peaks in each GB state. (Right) Topic–peak score for selected Topics. Topics identify distinct groups of co-accessible peaks within each GB state, reflecting different gene-regulatory programs active in those states. b, Genomic distance distributions between peak–gene pairs inferred by scDORI or MOFA29. For each peak in a MOFA factor, we picked the closest gene that was also part of the same factor. Red lines mark the cis-distance (150 kb) constraint applied to scDORI. Black lines indicate the ±1 Mb assessment window, and interchromosomal peak–gene pairs are shown separately on the left. c, Comparison of cell type prediction in our GB dataset using three latent space embeddings: scDORI (50 Topics), MOFA (50 factors), and SCENIC+ (AUCell-based TF activity scores from 195 TFs). Logistic regression models were trained to predict cell type labels from the latent embeddings of each method, using n = 9,464 GB and n = 6,959 TME metacells as input. scDORI achieved higher mean per-cell type accuracy (88.0%) than MOFA (80.3%; 17/17 cell types, P = 8 × 10−6) and SCENIC+ (85.2%; 11/17 cell types, P = 2.7 × 10−3), with the advantage over SCENIC+ concentrated in malignant states. P-values were obtained from a one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test. d, Stability of scDORI gene programs across random initializations. Shown is the Jaccard similarity between the top 500 genes of the most active Topic in each GB state, comparing the reference run (Run 0) against three additional runs trained with different random seeds. A randomized version of the reference Topic–gene set serves as a negative control. Gene programs are recovered consistently across runs. e, Activity patterns of selected scDORI Topics derived from our patient atlas projected onto a reference single-cell GB atlas from Neftel et al.10. Colour denotes average Topic activity, and bars on the left show the proportion of cells from each state in our atlas among the top 5,000 cells for each scDORI Topic. The mapping of scDORI Topics to GB cell states is highly concordant across datasets. f, Activity of selected scDORI Topics within malignant cells of the Neftel GB atlas in e, visualized on a UMAP embedding. Neftel state annotations and Leiden-clustered subpopulations are indicated. g, Performance of scDORI and SCENIC+ eGRNs in predicting DEGs between the Neftel GB cell states shown in e, following the GRaNPA21 framework. For each state pair a logistic regression model was trained to predict whether each gene is up- or downregulated based on the signed TF–gene links in each eGRN. Genes were split into four cross-validation folds, with test genes held out from training. AUPRC is shown for all state pairs. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Both methods outperform randomized control eGRNs (P = 3.1 × 10−5 for each, one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 15 pairs) and perform comparably to each other. h, Performance of scDORI and SCENIC+ in predicting DEGs between the Leiden clusters shown in f, computed as in g. AUPRC is shown for every cluster pair, considering either scDORI or SCENIC+ eGRNs. Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Both methods outperform randomized control eGRNs (P = 4.4 × 10−19 and P = 4.3 × 10−19, respectively; one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 104 pairs).

a, Quality control of the gain-of-function screen described in Fig. 3. Shown are distributions of UMI counts, detected genes, and mitochondrial read fractions, stratified by seeding density (High: 14,000 cells/cm2; low: 9,000 cells/cm2) and biological replicate, separately for each PDGC line (S24, P3XX, and BG5). b, Cells recovered after quality control and barcode demultiplexing. Left: Relative contribution of each cell line, replicate, and seeding density to the total of 261,566 cells. Right: Fraction of cells recovered per TF perturbation, shown for the pooled dataset and for each patient line. TF representation is balanced across lines. n = 3 (BG5) and n = 6 (S24, P3XX). c, Expression bimodality coefficients (BC) of all screened TFs in OE and control cells from b. Each dot is a TF (n = 55). Violin centre line, median; error bars, extrema. Expression is bimodal (BC > 0.555) for every TF in the OE populations and for 54 of 55 TFs in the controls, reflecting heterogeneous expression of the targeted TFs and motivating exclusion of low- and high TF-expressing cells from respective populations in each OE-versus-control comparison. Inset: ASCL1 expression in control and ASCL1-overexpressing cells. d, Effect of the endogenous-expression filter on control cell heterogeneity in b. Each dot is one TF from the OE screen (n = 55), showing the change in state proportions (left) or in average entropy (right) after removing control cells with high endogenous expression of that TF (above the tenth percentile). Centre line, mean; error bars, s.d. Filtering left state heterogeneity essentially unchanged: change in entropy did not differ from zero (P = 0.14, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 220) and mean changes in individual state proportions were at most 0.025. e, Proportion of cells from each GB state in unperturbed control populations across pooled or individual PDGC lines in b. Total cell counts per condition indicated above. All GB states are, to varying degrees, represented in control cells across all lines. f, Validation of state regulator ranking by scDORI and SCENIC+. For each GB state, the average change in state probability (Δ state score, OE versus control) is shown for the top N predicted regulators of that state, with the average change in the remaining TFs (54 − N) plotted below for comparison. Shaded regions indicate s.d. intervals. Regulators nominated by scDORI induced their predicted state more strongly than those nominated by SCENIC+ (P = 8.2 × 10−10, one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 40 state × N combinations, scDORI higher in 34 of 40), most notably for the neuronal-like and AC-like states. g, Induction of Topic programs after gain-of-function of scDORI-predicted regulators of each Topic. For each top regulator (scDORI regulator score > 0.25), the change in activity of its predicted Topic is shown (Δ Topic score, OE vs. control). Dot size denotes the number of PDGC lines in which the effect was significant (label-permutation test, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR < 0.05) and colour denotes the scDORI regulator score. Regulators of nearly all Topics induced their predicted Topic program. All Topic-level effects per TF are provided in Supplementary Table 3. h, Concordance of Topic- and state-level effects after OE of scDORI-predicted regulators. Each point corresponds to one TF-Topic prediction, positioned by the change it induced in that Topic (x-axis) and in the corresponding state (y-axis), relative to control cells. TFs predicted to regulate several Topics appear once per Topic. Colour denotes the predicted Topic and dot style the significance category (label-permutation test, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR < 0.05). Most regulators induced Topic and state changes consistent with scDORI predictions (Supplementary Table 3). i, Number of DEGs per TF OE condition versus the number of OE cells, per cell line in b. The dashed line depicts a linear regression fit. DEG count scaled positively with the number of OE cells (Spearman r = 0.87, P = 1.9 × 10−50, n = 162 TF × cell-line conditions), reflecting increased statistical power with greater cell coverage. j, Number of upregulated and downregulated genes in TF-overexpressing cells relative to control cells in each PDGC line in b. Bars show the mean ± s.d. of each direction. n = 3 (BG5) and n = 6 (S24, P3XX). Top 100 DEGs per condition are reported in Supplementary Table 3.

a, Availability of TRs across GB states. Left: Schematic illustrating how a TR can be selectively expressed in its native Topic but epigenetically primed in cells of alternative states. Right: Mean chromatin accessibility (colour intensity) and mean expression (dot size) of indicated TRs across GB Topics. Bars on top indicate availability of TRs in Topics of alternative states, either by expression (scaled expression>0.5; purple) or epigenetic priming (scaled accessibility>0.5, scaled expression<0.3; green). b, Average expression (left) and chromatin accessibility (right) of the top TRs (activity score>0.05) of each target Topic within cells of each source Topic. TR expression is largely confined to Topics of the same GB state, whereas TR accessibility extends broadly to Topics of alternative states, indicating epigenetic priming for future activation. c, TAP between Topic pairs, scaled by the number of expressed TFs in the source Topic and by the weight of self-regulatory links in the target Topic. Asterisks denote significant links, defined as those exceeding the 95th percentile of a null distribution from 1,000 randomized GRNs (one-sided permutation test). OPC-NPC-like (25, 34) and AC-like (9, 44) tTopics show multiple strong links towards alternative state Topics, whereas links from neuronal-like Topics remain largely within their own state. Full list of TAP scores provided in Supplementary Table 4. d, Changes in TAP scores when using TR accessibility or expression in source Topic for computation. Positive values indicate TAP links mainly influenced by epigenetic priming of TRs, which encompass many of the links between different states. e, Number of top TRs from alternative states (activity score>0.5) that are epigenetically primed in each GB state. The epigenetic priming of alternative state TRs reflects transition potential patterns. f, Variance component analysis of TAP scores across Topic pairs. Each bar shows the proportion of variance explained by a single biological feature, fitted separately in an ordinary least squares model and stratified by whether the target Topic belongs to the same/related state (yellow; n = 77 Topic pairs), an alternative state (orange; n = 212), or any state (purple; n = 289). Regulatory links inferred from the eGRNs explain the largest share of TAP variance. For transitions towards alternative states, epigenetic priming of TRs contributes more than their expression level. g, TRS values between pairs of Topics. Neuronal-like Topics (24, 37) exert the highest repressive effects towards alternative state Topics. Asterisks label significant TRS links, estimated as in c. Full list of TRS values provided in Supplementary Table 4. h, Repression exerted by each source Topic towards the top 50 marker genes from each state identified by the linear model in Fig. 1b, instead of TRs. Similar to TR-level repression, neuronal-like Topics (24, 49) exert the strongest repression towards genes of alternative states. i, Cumulative repression exerted by individual source Topics towards genes of alternative Topics or states. Neuronal-like Topic 24 exerts the strongest repression against alternative identities. j,k, Net transition potential between Topics, as determined by the difference between TAP and TRS values between Topic pairs. Three distinct regulatory mechanisms underlie net transition potential interactions with alternative Topics: (i) predominant repression (Topic 24), (ii) predominant activation (Topics 9 and 34), and (iii) limited activation or repression (Topic 19). Raw values are provided in Supplementary Table 4. Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Schematic of dorsal telencephalon development, depicting neurogenic and gliogenic differentiation trajectories from radial glia towards differentiated neuronal and glial cell types. The shown differentiation hierarchy was reconstructed from available lineage-tracing studies49,50,51. NPC: Neural progenitor cell, OPC: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell, GPC: Glial progenitor cell. b, Activity of selected Topics inferred by scDORI from a developmental brain atlas (n = 12 donors)48. Colour denotes average Topic activity scaled across cell types of dorsal telencephalic origin, collected during early fetal, late fetal, and post-natal development stages. Topic-regulated programs are labelled on the right, determined based on Topic activity patterns, associated genes, and TF regulators. UL: Upper-layer, DL: Deep-layer. Full list of inferred Topics reported in Supplementary Table 5. c, TRs identified in developmental Topics in b recovered canonical lineage regulators, including PAX6 and GLI3 in radial glia114, SOX11 in fetal neurons115, CUX2 in UL neurons116, FOXP2 in DL neurons117, SOX9 in astrocytes118, OLIG1 in OPCs119, and MYRF in oligodendrocytes120, indicating high-confidence prediction of bona fide fate regulators. d, TAP, TRS and net transition potential (TAP–TRS) between pairs of developmental Topics in b. Shown are the respective values scaled by the number of TFs in the source Topic and self-activation in the target Topic. Asterisks denote significant links, defined as those exceeding the 95th percentile of a null distribution from 1,000 randomized GRNs (one-sided permutation test). Progenitor Topics show broad transition potential toward downstream lineages, whereas terminally differentiated cell type Topics show little or no transition potential towards alternative lineages, often constrained by repression. These results reflect the canonical differentiation hierarchy shown in a, as well as dedifferentiation potentials described for OPCs and astrocytes51,52, demonstrating that our transition model captures biologically coherent relationships. Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Schematic of the approach used to compute spatial co-activity of Topics across 97 matched tumour sections profiled by Visium spatial transcriptomics. For every section and Topic pair, the pairwise Euclidean distance between Topic A and Topic B spots is computed. Spatial co-activity is defined as the fraction of sections in which the closest 10% of spot pairs are spatially overlapping. Because spatial distance is symmetric by construction, net transition potentials (TAP–TRS) are symmetrized before row-wise Pearson correlation. b, Number of Visium sections and patients represented per Topic pair in the analysis described in a. All Topic pairs were covered by at least 20 sections derived from at least 7 patients, supporting the generalizability of the reported spatial co-activity patterns. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Average spatial co-activity between Topic pairs computed as described in a (right), compared to their symmetric net transition potentials (left). Topic pairs with high net transition potential tend to be spatially co-active, as evidenced by row-wise correlations (Pearson r, right bar). Asterisks denote correlation P < 0.05. A full list of spatial co-activity values between Topics is provided in Supplementary Table 6. d, Schematic of how temporal co-activity of Topics was computed across pseudotime-aligned clonal trajectories. For each Topic pair, we averaged the cosine similarity of their temporal profiles across the top 10% of trajectories in which the two Topics were most temporally proximal, and compared the resulting matrix to net transition potential using column-wise (r1) and row-wise (r2) Pearson correlations, which capture incoming and outgoing transition relationships, respectively. e, Number of clonal populations per patient considered for the temporal analysis in d. A total of 57 clonal trajectories from all 12 patients were considered. f, Average temporal co-activity of Topics as described in d,e compared to net transition potentials (left). Topic pairs with high net transition potential tended to be temporally co-active for incoming and outgoing transitions, as evidenced by column-wise (top bar) and row-wise (right bar) correlations. Asterisks denote correlation P < 0.05. A full list of temporal co-activity values between Topics is provided in Supplementary Table 7. g, Correlation between Topic spatial co-activity and symmetric net transition potentials associated with each source Topic (n = 17). TAP and TRS values were computed using Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs, a union scDORI eGRN pooling links across Topics, SCENIC+ eGRNs, or random eGRNs. Dot colour represents the source Topic. Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs result in significantly higher correlation with spatial co-activity patterns than those derived using alternative GRNs (P = 0.0057 vs. Union; P = 0.0117 vs SCENIC+; paired two-sided t-test). h, Same as in g, but correlating temporal co-activity patterns in f and net transition potentials. Values denote the average between column-wise (incoming links, r1) and row-wise (outgoing links, r2) correlations for each Topic. Net transition potential values estimated with Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs positively correlated with temporal co-activity, significantly outperforming those derived from alternative methods (P = 0.0052 vs. Union; P = 0.0026 vs SCENIC+; paired two-sided t-test). i, Average epigenetic plasticity of cells in each Topic (as in Fig. 1c, top 5,000 cells per Topic) compared with (i) the cumulative net transition potential towards alternative state Topics (Topic-driven plasticity) and (ii) the total repression exerted by each Topic, both computed from Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs, a union scDORI eGRN pooling links across Topics, or SCENIC+ eGRNs. Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs best recapitulate observed epigenetic plasticity, with modelled plasticity and repression showing significant positive (r = 0.71, P = 0.002) and negative (r = −0.512, P = 0.036) correlations, respectively. Yellow boxes indicate P < 0.05. Box plots in g,h show median and IQR; whiskers are 1.5 × IQR. Illustrations in a,d created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

a, Predicted regulatory roles of indicated neuronal-like TFs based on scDORI. Heat map colours indicate differences in the number of activated and repressed marker genes of each Topic (top 250). Dot size and colour denote TF-driven regulation of target TRs (TAP/TRS analysis, Supplementary Table 4). Repressors are predicted to broadly silence non-neuronal-like Topics, while activators selectively induce neuronal-like programs. b, OE levels of neuronal-like TFs in a at day 3 post-transduction in S24 PDGCs, quantified by qPCR, normalized to GFP vector controls (n = 3 independent transductions). Data are presented as mean ± s.d. c, Proportion of scDORI or SCENIC+ predicted target genes showing concordant changes in both ATAC-seq and RNA-seq after OE of neuronal-like TFs as in b. PBX1 and SOX4 were excluded because of insufficient changing gene sets (<500). Despite differences in regulon size across methods, the proportion of targets responding to perturbation was comparable. d, Percentage of target gene-regulatory directions accurately (green) or incorrectly (brown) predicted by scDORI or SCENIC+ based on gain-of-function perturbations in b. scDORI more accurately predicted regulatory directionality than SCENIC+, particularly for repressed targets. e, Percentage of Topic peaks (Topic-association score>0.95) opened after OE of neuronal-like TFs as in b, determined by ATAC-seq. Significance determined by one-sided hypergeometric test (BH-corrected FDR < 0.05). Only the pioneer TF ASCL1 induced a strong and significant increase in chromatin accessibility across neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like Topic regions. f, Expression of top neuronal-like state regulators in GB states (left) and TME neurons (right) in our patient atlas. Dot colour and size indicate average expression and percentage of TF-expressing cells. MYT1L is the only TF exclusively expressed in neuronal-like GB cells at levels comparable to TME neurons. g, Genomic distribution of MYT1L-bound regions (n = 20,620) in S24 PDGCs determined by CUT&RUN after 8 days of MYT1L OE (n = 3) (top). Intensity of CUT&RUN peaks within ± 1 kb from peak summit in OE and control conditions (bottom). h, Differentially accessible regions (DARs) after MYT1L OE compared to control PDGCs in neurospheroid monoculture or co-culture with primary cortical cells (n = 3 each). Shown are the proportion of opening and closing regions, bound or not bound by MYT1L, and their genomic annotation. MYT1L predominantly closes chromatin by binding enhancer and promoter regions. i, Representative genome browser examples of MYT1L-bound TRs closed after MYT1L OE, as in b,g. j, Precision of MYT1L downstream target prediction, assessed at the level of target TFs and all target genes. Predicted MYT1L targets were derived from an average scDORI eGRN across neuronal-like Topics and compared against those of a SCENIC+ eGRN trained on neuronal-like cells. Blue boxes indicate the proportion of predicted targets directly bound by MYT1L (CUT&RUN as in g). Colours denote directional concordance with ATAC-seq and RNA-seq changes after MYT1L OE as in b. scDORI outperformed SCENIC+ in MYT1L regulon prediction, particularly at the TF level. #1384. Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”

For all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage said. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

“It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really important to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”

With only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

Jaydee Canvot glances the ball into his own net and Brighton lead! 🔵 https://t.co/subm9ggwId

But the hint of self-immolation in Palace’s display should not obscure the swagger of Brighton’s performance. Despite losing Danny Welbeck, last year’s top scorer, Brighton have scored 23 goals already this Premier League campaign, the most in the league. This tally includes one of the most extraordinary goals in Premier League history.

Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Receiving a short pass from Olivier Boscagli just inside his own half, Gómez could have sought to pick out a team-mate. Instead, his scanning of the pitch before receiving the ball had revealed that goalkeeper Walter Benítez was off his line and Brighton’s attacking players were being tightly guarded by defenders. And so, just as he entered the centre circle in the opposition half, Gómez attempted the absurd.

"Would you look at that!" DIEGO GOMEZ SCORES FROM THE HALFWAY LINE! 🤯 https://t.co/qmagVbGEb4

“I’m not training with Diego Gómez shooting from 50 metres in training,” head coach Fabian Hürzeler said while breaking into a smile. “It’s just about making the players quick in their minds.

“In these moments it’s about being very precise with his long kick. The perception to recognise the keeper and being quick to go to the action was impressive.”

The presence of mind to attempt something outlandish was one thing; the execution was quite another. With Benítez vulnerable, Gómez took just one touch with his right foot before taking his shot, not giving the keeper enough time to scramble back to cover his line. As he looked up to confirm the opportunity, the 23-year-old struck the ball over Benítez with such venom that it did not even bounce until it reached the goal.

All that remained was for the Paraguayan international to hurtle towards the corner flag, engulfed by his ecstatic team-mates. For the Brighton fans, soaked by showers at the Amex, rain can never have felt so sweet.

Gómez’s goal will earn comparisons with David Beckham’s lob from the halfway line at Wimbledon. The advancements in pressing and conditioning in the 30 years since, with space ever more congested, makes such a strike even harder today. Not since Wayne Rooney in 2017 has a player scored a Premier League goal from further out than Gómez’s 56 yards.

Gómez may well attempt an encore. He shot from even further out at the Stadium of Light a week ago. When October ends, three of the last four Premier League goal-of-the-month winners will be Brighton players. Alongside his meticulous emphasis on set-pieces, Hürzeler empowers flair in open play.

Diego Gomez has history for scoring stunners by the way 🤯 The Brighton forward scored this in the @Carabao_Cup last year ⚽️ https://t.co/beBoDK8Rk8

While Brighton’s second goal owed to individual brilliance, their third was a sumptuous team strike. Charalampos Kostoulas’s back-heel on the right-hand side set up Yasin Ayari to tuck home. Dropping back and then running over the top, Kostoulas was a constant menace, fully deserving his goal in the 49th minute, when Ayari’s deflected shot fell into his path. Aged 19, Kostoulas is shaping up as Brighton’s next great discovery.

Only once has an M23 derby been more one-sided, when Palace thrashed Brighton 6-0 in 1950. The refrain of Brighton’s exultant fans on the train home – “Who put the ball in the Palace net? Half the f---ing team did” – will, you suspect, become a staple at the Amex.

Calvert-Lewin cancels out Mbeumo’s opener as the points are shared at Elland Road. It is to be seen whether the result relieves pressure from Carrick’s shoulders. United are 14th in the league while Leeds move into the top seven.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German said: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

You can also follow the latest updates from Manchester United’s crucial trip to Elland Road in our sister blog here.

#1383. Martin O'Neill relaxed over Kasper Hogh scoring drought as Celtic boss hails Dane's display against Besiktas

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EDT, 6 November 2026

Martin O'Neill is adamant that he’s not overly concerned about Kasper Hogh’s goal drought — despite the Dane failing to find the net in 15 matches.

Celtic’s record signing at £11million from Bodo/Glimt, the forward looked set to be a huge hit when he scored a hat-trick at Kilmarnock on August 9 only to go off the boil.

His hopes of ending a barren run against Besiktas on Thursday ended when he was taken off 13 minutes from time, with substitutes Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran climbing off the bench to seal a dramatic 3-2 for O’Neill’s men.

But while O’Neill shared Hogh’s frustration at not getting among the goals again, he made a point of telling him that he should have been proud of his other work on the night.

‘I did, absolutely,’ he explained. ‘I want centre-forwards to be able to hold it and that is what he did.

‘He is not Duran, he is not a dribbler. But if he can do this for us against strong opposition it will stand him in good stead.’

O'Neill admits his record-signing is currently struggling for confidence in front of goal

Hogh hasn't found the net since firing a hat-trick in a 5-1 win over Kilmarnock on August 9

With his player not in the latest Denmark squad, O’Neill believes confidence may be an issue. But he stressed: ‘I think Thursday night will be good for him. I said to him that I’m not worried about whether he scores a goal.

‘Of course, you want centre-forwards to score and, of course, centre-forwards live on them. But I said to him that last night I wanted him to be strong and fight when the ball is played up to him.

'I thought in terms of holding the ball up and bringing people into the game, that he did really well.’

Duran stole the headlines against the Turks, though, with his double securing Celtic’s first win in the Europa League and bringing his personal tally for the season to 13.

‘At this minute, he is on fire,’ O’Neill said of the Colombian. ‘He can play wide right, he has done that. He has played wide left for his other club. But centre forward is where he is dynamic.’

Asked if it was increasingly difficult to start Hogh ahead of Duran through the middle, O’Neill said: ‘We will see. We made five changes on Thursday night because it was necessary.

‘Centre-forwards need a goal but that performance there against European opposition will give him confidence.

‘I don’t know what side we will play on Sunday. But this lad has scored goals in the Champions League remember.

'He will get a confidence boost from Thursday night in terms of doing that part of the game well. But it will be nice for him to score a goal.’

While O’Neill’s side now focus on Kilmarnock, the win over Besiktas has breathed new life into their European campaign. With three points on the board at the midway point, two further wins from their matches with Torreense, Omonia, Marseille and Union Saint-Gilloise may see them qualify for the knockout round.

‘It was really pleasing and really important,’ O’Neill said of Thursday’s dramatic victory. ‘We conceded some ground in the game which was to be expected, but I thought defensively we were really, really strong.

‘From the European side, we have given ourselves a chance. We will have to go and win away from home and it will not be easy. We are looking forward to Sunday and we will look to take it on.’

#1382. Some are calling this 'Tuchel 2.0' and his latest squad does feel like that. Here's why England think a tilt at the European Championship is within reach, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 17:35 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 17:39 EDT, 6 November 2026

One of Thomas Tuchel’s favourite analogies when it comes to the development of his England team is that of a train leaving a station with only the chosen few on it. As time moves on, the bodies lying on the tracks are growing greater in number.

Consider this statistic. Of the 26 players who travelled to the World Cup in America 13 are not in the squad chosen by England manager Tuchel for next week’s Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. And that does not include Cole Palmer and Phil Foden who, after missing out in the summer, were expected by many of us to have forced a way back in by now.

Tuchel’s latest selection has been affected by injuries, of course. But more significant is that the experienced German believes he is now starting to see an England team and squad develop in a way and in a direction that even he hadn’t envisaged once Argentina ended his World Cup hopes in that dismal Atlanta semi-final in July.

Different feelings, different style of play and, to a degree, different players.

Some are calling this ‘Tuchel 2.0’ and it does feel a little bit like that. The start of the second phase of Tuchel’s tenure, the start of the road towards a tilt at another trophy, the European Championships of 2028.

Having admitted to some worry ahead of the four-game international break FIFA saddled us all with last month, Tuchel sat down yesterday looking and sounding like a man once again certain of himself.

Tuchel sat down with the media looking and sounding like a man once again certain of himself

The inclusion of Jobe Bellingham — Jude’s younger brother (right) — was the headline act but there were other messages written within

Certain enough of a direct, quick, athletic style of play that helped England to two wins over Czech Republic and one – by seven goals – against Croatia in Rijeka. And certain that a dependence on players like Jordan Henderson, Dan Burn and John Stones for what we may politely call ‘squad culture management’ lies now in the past.

All of this may crash down in Madrid next Sunday. Spain have already beaten Tuchel’s England once – at Wembley in late September – and a repeat this month would ask familiar questions about England against the really good teams.

But for now, Tuchel is confident enough to claim that he has found his path.

‘We said at some point we need to take the next step, to build on what we have, to get better and to improve otherwise you’re just left behind,’ said Tuchel yesterday.

‘That’s how football works. You have been champion in one season but you need to improve, you need to bring in new players for competition, young players, new energy, fresh energy. It’s also the way, naturally, the national team goes.

‘We cannot be stuck in the same personnel and in the same style of play.

‘I agreed with you last month. I was the first to admit I was not 100 per cent happy with the pure level of football we played in the US. I saw a higher level in training [than on the field], I saw a higher level in glimpses.

‘We adjusted some things tactically, created some new positions and took the next steps.’

The Tuchel we sat down with in late September still wore the scars of the summer’s disappointment – and the criticism that came with it – rather visibly. It was the first time we had seen him like that in his two years in the job. He was tetchy and easily provoked. Call it the Argentina effect if you like.

Here, he appeared rather healed. Good results tend to do that for a manager and a little time helps too. If he believes his team has moved on then maybe he has also and he had to.

Certainly, his selection squad speaks to that. The inclusion of Jobe Bellingham – Jude’s younger brother – was the headline act but there were other messages written within.

Henderson and Burn are available but not included. So too Arsenal’s Noni Madueke, excluded to the benefit of the more direct Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha.

‘We need runners who will go between the lines,’ said Tuchel. A clear indication, there, that too much of England’s summer wing play was too slow and too conservatively narrow.

Palmer, Foden and Kobbie Mainoo are also on the outside looking in once again and the case of the Manchester United midfielder is perhaps indicative of how Tuchel now operates.

Moved to apologise to him in front of the whole squad in July for his lack of minutes at the World Cup, Tuchel was determined Mainoo would play in the opening four games of the Nations League campaign.

‘I was desperate to give him the minutes and desperate to include him in this new start,’ explained Tuchel.

‘But then he pulled out. He missed an excellent camp and also entered a difficult, difficult spell for himself.

‘Man United fell off a cliff a little bit performance-wise. So this is why he now suffers.’

We can talk about the whys and wherefores of that logic. If Mainoo was good enough in September then why is he not good enough now? How desperate could Tuchel really have been to play him that one withdrawal with injury closed the door for the next camp and opened it instead for Bellingham jnr?

This, though, is how Tuchel works. He is an adept tactician but he’s also a mood coach, someone who – after sobering club experiences at places like PSG, Chelsea and Bayern Munich – places huge emphasis on environments and gut feels and culture. If he feels something works, he doesn’t like to pick it apart without good reason.

This is why for example the growing voice and influence of Elliot Anderson has left Jordan Henderson suddenly surplus. Tuchel says the door is not closed on a player who will be 38 by the time the next Euros are played and he called him this week to say so. In Tuchel’s mind, though, England will now move without the veteran and others of his ilk.

‘I was concerned before the last camp that we missed the players who kept our standards,’ said Tuchel.

‘I was worried that we missed so many of them. But then this group found their own way and their own voices.

It’s also reasonable to ask why our head coach can’t find room in his squad – if not his team – for the game changing duo of Palmer and Foden

‘I know what the others did. They built a platform on which these ones can build.’

Time will tell. To a degree, Spain will tell. Can England play the kind of higher tempo, front foot football we saw against Croatia and the Czechs against the world and European champions next Sunday? They embarrassed us when we didn’t have the ball at Wembley.

It’s also reasonable to ask why our head coach can’t find room in his squad – if not his team – for the game-changing duo of Palmer and Foden. England lacked good substitutes at the World Cup. There was too much like for like.

England need to win in order for such decisions to be vindicated and Tuchel knows that.

Asked yesterday if he felt as invigorated as he looked he said he did. ‘The last camp gave me a lot of energy, gave me a lot of extra belief,’ he said.

‘It gave me a lot of optimism to not compromise on the way England teams should play. Be physical but also step up in the pure level of performances.’

It’s certainly time for this now. The summer only served to expose English shortcomings. Tuchel’s train must arrive in Madrid next weekend, not only with fresh personnel but also new ideas clearly apparent.
